metadata.title: An algebraic approach to virtual fundamental cycles on moduli spaces of pseudo-holomorphic curves

extraction_notes.note: Sections 1-2 are expository previews of later formal definitions and results (implicit atlas with boundary, product atlas, S^1-equivariant atlas, S^1-localization); per 'one node per repeated statement' these previews got no nodes, only the worked examples and constructions unique to Section 2 did.
Remark environment 'Orbifold fiber product' retyped as an external definition: its content is the (standard, Thurston-cited) definition of the orbifold fiber product.
Single-chart S^1-localization argued in the technical introduction kept as a claim with its prose proof; it is the special case of Theorem 8.6.14 (specializes edge) rather than a restated copy.

The same Convention text is repeated verbatim at the start of Sections 4, 5, 6 (and 8); each scopes its own section, so each is kept as its own assumption node rather than merged as a repeated statement.
Remark environment whose content defines Morse--Smale flow category diagrams; retyped as definition.
Convention environment fixing the ground ring and invertibility of covering-group orders; typed assumption (could be remark).
Definition environment 'Gysin sequence' states the standard Gysin long exact sequence with a justification; typed theorem (external, standard) rather than definition.
Remarks 8.4.9 and 8.7.17 have identical text but sit in different contexts (two different chain models); both kept as separate nodes rather than treated as one repeated statement.
Section 8.4 develops the chain model C^{S^1} in running prose; the list of required properties was taken as one definition node and the spectral-sequence verification as a self-contained remark.
Definition 9.3.14 says it is well-defined by the next lemma, while that lemma uses the defined invariant; to avoid reciprocal uses edges only the definition-to-lemma edge is kept.
Theorem 10.7.24 and the Arnold conjecture corollary are reproofs of results the paper attributes to Liu-Tian, Fukaya-Ono and Ruan, so they are marked external; their proofs are the paper's.
Remark environment whose whole content is an unresolved question (does stalk cohomology imply weak vanishing?); typed open_problem rather than remark.

Theorem B.1.1 parts (i)-(iii) are proved in the proof environment of B.12 and part (iv) in prose in B.13; following 'parts proved separately are claims', each item is a claim nested in the theorem and the proves edges target the parts.

The regular-locus definition and the choice of Q_{0,0} each introduce several auxiliary symbols (B, the bundle, x_i; q_i, V_i, E'', L_0, W) in one construction paragraph; kept as one definition node each.

Appendix C.2 states its main gluing result only as 'the construction of a germ of a local chart' (eq. HFgluinggoal); taken as a prose claim, with the sentence reducing Propositions 10.3.10 and 10.6.21 to it as a prose proof.
The definitions of the cutoff chi and of the torsion T_nabla in C.3/C.5 repeat Appendix B word for word; no prose node here (one node per repeated statement), F880 carries the cutoff formula.
The 'well-known' exponential decay statement in C.1.6 restates Proposition C.11.24 (neckestimateHF); no separate node, the definition of the weights delta_i uses the proposition instead.

Subsection C.12 is a prose continuation of the proof of the Hamiltonian Floer gluing proposition (HFgluingneeded, Prop. 10.3.10) begun earlier in Appendix C; emitted as a separate proof part with a proves edge to that proposition.
Proposition C.11.24 is a known exponential-decay estimate (Floer; proof adapted from Salamon) re-proved here; marked origin external with a paper proof.

Appendix C (Floer gluing) re-introduces its own versions of symbols and terms first defined in Appendix B ($\overline{\mathcal M}$, $C_0$, $j_y$, neck, cylindrical end); defined-term warnings from the B definitions to C nodes were left without edges, since the C nodes rely on their own C definitions.

The symbols $E_I$ and $E_A$ are first introduced inside informal previews in the introduction (no node by the repeated-statement rule); their formal introduction is in Definition 3.1.1, which carries the dependency edges.

metadata.extraction_comment: This 990-environment paper was extracted in nine section-range passes and merged; cross-range defined-term edges were reconciled at merge time, but generic words defined in Appendix A conventions ('space', 'complex', 'support') were deliberately not linked outside that appendix.

nodes.name: VFC paradigm diagram
nodes.statement: \begin{matrix}\text{Symplectic}\cr\text{manifold}\end{matrix}\;\Longrightarrow\;\begin{matrix}\text{Moduli space(s) of}\cr\text{pseudo-holomorphic curves}\end{matrix}\;\overset{\text{VFC}}\Longrightarrow\;\begin{matrix}\text{Desired}\cr\text{invariant}\end{matrix}
nodes.label: paradigm

nodes.name: Local chart of a moduli space
nodes.statement: \begin{tikzcd} X\ar[hookleftarrow]{r}{\text{open}}&s_\alpha^{-1}(0)\ar[hook]{r}{\text{closed}}&X_\alpha\ar{r}{s_\alpha}&E_\alpha \end{tikzcd}
nodes.label: localchart

nodes.name: Implicit atlases versus derived manifolds
nodes.statement: From a theoretical standpoint, it would be desirable to endow the moduli space $X$ with the canonical structure of a ``derived manifold'' (a notion which should be more intrinsic than the notion of an implicit atlas on $X$). A good notion of a ``derived smooth manifold'' exists (due to Spivak \cite{spivak}, Borisov--Noel \cite{borisovnoel}, and Joyce \cite{joyceI,joyceII}), and it is reasonable to expect that a parallel topological theory exists as well. By nature, the theory of derived manifolds uses the language of higher category theory. An implicit atlas on $X$ may be thought of as giving a ``presentation'' of $X$ as a derived manifold (just as a collection of open sets of $\mathbb R^n$ and gluing data can be used to present an ordinary manifold). The ``atlas'' approach which we follow here, while being less intrinsic, has the advantage of being more concrete and more elementary. We believe that a more intrinsic approach is unlikely to lead to any simplification in the construction of this extra structure (implicit atlas or derived manifold structure) on moduli spaces of pseudo-holomorphic curves. However, it would likely make it easier to work with (and, in particular, calculate) virtual fundamental cycles on such spaces.
nodes.statement_short: An implicit atlas can be viewed as a presentation of a derived manifold; the atlas approach is more concrete and elementary.

nodes.name: Fundamental isomorphism (introduction)
nodes.statement: \check H^\bullet(X)\xrightarrow\sim H^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(X;A)
nodes.label: fundisointro

nodes.name: Chain-level pushforward $s_\ast$ (introduction)
nodes.statement: C^{d+\bullet}_\mathrm{vir}(X;A)\xrightarrow{s_\ast}C_{\dim E_A-\bullet}(E_A,E_A\setminus 0)
nodes.label: spushforwardintro

nodes.name: Single global chart diagram
nodes.statement: \check H^{\dim X_\alpha^\mathrm{reg}-\dim E_\alpha}(X)\xrightarrow\sim H_{\dim E_\alpha}(X_\alpha^\mathrm{reg},X_\alpha^\mathrm{reg}\setminus X)\xrightarrow{(s_\alpha)_\ast}H_{\dim E_\alpha}(E_\alpha,E_\alpha\setminus 0)=\mathbb Z

nodes.name: Perturbation computes the virtual fundamental class
nodes.statement: Though our definition of the virtual fundamental cycle does not involve perturbation, we do in some sense show that perturbation is a valid way to compute the virtual fundamental class (in fact, this is an easy corollary of some of its formal properties).
nodes.statement_short: Although the definition avoids perturbation, perturbation is shown to compute the virtual fundamental class.

nodes.name: Bordism-valued virtual fundamental cycles
nodes.statement: In this paper, we only construct virtual fundamental cycles in ordinary homology, which is thus inadequate for applications of moduli spaces of pseudo-holomorphic curves involving their fundamental class in smooth (or framed) bordism (e.g.\ as in Abouzaid \cite{abouzaid} or Ekholm--Smith \cite{ekholmsmith}). However, in discussions with Abouzaid, we realized that by working on the space level, one can probably upgrade our construction to yield a virtual fundamental cycle in the (Steenrod) framed bordism group of $X$, twisted by a certain ``virtual spherical normal bundle''.
nodes.statement_short: Only ordinary homology is treated; a space-level upgrade to framed bordism is probably possible.
nodes.label: smoothcandomaybe

nodes.name: Virtual fundamental cycle as a global section of a homotopy sheaf
nodes.statement: In broad philosophical outline, the strategy we follow to define the virtual fundamental cycle is the following. The functor $U\mapsto C_\bullet(U\operatorname{rel}\partial U)$ (or Borel--Moore chains $C_\bullet^\mathrm{BM}(U)$) is homotopy sheaf on $X$, and the virtual fundamental cycle is a global section thereof. Hence we may define the virtual fundamental cycle by \emph{specifying it on a convenient finite open cover and giving patching data on all higher overlaps} (in our case, the particular cover being $X=\bigcup_{I\subseteq A}\psi_{\varnothing I}((s_I|X_I^\mathrm{reg})^{-1}(0))$ for finite $A$). This philosophy is very natural and could apply quite generally.
nodes.statement_short: Chains rel boundary form a homotopy sheaf; the VFC is specified on a finite cover with patching data on overlaps.
nodes.label: chainsishomotopysheaf

nodes.name: Infinity-categories as a natural setting
nodes.statement: The language of $\infty$-categories as developed by Lurie \cite{luriehtt} seems to be a natural setting for the VFC package and, more generally, for a good theory of derived manifolds and their virtual fundamental cycles (indeed, the existing theory of derived smooth manifolds is by necessity written in the language of higher category theory). We have avoided $\infty$-categories in this paper for sake of concreteness (though at the cost of needing to use lots of explicit homotopy colimits). However, we expect that in this more abstract framework, one could ultimately develop the most flexible calculational tools (computing virtual fundamental cycles directly from our defintion seems rather difficult, due to the inexplicit nature of the isomorphism \eqref{fundisointro}).
nodes.statement_short: Lurie's infinity-categories would be a natural framework; avoided here for concreteness at the cost of explicit homotopy colimits.
nodes.label: inftycategoriesbetter

nodes.name: Implicit atlas (proto version)
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a compact Hausdorff space. A \emph{(proto) implicit atlas} of dimension $d$ on $X$ is an index set $A$ along with the following data: \begin{rlist} \item(Obstruction spaces) A finite-dimensional $\mathbb R$ vector space $E_\alpha$ for all $\alpha\in A$ (let $E_I:=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}E_\alpha$). \item(Thickenings) A Hausdorff space $X_I$ for all finite $I\subseteq A$, and a homeomorphism $X\to X_\varnothing$. \item(Kuranishi maps) A function $s_\alpha:X_I\to E_\alpha$ for all $\alpha\in I\subseteq A$ (for $I\subseteq J$, let $s_I:X_J\to E_I$ denote $\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}s_\alpha$). \item(Footprints) An open set $U_{IJ}\subseteq X_I$ for all $I\subseteq J\subseteq A$. \item(Footprint maps) A function $\psi_{IJ}:(s_{J\setminus I}|X_J)^{-1}(0)\to U_{IJ}$ for all $I\subseteq J\subseteq A$. \end{rlist} which must satisfy the following ``compatibility axioms'': \begin{rlist} \item$\psi_{IJ}\psi_{JK}=\psi_{IK}$ and $\psi_{II}=\operatorname{id}$. \item$s_I\psi_{IJ}=s_I$. \item$U_{IJ_1}\cap U_{IJ_2}=U_{I,J_1\cup J_2}$ and $U_{II}=X_I$. \item$\psi_{IJ}^{-1}(U_{IK})=U_{JK}\cap(s_{J\setminus I}|X_J)^{-1}(0)$. \item(Homeomorphism axiom) $\psi_{IJ}$ is a homeomorphism. \setcounter{rcountsave}{\value{rcounti}} \end{rlist} and the following ``transversality axioms'': \begin{rlist} \setcounter{rcounti}{\value{rcountsave}} \item(Submersion axiom) $s_{J\setminus I}:X_J\to E_{J\setminus I}$ is locally modeled on the projection $\mathbb R^{d+\dim E_J}\to\mathbb R^{\dim E_{J\setminus I}}$ over $0\in E_{J\setminus I}$ for $\#I\geq 1$ (in particular, taking $I=J$ implies that $X_I$ is a topological manifold dimension $d+\dim E_I$ for $\#I\geq 1$). \item(Covering axiom) $X_\varnothing=\bigcup_{\varnothing\ne I\subseteq A}\psi_{\varnothing I}((s_I|X_I)^{-1}(0))$. \end{rlist}
nodes.statement_short: Simplified implicit atlas: obstruction spaces, thickenings, Kuranishi maps, footprints and footprint maps with compatibility, submersion and covering axioms.
nodes.genus: index set $A$ along with the following data
nodes.label: IAproto

nodes.name: Kuranishi structures are indexed by points
nodes.statement: The basic charts of a Kuranishi structure are indexed by the points of $X$. Hence to define a Kuranishi structure on a space $X$, one must make a choice for each $p\in X$. The charts of an implicit atlas are indexed by an abstract set $A$, and hence we can define implicit atlases without making any choices (see \S\ref{constructintro}).
nodes.statement_short: Kuranishi charts are indexed by points of X, requiring choices; implicit atlas charts are indexed by an abstract set, so no choices are needed.

nodes.name: Uniform treatment of empty and nonempty I
nodes.statement: Most of the axioms of an implicit atlas are stated without reference to whether $I$ is empty or nonempty. This contrasts with other approaches, where there is an axiomatic and notational distinction between the $X_I$, $\psi_{IJ}$, or $U_{IJ}$ depending on whether $I$ is empty or nonempty. We believe that our uniform treatment makes implicit atlases simpler notationally and conceptually, and this is a novel aspect of our approach.
nodes.statement_short: Axioms make no distinction between empty and nonempty index subsets, a novel simplification.
nodes.label: Iemptynotspecial

nodes.name: Why use the regular locus $X_I^\mathrm{reg}$
nodes.statement: The requirement that $X_I$ be a manifold \emph{whenever $I$ is nonempty} is rather unnatural (c.f.\ Remark \ref{Iemptynotspecial}) and is too strong of an assumption for two different reasons. First, we do not know how to construct implicit atlases with this property on moduli spaces of pseudo-holomorphic curves (it is a subtle question of choosing good neighborhoods to ensure transversality over all $X_I$ if $\#I\geq 1$). Second, with this axiom we cannot form the ``product implicit atlas'' (Definition \ref{productimplicitatlas}) which is crucial for understanding coherence of virtual fundamental cycles between moduli spaces when treating Floer-type homology theories. Thus in the real definition of an implicit atlas (Definition \ref{implicitatlasdefinition}), there is no such requirement on $X_I$. Rather, we specify open subsets $X_I^\mathrm{reg}\subseteq X_I$ for all $I\subseteq A$ (morally, this is the locus where $X_I$ is cut out transversally), and we modify the transversality axioms appropriately.
nodes.statement_short: Requiring X_I to be manifolds for nonempty I is too strong (not constructible, incompatible with product atlases), so regular loci are used instead.
nodes.label: bettertouseXSreg

nodes.name: Equivalence and cobordism of implicit atlases
nodes.statement: The most natural notion of ``equivalence'' between two implicit atlases $A$ and $B$ on a space $X$ seems to be the existence of a chain of inclusions of implicit atlases $A\subseteq C_1\supseteq\cdots\subseteq C_n\supseteq B$. It is common to speak of ``cobordisms'' between Kuranishi structures or Kuranishi atlases; the analogous notion of cobordism between implicit atlases (say on the same index set $A$) on a space $X$ is an implicit atlas with boundary on $X\times[0,1]$ whose restriction to the boundary coincides with the first (resp.\ second) implicit atlas on $X\times\{0\}$ (resp.\ $X\times\{1\}$). It is an easy consequence of the VFC machinery that the virtual fundamental class is invariant under both notions of equivalence.
nodes.statement_short: Equivalence of atlases is a zigzag of inclusions; cobordism is an atlas with boundary on X x [0,1]; the VFC is invariant under both.
nodes.label: equivalenceofIA

nodes.statement: Fix a smooth orbifold $X$ and let $\{X_\alpha/\Gamma_\alpha=V_\alpha\subseteq X\}_{\alpha\in A}$ be an open cover, where each $X_\alpha$ is a smooth manifold with a smooth action by a finite group $\Gamma_\alpha$ (let us call this the ``covering group''). Then for any finite subset $I=\{\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n\}\subseteq A$, there is an ``overlap chart'': \begin{align} X_I&:=X_{\alpha_1}\underset X\times\cdots\underset X\times X_{\alpha_n}\\ \Gamma_I&:=\Gamma_{\alpha_1}\times\cdots\times\Gamma_{\alpha_n} \end{align} (where \eqref{fpoverorbifold} is the ``orbifold fiber product''; see Remark \ref{orbifoldfiberproductrmk} below). It is easy to check that $X_I$ is a smooth manifold with a smooth action by $\Gamma_I$ and that: \begin{equation} X_I/\Gamma_I=V_{\alpha_1}\cap\cdots\cap V_{\alpha_n}\subseteq X \end{equation} As an exercise, the reader may check that this system of charts described above gives an implicit atlas in the sense of Definition \ref{implicitatlasdefinition} where every $E_\alpha=0$.
nodes.name: Implicit atlas on a smooth orbifold
nodes.statement_short: Orbifold charts with finite covering groups and their orbifold fiber products form an implicit atlas with all obstruction spaces zero.
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Implicit atlases on spaces with nontrivial isotropy

nodes.name: Orbifold fiber product overlap chart
nodes.statement: X_I&:=X_{\alpha_1}\underset X\times\cdots\underset X\times X_{\alpha_n}\\ \Gamma_I&:=\Gamma_{\alpha_1}\times\cdots\times\Gamma_{\alpha_n}
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Implicit atlases on spaces with nontrivial isotropy
nodes.label: fpoverorbifold

nodes.name: Quotient of overlap chart
nodes.statement: X_I/\Gamma_I=V_{\alpha_1}\cap\cdots\cap V_{\alpha_n}\subseteq X
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Implicit atlases on spaces with nontrivial isotropy

nodes.name: Orbifold fiber product
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal X,\mathcal Y,\mathcal Z$ be orbifolds, and fix maps of orbifolds $\mathcal X,\mathcal Y\to\mathcal Z$. Then the \emph{orbifold fiber product} $\mathcal X\times_\mathcal Z\mathcal Y$ is simply the categorical $2$-fiber product in the weak $2$-category of orbifolds. It exists whenever $\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\to\mathcal Z\times\mathcal Z$ is transverse to the diagonal $\mathcal Z\to\mathcal Z\times\mathcal Z$ (in particular, it exists if at least one of the maps $\mathcal X,\mathcal Y\to\mathcal Z$ is \emph{\'etale} as in the above example of $X_\alpha\to X$). Thurston \cite[Proof of Proposition 13.2.4]{thurston} gives an explicit hands-on definition of $\mathcal X\times_\mathcal Z\mathcal Y$ in the case $\mathcal X,\mathcal Y\to\mathcal Z$ are both \'etale by working locally on $\mathcal Z$ and then gluing. In a more modern perspective (defining orbifolds as certain stacks on the site of smooth manifolds), we may define the orbifold fiber product by the following universal property: \begin{equation} \operatorname{Hom}(S,\mathcal X\times_\mathcal Z\mathcal Y):=\operatorname{Hom}(S,\mathcal X)\times_{\operatorname{Hom}(S,\mathcal Z)}\operatorname{Hom}(S,\mathcal Y) \end{equation} for any smooth manifold $S$. The right hand side denotes the $2$-fiber product in the weak $2$-category of groupoids, which admits the explicit description: \begin{equation} G_1\times_HG_2:=\Bigl\{(g_1,g_2,\theta)\Bigm|g_1\in G_1,\,g_2\in G_2,\,\theta\!:\!f_1(g_1)\to f_2(g_2)\Bigr\} \end{equation} (with the obvious notion of isomorphism between triples $(g_1,g_2,\theta)$) for groupoids $G_1,G_2,H$ and functors $f_i:G_i\to H$. The orbifold fiber product usually does not coincide with the fiber product of the underlying topological spaces $X\times_YZ$, though there is at least always a map $\mathcal X\times_\mathcal Z\mathcal Y\to X\times_ZY$. The construction \eqref{fpoverorbifold} would not work if we used the fiber product of topological spaces.
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Implicit atlases on spaces with nontrivial isotropy
nodes.statement_short: The orbifold fiber product is the 2-fiber product in the 2-category of orbifolds, characterized by a universal property on Hom-groupoids.
nodes.label: orbifoldfiberproductrmk

nodes.name: Universal property of orbifold fiber product
nodes.statement: \operatorname{Hom}(S,\mathcal X\times_\mathcal Z\mathcal Y):=\operatorname{Hom}(S,\mathcal X)\times_{\operatorname{Hom}(S,\mathcal Z)}\operatorname{Hom}(S,\mathcal Y)
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Implicit atlases on spaces with nontrivial isotropy

nodes.name: 2-fiber product of groupoids
nodes.statement: G_1\times_HG_2:=\Bigl\{(g_1,g_2,\theta)\Bigm|g_1\in G_1,\,g_2\in G_2,\,\theta\!:\!f_1(g_1)\to f_2(g_2)\Bigr\}
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Implicit atlases on spaces with nontrivial isotropy

nodes.statement: Suppose we have a smooth manifold $B$, a smooth vector bundle $p:E\to B$, and a smooth section $s:B\to E$ with $s^{-1}(0)$ compact. Let us now construct an implicit atlas $A$ of dimension $d:=\dim B-\dim E$ on $X:=s^{-1}(0)$. We will revisit this example in \S\ref{vfcobsbundspace}, so the reader may also refer there for more details. We set $A$ to be the set of all \emph{thickening datums} where a thickening datum $\alpha$ is a triple $(V_\alpha,E_\alpha,\lambda_\alpha)$ consisting of: \begin{rlist} \item An open set $V_\alpha\subseteq B$. \item A finite-dimensional vector space $E_\alpha$. \item A smooth homomorphism of vector bundles $\lambda_\alpha:V_\alpha\times E_\alpha\to p^{-1}(V_\alpha)$. \end{rlist} Now our thickenings are: \begin{equation} X_I:=\Bigl\{(x,\{e_\alpha\}_{\alpha\in I})\in\bigcap_{\alpha\in I}V_\alpha\times\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}E_\alpha\Bigm|s(x)+\sum_{\alpha\in I}\lambda_\alpha(x,e_\alpha)=0\Bigr\} \end{equation} The function $s_\alpha:X_I\to E_\alpha$ is simply projection to the $E_\alpha$ component. The set $U_{IJ}\subseteq X_I$ is the locus where $x\in\bigcap_{\alpha\in J}V_\alpha$, and the footprint map $\psi_{IJ}$ is simply the natural map forgetting $e_\alpha$ for $\alpha\in J\setminus I$. It may be a good exercise for the reader to verify the compatibility axioms in this particular case.
nodes.name: Implicit atlas on the zero set of a smooth section
nodes.statement_short: Thickening datums (V, E_alpha, lambda_alpha) give thickenings X_I = solutions of s + sum lambda_alpha(e_alpha) = 0, an implicit atlas on s^{-1}(0).
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Zero set of a smooth section

nodes.name: Thickening for the zero set of a section
nodes.statement: X_I:=\Bigl\{(x,\{e_\alpha\}_{\alpha\in I})\in\bigcap_{\alpha\in I}V_\alpha\times\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}E_\alpha\Bigm|s(x)+\sum_{\alpha\in I}\lambda_\alpha(x,e_\alpha)=0\Bigr\}
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Zero set of a smooth section
nodes.label: fredholmsectionchart

nodes.name: Index set of thickening datums is a groupoid
nodes.statement: The reader may rightfully object that the index set $A$ defined above is not a set but rather a groupoid (just as there is no ``set of all finite sets'' or ``set of all compact smooth manifolds''). There are two ways of resolving this issue. The simplest solution is to add appropriate ``rigidifying data'' to turn $A$ into a set (e.g.\ we could add the data of an isomorphism $E_\alpha\xrightarrow\sim\mathbb R^{\dim E_\alpha}$ to the definition of a thickening datum). Another (more cumbersome, and ultimately unnecessary) solution would be to just check that the notion of an implicit atlas and the accompanying theory of virtual fundamental cycles remains valid for $A$ a groupoid instead of a set (see also Remark \ref{bettertouseovercategory} for more details).
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Zero set of a smooth section
nodes.statement_short: All thickening datums form a groupoid rather than a set; fix by adding rigidifying data.
nodes.label: notsetremark

nodes.name: Canonicity of the index set of all thickening datums
nodes.statement: The index set $A$ consists of \emph{all} possible thickening datums. It is thus canonical in the sense that it does not depend on any auxiliary choice. For the purposes of extracting the virtual fundamental cycle from an implicit atlas, the only choice we will need to make is that of a finite subatlas; the independence of this choice is part of the VFC machinery.
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Zero set of a smooth section
nodes.statement_short: Taking all thickening datums makes the atlas canonical; only a finite subatlas needs to be chosen.

nodes.name: Direct sum of obstruction spaces is essential
nodes.statement: To construct the overlap charts $X_I$, it is crucial that we are able to take the abstract direct sum of the obstruction spaces $E_\alpha$. Hence, it is better to think of them as abstract vector spaces equipped with maps to $E$ over $V_\alpha$, rather than as trivialized subbundles of $E$ over $V_\alpha$ (which also imposes the unnecessary restriction that $\lambda_\alpha$ be injective), since the latter category is not closed under direct sum. To illustrate this distinction further, let us mention a problematic alternative version of \eqref{fredholmsectionchart}: \begin{equation} X_I:=\Bigl\{x\in\bigcap_{\alpha\in I}V_\alpha\Bigm|s(x)\in\Bigl(\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}\lambda_\alpha\Bigr)(E_I)\Bigr\} \end{equation} This definition agrees with \eqref{fredholmsectionchart} if the following map is injective: \begin{equation} \bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}\lambda_\alpha:\bigcap_{\alpha\in I}V_\alpha\times\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}E_\alpha\to p^{-1}\Bigl(\bigcap_{\alpha\in I}V_\alpha\Bigr) \end{equation} but in general it can be different, and indeed, if \eqref{lambdatotal} fails to be injective, the definition \eqref{fredholmsectionchartwrong} isn't particularly useful. Note that this can occur even if we add the requirement that each $\lambda_\alpha$ be injective. The importance of using the direct sum was independently observed by McDuff--Wehrheim \cite{mcduffwehrheim}, and it is implicit in Fukaya--Oh--Ohta--Ono \cite{foootechnicaldetails}.
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Zero set of a smooth section
nodes.statement_short: Obstruction spaces must be abstract spaces with maps to E so direct sums can be taken; the image-based alternative fails when the total map is not injective.
nodes.label: directsumisbetter

nodes.name: Problematic alternative thickening
nodes.statement: X_I:=\Bigl\{x\in\bigcap_{\alpha\in I}V_\alpha\Bigm|s(x)\in\Bigl(\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}\lambda_\alpha\Bigr)(E_I)\Bigr\}
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Zero set of a smooth section
nodes.label: fredholmsectionchartwrong

nodes.name: Total obstruction map
nodes.statement: \bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}\lambda_\alpha:\bigcap_{\alpha\in I}V_\alpha\times\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}E_\alpha\to p^{-1}\Bigl(\bigcap_{\alpha\in I}V_\alpha\Bigr)
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Zero set of a smooth section
nodes.label: lambdatotal

nodes.statement: Specifically, we construct an implicit atlas $A$ on the moduli space of stable maps $\overline{\mathcal M}_{0,0}(X,B)$ (we fix a symplectic manifold $X$, a smooth $\omega$-tame almost complex structure $J$, and a homology class $B\in H_2(X;\mathbb Z)$). The reader impatient for the full details may also wish to refer to \S\ref{gromovwittensection} where we give a full treatment. Here we have simplified things by assuming that $(g,n)=(0,0)$, $\Gamma_\alpha=S_{r_\alpha}$ and $\overline{\mathcal M}_\alpha=\overline{\mathcal M}_{0,r_\alpha}$ (which is a smooth manifold!). We define $A$ to be the set of all \emph{thickening datums} where a thickening datum is a $4$-tuple $(r_\alpha,D_\alpha,E_\alpha,\lambda_\alpha)$ consisting of: \begin{rlist} \item An integer $r_\alpha>2$; let $\Gamma_\alpha:=S_{r_\alpha}$. \item A smooth compact codimension two submanifold $D_\alpha\subseteq X$ with boundary. \item A finite-dimensional $\mathbb R[S_{r_\alpha}]$-module $E_\alpha$. \item A $S_{r_\alpha}$-equivariant map $\lambda_\alpha:E_\alpha\to C^\infty(\overline{\mathcal C}_{0,r_\alpha}\times X,\Omega^{0,1}_{\overline{\mathcal C}_{0,r_\alpha}/\overline{\mathcal M}_{0,r_\alpha}}\otimes_\mathbb C TX)$ (where $\overline{\mathcal C}_{0,r_\alpha}\to\overline{\mathcal M}_{0,r_\alpha}$ is the universal family over the Deligne--Mumford moduli space) supported away from the nodes and marked points of the fibers. \end{rlist} Let us remark that the analogue of the open set $V_\alpha$ from \S\ref{constructFredholmimplicitatlasintro} is the set of maps $u:C\to X$ satisfying the conditions appearing in (\ref{firstcondition}) below. Now our thickening $\overline{\mathcal M}_{0,0}(X,B)_I$ (any finite $I\subseteq A$) is defined as the set of: \begin{rlist} \item A smooth map $u:C\to X$ where $C$ is a nodal curve of genus $0$ so that for all $\alpha\in I$, we have $u\pitchfork D_\alpha$ (meaning $u^{-1}(\partial D_\alpha)=\varnothing$ and for all $p\in u^{-1}(D_\alpha)$, the differential $(du)_p:T_pC\to T_{u(p)}X/T_{u(p)}D_\alpha$ is surjective and $p$ is not a node of $C$) with $\#u^{-1}(D_\alpha)=r_\alpha$ such that adding these $r_\alpha$ intersections as marked points makes $C$ stable. \item Elements $e_\alpha\in E_\alpha$ for all $\alpha\in I$ \item Labellings of $u^{-1}(D_\alpha)$ by $\{1,\ldots,r_\alpha\}$ for all $\alpha\in I$. \end{rlist} such that: \begin{equation} \bar\partial u+\sum_{\alpha\in I}\lambda_\alpha(e_\alpha)(\phi_\alpha,u)=0 \end{equation} where $\phi_\alpha:C\to\overline{\mathcal C}_{0,r_\alpha}$ is the unique isomorphism onto a fiber respecting the labeling of $u^{-1}(D_\alpha)$. There is an action of $\Gamma_\alpha=S_{r_\alpha}$ on $\overline{\mathcal M}_{0,0}(X,B)_I$ (for $\alpha\in I$) given by changing the labelling of $u^{-1}(D_\alpha)$ and by its given action on $e_\alpha\in E_\alpha$. There are obvious projection maps $s_\alpha:\overline{\mathcal M}_{0,0}(X,B)_I\to E_\alpha$ and forgetful maps $\psi_{IJ}:(s_{J\setminus I}|X_J)^{-1}(0)\to U_{IJ}$, where $U_{IJ}\subseteq\overline{\mathcal M}_{0,0}(X,B)_I$ is the locus of curves satisfying the conidition in (\ref{firstcondition}) above for all $\alpha\in J$. Thus we have specified the atlas data for $A$. The compatibility axioms are rather trivial (as in \S\ref{constructFredholmimplicitatlasintro}), though for the homeomorphism axiom requires a bit of thought.
nodes.name: Implicit atlas on genus zero stable maps (simplified)
nodes.statement_short: Thickening datums (r, D, E, lambda) with divisor intersections stabilizing the domain give thickened moduli spaces solving a thickened d-bar equation.

nodes.name: Thickened d-bar equation (introduction)
nodes.statement: \bar\partial u+\sum_{\alpha\in I}\lambda_\alpha(e_\alpha)(\phi_\alpha,u)=0
nodes.label: thickenedintro

nodes.name: Intrinsic definition of thickened moduli spaces
nodes.statement: The thickened moduli spaces $\overline{\mathcal M}_{0,0}(X,B)_I$ are defined as moduli spaces of solutions to the ``$I$-thickened $\bar\partial$-equation'' \eqref{thickenedintro}. With this intrinsic definition, the convenient overlap properties of the charts (the compatibility axioms) follow rather trivially. The atlas also clearly does not depend on any choice of Sobolev norms or ``gluing profile''. On this point, it is useful to compare with other approaches, which often take the perspective of defining thickened moduli spaces as subsets of some particular Banach manifold of maps. In this context, achieving good overlap properties seems to be more difficult and less conceptual. Another inconvenience of this setting is the lack of differentiability of the reparameterization action (and large reparameterization groups for bubbles).
nodes.statement_short: Defining thickenings via the thickened d-bar equation makes compatibility axioms trivial and avoids Sobolev/gluing-profile choices.

nodes.name: Analysis is confined to openness and submersion axioms
nodes.statement: In our approach, the most serious analytic questions are encountered in verifying the openness and submersion axioms (that is, in proving the necessary gluing theorems). We remark that these only concern the local properties of the thickened moduli spaces, and, in particular, are separated from the other technical aspects of the construction of the implicit atlas (e.g.\ the compatibility axioms, the action of the groups $\Gamma_I$, or the action of a larger symmetry group on the entire atlas).
nodes.statement_short: The serious analysis (gluing) only concerns local properties of thickened moduli spaces.

nodes.name: Standard gluing suffices; stratified smooth structure
nodes.statement: Standard gluing techniques suffice to verify the openness and submersion axioms for the implicit atlases we construct on moduli spaces of pseudo-holomorphic curves. In fact, the transition maps between gluing charts are clearly smooth when restricted to each stratum (i.e.\ for a fixed topological type of the domain), and this yields a canonical ``stratified smooth structure'' on each $X_I^\mathrm{reg}$. If one wanted to obtain a smooth structure on the $X_I^\mathrm{reg}$, one would need to construct gluing charts whose transition maps are truly smooth. This would require a choice of ``gluing profile'' (on which the resulting smooth structure would depend) and is slightly more delicate (see Fukaya--Oh--Ohta--Ono \cite{FOOOII,foootechnicaldetails} or Hofer--Wysocki--Zehnder \cite{polyfoldGW}). Such methods might yield smooth implicit atlases (see Definition \ref{smoothIAdef}).
nodes.statement_short: Standard gluing verifies openness and submersion; truly smooth charts would need a gluing profile.

nodes.statement: The \emph{dual of \v Cech cohomology} $\check H^\bullet(X)^\vee:=\operatorname{Hom}(\check H^\bullet(X),\mathbb Z)$ is a good candidate (and it is what we choose to use, though see Remark \ref{alsogetsteenrod} for further discussion).
nodes.name: Dual of Cech cohomology
nodes.section: 2.3.1 What ``homology group'' does the virtual fundamental class live in?

nodes.name: Insufficiency of singular homology
nodes.statement: Consider the Warsaw circle $W\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ as illustrated in Figure \ref{warsawfigure}; note that singular $H_1(W)=0$. Now $\mathbb R^2\setminus W$ has two connected components; let $s:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ be positive on one component and negative on the other; this gives the data of an implicit atlas on $W=s^{-1}(0)$. Using any reasonable definition, we certainly want $[W]^\mathrm{vir}\in\check H^1(W)^\vee\cong\mathbb Z$ to be a generator, however this is clearly not in the image of singular homology under the natural map $H_\bullet(W)\to H^\bullet(W)^\vee\to\check H^\bullet(W)^\vee$. Alternatively, the pushforward of $[W]^\mathrm{vir}$ to a small annular neighborhood $A\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ of $W$ should be a generator of $H_1(A)\cong\mathbb Z$ (as one can see by perturbing $s$).
nodes.section: 2.3.1 What ``homology group'' does the virtual fundamental class live in?
nodes.statement_short: The Warsaw circle has trivial singular H_1 but its virtual fundamental class should generate the dual of Cech H^1.
nodes.label: singularhomologyisbad

nodes.statement: We have a space $X$, and the implicit atlas $A=\{\alpha\}$ consists of the following data. We have a topological manifold $X_\alpha$ (not necessarily compact), a vector space $E_\alpha$, and a continuous function $s_\alpha:X_\alpha\to E_\alpha$. We also have an identification $X=s_\alpha^{-1}(0)$ (see Figure \ref{implicitatlaspicture}\subref{pica}). We define the virtual fundamental class via the following diagram, which we explain below: \begin{equation} \check H^d(X)=H_{\dim E_\alpha}(X_\alpha,X_\alpha\setminus X)\xrightarrow{(s_\alpha)_\ast}H_{\dim E_\alpha}(E_\alpha,E_\alpha\setminus 0)\xrightarrow{[E_\alpha]\mapsto 1}\mathbb Z \end{equation} (recall that $\dim X_\alpha=d+\dim E_\alpha$). Poincar\'e duality gives a canonical\footnote{For the moment, we ignore the necessary twist by the orientation sheaf.} identification $\check H^\bullet(X)=H_{\dim X_\alpha-\bullet}(X_\alpha,X_\alpha\setminus X)$, which gives the first equality in \eqref{singlechartFC} (this is a rather strong version of Poincar\'e duality, valid for any compact subset $X$ of a manifold $X_\alpha$; we will say more about how to prove it in \S\ref{homotopysheavesintrosec}). We think of the composite of the maps in \eqref{singlechartFC} as an element $[X]_A^\mathrm{vir}\in\check H^d(X)^\vee$, which we call the virtual fundamental class.
nodes.name: Virtual fundamental class from a single chart
nodes.statement_short: For a single global chart, the VFC is Poincare duality H^d(X)=H(X_alpha, X_alpha minus X) followed by pushforward along s_alpha to H(E,E minus 0)=Z.
nodes.section: 2.3.2 Virtual fundamental class from a single chart

nodes.name: Single-chart virtual fundamental class diagram
nodes.statement: \check H^d(X)=H_{\dim E_\alpha}(X_\alpha,X_\alpha\setminus X)\xrightarrow{(s_\alpha)_\ast}H_{\dim E_\alpha}(E_\alpha,E_\alpha\setminus 0)\xrightarrow{[E_\alpha]\mapsto 1}\mathbb Z
nodes.section: 2.3.2 Virtual fundamental class from a single chart
nodes.label: singlechartFC

nodes.statement: The algebraic approach is more general (it does not require a smooth structure on $X_\alpha$), and it is easy to see that it gives the same answer as the perturbation approach when $X_\alpha$ has a smooth structure.
nodes.name: Algebraic and perturbative single-chart classes agree
assumptions: when $X_\alpha$ has a smooth structure
conclusions: it gives the same answer as the perturbation approach
nodes.section: 2.3.2 Virtual fundamental class from a single chart

nodes.name: Virtual fundamental class of $s(x)=x^n$ and $s(z)=z^n$
nodes.statement: Let $X=\{0\}$, $X_\alpha=E_\alpha=\mathbb R$, and $s_\alpha(x)=x^n$ ($n\geq 1$). The reader may easily check that with our definition, the virtual fundamental class is $1$ if $n$ is odd and $0$ if $n$ is even (as is consistent with the perturbation picture). Let $X=\{0\}$, $X_\alpha=E_\alpha=\mathbb C$ (considered as an $\mathbb R$-vector space), and $s_\alpha(z)=z^n$ ($n\geq 1$). The reader may check that in this case, the virtual fundamental class is $n$.
nodes.section: 2.3.2 Virtual fundamental class from a single chart
nodes.statement_short: For s(x)=x^n on R the class is 1 or 0 by parity of n; for s(z)=z^n on C it is n.

nodes.statement: We have a space $X$, and the implicit atlas $A=\{\alpha\}$ consists of the following data. We have a topological manifold $X_\alpha$ (not necessarily compact), a vector space $E_\alpha$, and a continuous function $s_\alpha:X_\alpha\to E_\alpha$. We have a finite group $\Gamma_\alpha$ acting on $X_\alpha$ and (linearly) on $E_\alpha$ so that $s_\alpha$ is $\Gamma_\alpha$-equivariant. Finally, we have an identification $X=s_\alpha^{-1}(0)/\Gamma_\alpha$. We must now work over the coefficient ring $R=\mathbb Z[\frac 1{\#\Gamma_\alpha}]$. To define the virtual fundamental class we consider: \begin{equation} \check H^d(s_\alpha^{-1}(0);R)^{\Gamma_\alpha}=H_{\dim E_\alpha}(X_\alpha,X_\alpha\setminus s_\alpha^{-1}(0);R)^{\Gamma_\alpha}\xrightarrow{(s_\alpha)_\ast}H_{\dim E_\alpha}(E_\alpha,E_\alpha\setminus 0;R)^{\Gamma_\alpha}\xrightarrow{[E_\alpha]\mapsto 1}R \end{equation} Now it is a general property of \v Cech cohomology that $\check H^\bullet(Y;R)^\Gamma=\check H^\bullet(Y/\Gamma;R)$ for a compact Hausdorff space $Y$ acted on by a finite group $\Gamma$ as long as $R$ is a module over $\mathbb Z[\frac 1{\#\Gamma}]$. We precompose \eqref{singlechartisotropyFC} with the canonical isomorphism $\check H^d(X;R)\to\check H^d(s_\alpha^{-1}(0);R)^{\Gamma_\alpha}$ given as $\frac 1{\#\Gamma_\alpha}$ times the pullback. This gives an element $[X]_A^\mathrm{vir}\in\check H^d(X;R)^\vee$, which we call the virtual fundamental class.
nodes.name: Virtual fundamental class from a single chart with covering group
nodes.definiendum: virtual fundamental class $[X]_A^\mathrm{vir}$ (single chart with covering group)
nodes.statement_short: With a finite covering group, work over Z[1/#Gamma], take Gamma-invariants, and precompose with 1/#Gamma times pullback.
nodes.section: 2.3.3 Virtual fundamental class from a single chart (with covering group)

nodes.name: Single-chart virtual fundamental class diagram with covering group
nodes.statement: \check H^d(s_\alpha^{-1}(0);R)^{\Gamma_\alpha}=H_{\dim E_\alpha}(X_\alpha,X_\alpha\setminus s_\alpha^{-1}(0);R)^{\Gamma_\alpha}\xrightarrow{(s_\alpha)_\ast}H_{\dim E_\alpha}(E_\alpha,E_\alpha\setminus 0;R)^{\Gamma_\alpha}\xrightarrow{[E_\alpha]\mapsto 1}R
nodes.section: 2.3.3 Virtual fundamental class from a single chart (with covering group)
nodes.label: singlechartisotropyFC

nodes.name: Two-chart implicit atlas data
nodes.statement: s_\alpha:X_\alpha&\to E_\alpha&s_\alpha^{-1}(0)=U_\alpha\subseteq X\text{ (open subset)}\\ s_\beta:X_\beta&\to E_\beta&s_\beta^{-1}(0)=U_\beta\subseteq X\text{ (open subset)}\\ s_\alpha\oplus s_\beta:X_{\alpha\beta}&\to E_\alpha\oplus E_\beta&(s_\alpha\oplus s_\beta)^{-1}(0)=U_{\alpha\beta}=U_\alpha\cap U_\beta\subseteq X
nodes.section: 2.3.4 Virtual fundamental class from two charts

nodes.name: Local virtual fundamental cycle
nodes.statement: The complex $C_{\dim X_\alpha-\bullet}(X_\alpha,X_\alpha\setminus U_\alpha)$ calculates $\check H^\bullet_c(U_\alpha)$, and the map $s_\ast:C_\bullet(X_\alpha,X_\alpha\setminus U_\alpha)\to C_\bullet(E_\alpha,E_\alpha\setminus 0)$ should be thought of as the chain level ``local virtual fundamental cycle'' $[X]^\mathrm{vir}\in\check H^{\dim X_\alpha-\dim E_\alpha}_c(U_\alpha)^\vee$, which we would like to glue together into the global virtual fundamental cycle.
nodes.section: 2.3.4 Virtual fundamental class from two charts
nodes.statement_short: Chains of X_alpha rel complement of U_alpha compute compactly supported Cech cohomology; s_* is the chain-level local VFC to be glued.

nodes.name: Need for a uniform functorial definition
nodes.statement: Technically speaking, it is very important to have a uniform functorial definition of the virtual cochain complexes (one which does not require making any extra choices).
nodes.section: 2.3.4 Virtual fundamental class from two charts

nodes.statement: As a first try towards gluing the desired complexes together, let us consider using the mapping cone of the following chain map: \begin{equation} C_{\dim X_{\alpha\beta}-\bullet}(X_{\alpha\beta},X_{\alpha\beta}\setminus U_{\alpha\beta})\xrightarrow{\cap[s_\beta^{-1}(0)]\oplus\cap[s_\alpha^{-1}(0)]}\begin{matrix}C_{\dim X_\alpha-\bullet}(X_\alpha,X_\alpha\setminus U_\alpha)\cr\oplus\cr C_{\dim X_\beta-\bullet}(X_\beta,X_\beta\setminus U_\beta)\end{matrix} \end{equation} where the maps are intersection of chains with the (transversely cut out!) submanifolds $s_\beta^{-1}(0)$ and $s_\alpha^{-1}(0)$ of $X_{\alpha\beta}$. There is the question, though, of how these maps are to be defined on the chain level. There are various direct ways to define these maps\footnote{One could use very fine chains, do a (chain level) cap product with a choice of cochain level Poincar\'e dual of the relevant submanifold and then project ``orthogonally'' onto the submanifold. Alternatively, one could just use ``generic'' chains (or perturb the chains) so they are transverse to the submanifold, and then triangulate the intersection in a suitable way.}, however (at least when attempted by the author) the multitude of ``choices'' one has to make invariably leads to a big mess.
nodes.name: First try: mapping cone of cap product maps
nodes.statement_short: Gluing via a mapping cone of cap products with the zero loci fails because chain-level definitions require messy choices.
nodes.section: 2.3.4 Virtual fundamental class from two charts

nodes.name: Mapping cone (first try)
nodes.statement: C_{\dim X_{\alpha\beta}-\bullet}(X_{\alpha\beta},X_{\alpha\beta}\setminus U_{\alpha\beta})\xrightarrow{\cap[s_\beta^{-1}(0)]\oplus\cap[s_\alpha^{-1}(0)]}\begin{matrix}C_{\dim X_\alpha-\bullet}(X_\alpha,X_\alpha\setminus U_\alpha)\cr\oplus\cr C_{\dim X_\beta-\bullet}(X_\beta,X_\beta\setminus U_\beta)\end{matrix}
nodes.section: 2.3.4 Virtual fundamental class from two charts
nodes.label: mappingconefirsttry

nodes.statement: As a second try, let us try to glue together the complexes: \begin{align} C_{\dim X_{\alpha\beta}-\bullet}&(X_\alpha\times E_\beta,[X_\alpha\setminus U_\alpha]\times E_\beta)\\ C_{\dim X_{\alpha\beta}-\bullet}&(E_\alpha\times X_\beta,E_\alpha\times[X_\beta\setminus U_\beta])\\ C_{\dim X_{\alpha\beta}-\bullet}&(X_{\alpha\beta},X_{\alpha\beta}\setminus U_{\alpha\beta}) \end{align} This should let us let us avoid the cap product maps (since there is no ``dimension shift'' between these complexes). Each of these complexes has a canonical map to $C_{\dim X_{\alpha\beta}-\bullet}(E_\alpha\oplus E_\beta,E_\alpha\oplus E_\beta\setminus 0)$, but it is not clear how to glue them together in a manner compatible with this map. In particular, there is no reason for there to exist commuting diagrams: \begin{equation} \begin{tikzcd}[column sep = tiny] U_{\alpha,\alpha\beta}\times E_\beta\arrow{rr}\arrow{dr}[swap]{s_\alpha\oplus\operatorname{id}}&&X_{\alpha\beta}\arrow{dl}{s_{\alpha\beta}}\\ &E_\alpha\oplus E_\beta \end{tikzcd} \qquad \begin{tikzcd}[column sep = tiny] E_\alpha\times U_{\beta,\alpha\beta}\arrow{rr}\arrow{dr}[swap]{\operatorname{id}\oplus s_\beta}&&X_{\alpha\beta}\arrow{dl}{s_{\alpha\beta}}\\ &E_\alpha\oplus E_\beta \end{tikzcd} \end{equation} Moreover, it is technically very inconvenient (functoriality of the construction is a mess) to have a complex which depends on a choice of maps \eqref{strongtubularneighborhood} (even if this turns out to be a contractible choice, and thus morally irrelevant).
nodes.name: Second try: gluing via product complexes
nodes.statement_short: Gluing equal-dimension product complexes avoids cap products but needs non-canonical tubular neighborhood diagrams.
nodes.section: 2.3.4 Virtual fundamental class from two charts

nodes.name: Complexes to glue (second try)
nodes.statement: C_{\dim X_{\alpha\beta}-\bullet}&(X_\alpha\times E_\beta,[X_\alpha\setminus U_\alpha]\times E_\beta)\\ C_{\dim X_{\alpha\beta}-\bullet}&(E_\alpha\times X_\beta,E_\alpha\times[X_\beta\setminus U_\beta])\\ C_{\dim X_{\alpha\beta}-\bullet}&(X_{\alpha\beta},X_{\alpha\beta}\setminus U_{\alpha\beta})
nodes.section: 2.3.4 Virtual fundamental class from two charts

nodes.name: Strong tubular neighborhood diagrams
nodes.statement: \begin{tikzcd}[column sep = tiny] U_{\alpha,\alpha\beta}\times E_\beta\arrow{rr}\arrow{dr}[swap]{s_\alpha\oplus\operatorname{id}}&&X_{\alpha\beta}\arrow{dl}{s_{\alpha\beta}}\\ &E_\alpha\oplus E_\beta \end{tikzcd} \qquad \begin{tikzcd}[column sep = tiny] E_\alpha\times U_{\beta,\alpha\beta}\arrow{rr}\arrow{dr}[swap]{\operatorname{id}\oplus s_\beta}&&X_{\alpha\beta}\arrow{dl}{s_{\alpha\beta}}\\ &E_\alpha\oplus E_\beta \end{tikzcd}
nodes.section: 2.3.4 Virtual fundamental class from two charts
nodes.label: strongtubularneighborhood

nodes.statement: As a third try (which ends up working nicely), let us consider the following ``deformation to the normal cone'': \begin{equation} Y_{\alpha\beta}:=\left\{(e_\alpha,e_\beta,t,x)\in E_\alpha\times E_\beta\times[0,1]\times X_{\alpha\beta}\;\middle|\;\begin{matrix}s_\alpha(x)=t\cdot e_\alpha\hfill\cr s_\beta(x)=(1-t)\cdot e_\beta\hfill\end{matrix}\right\} \end{equation} We think of $Y_{\alpha\beta}$ as a family of spaces parameterized by $[0,1]$ (via the projection $Y_{\alpha\beta}\to[0,1]$). Observe that if $t\in(0,1)$, then $e_\alpha,e_\beta$ are determined uniquely by $x$. Therefore, over the open interval $(0,1)$, we see that $Y_{\alpha\beta}$ is a trivial product space $X_{\alpha\beta}\times(0,1)$. Over the point $t=0$, though, the fiber is $E_\alpha\times U_{\beta,\alpha\beta}$, which is the ``normal cone'' of the submanifold $U_{\beta,\alpha\beta}\subseteq X_{\alpha\beta}$ cut out (transversally!) by the equation $s_\alpha=0$. Similarly, over the point $t=1$, the fiber is $U_{\alpha,\alpha\beta}\times E_\beta$. Also observe that $Y_{\alpha\beta}$ is a manifold by the submersion axiom.
nodes.name: Deformation to the normal cone $Y_{\alpha\beta}$
nodes.statement_short: Y_ab is a family over [0,1], trivial over (0,1), whose end fibers are the normal cones E_a x U_b and U_a x E_b.
nodes.section: 2.3.4 Virtual fundamental class from two charts

nodes.name: Deformation to the normal cone $Y_{\alpha\beta}$
nodes.statement: Y_{\alpha\beta}:=\left\{(e_\alpha,e_\beta,t,x)\in E_\alpha\times E_\beta\times[0,1]\times X_{\alpha\beta}\;\middle|\;\begin{matrix}s_\alpha(x)=t\cdot e_\alpha\hfill\cr s_\beta(x)=(1-t)\cdot e_\beta\hfill\end{matrix}\right\}
nodes.section: 2.3.4 Virtual fundamental class from two charts

nodes.statement: Now we consider the mapping cone of the following: \begin{equation} \begin{matrix} C_{\dim X_{\alpha\beta}-\bullet}(U_{\alpha,\alpha\beta}\times E_\beta,U_{\alpha,\alpha\beta}\times E_\beta\setminus U_\alpha\times 0)\cr\oplus\cr C_{\dim X_{\alpha\beta}-\bullet}(E_\alpha\times U_{\beta,\alpha\beta},E_\alpha\times U_{\beta,\alpha\beta}\setminus 0\times U_\beta) \end{matrix} \to \begin{matrix} C_{\dim X_{\alpha\beta}-\bullet}(X_\alpha\times E_\beta,X_\alpha\times E_\beta\setminus U_\alpha\times 0)\cr\oplus\cr C_{\dim X_{\alpha\beta}-\bullet}(Y_{\alpha\beta},Y_{\alpha\beta}\setminus 0\times[0,1]\times U_{\alpha\beta})\cr\oplus\cr C_{\dim X_{\alpha\beta}-\bullet}(E_\alpha\times X_\beta,E_\alpha\times X_\beta\setminus 0\times U_\beta) \end{matrix} \end{equation} The maps are simply pushforward along the maps of spaces (with appropriate signs): \begin{align} U_{\alpha,\alpha\beta}\times E_\beta&\hookrightarrow X_\alpha\times E_\beta\\ U_{\alpha,\alpha\beta}\times E_\beta&\hookrightarrow Y_{\alpha\beta}\quad\text{(isomorphism onto $t=1$ fiber)}\\ E_\alpha\times U_{\beta,\alpha\beta}&\hookrightarrow Y_{\alpha\beta}\quad\text{(isomorphism onto $t=0$ fiber)}\\ E_\alpha\times U_{\beta,\alpha\beta}&\hookrightarrow E_\alpha\times X_\beta \end{align} There is also an evident map from (the mapping cone of) \eqref{multichartcomplex} to $C_\bullet(E_\alpha\oplus E_\beta,E_\alpha\oplus E_\beta\setminus 0)$ (namely pushforward on the three factors on the right hand side and zero on the left hand side).
nodes.name: Two-chart virtual cochain complex
nodes.statement_short: Glue chain complexes of the charts and the deformation space Y_ab by a mapping cone of pushforwards; it maps to chains on (E_a+E_b, minus 0).
nodes.section: 2.3.4 Virtual fundamental class from two charts

nodes.name: Two-chart virtual cochain complex (mapping cone)
nodes.statement: \begin{matrix} C_{\dim X_{\alpha\beta}-\bullet}(U_{\alpha,\alpha\beta}\times E_\beta,U_{\alpha,\alpha\beta}\times E_\beta\setminus U_\alpha\times 0)\cr\oplus\cr C_{\dim X_{\alpha\beta}-\bullet}(E_\alpha\times U_{\beta,\alpha\beta},E_\alpha\times U_{\beta,\alpha\beta}\setminus 0\times U_\beta) \end{matrix} \to \begin{matrix} C_{\dim X_{\alpha\beta}-\bullet}(X_\alpha\times E_\beta,X_\alpha\times E_\beta\setminus U_\alpha\times 0)\cr\oplus\cr C_{\dim X_{\alpha\beta}-\bullet}(Y_{\alpha\beta},Y_{\alpha\beta}\setminus 0\times[0,1]\times U_{\alpha\beta})\cr\oplus\cr C_{\dim X_{\alpha\beta}-\bullet}(E_\alpha\times X_\beta,E_\alpha\times X_\beta\setminus 0\times U_\beta) \end{matrix}
nodes.section: 2.3.4 Virtual fundamental class from two charts
nodes.label: multichartcomplex

nodes.name: Pushforward maps for the two-chart complex
nodes.statement: U_{\alpha,\alpha\beta}\times E_\beta&\hookrightarrow X_\alpha\times E_\beta\\ U_{\alpha,\alpha\beta}\times E_\beta&\hookrightarrow Y_{\alpha\beta}\quad\text{(isomorphism onto $t=1$ fiber)}\\ E_\alpha\times U_{\beta,\alpha\beta}&\hookrightarrow Y_{\alpha\beta}\quad\text{(isomorphism onto $t=0$ fiber)}\\ E_\alpha\times U_{\beta,\alpha\beta}&\hookrightarrow E_\alpha\times X_\beta
nodes.section: 2.3.4 Virtual fundamental class from two charts

nodes.name: Goal isomorphism $H^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(X;A)=\check H^\bullet(X)$
nodes.statement: H^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(X;A)=\check H^\bullet(X)
nodes.section: 2.3.5 Homotopy \texorpdfstring{$\mathcal K$}{K}-sheaves in the theory of virtual fundamental cycles
nodes.label: homotopyisogoal

nodes.statement: As an introduction to the language of sheaves and homotopy sheaves, let us first use it to give a proof of ordinary Poincar\'e duality (in fact, a strong version for arbitrary compact subsets of a manifold).\footnote{An easier proof (using the fact that \v Cech cohomology satisfies the ``continuity axiom'') is available if $M$ has a smooth structure (along the lines of \cite[pp887--888 Lemmas 3.1 and 3.3]{pardonHS}). This approach does not seem to apply to the more general setting we need to treat here.} The following argument appears in full detail in Lemma \ref{poincareduality}. Fix a closed manifold $M$ of dimension $n$. For any compact subset $K\subseteq M$, let $\mathcal F^\bullet(K)$ denote the complex $C_{n-\bullet}(M,M\setminus K)$. This object $\mathcal F^\bullet$ is a \emph{$\mathcal K$-presheaf\footnote{The prefix ``$\mathcal K$-'' indicates sections are given over compact sets instead of open sets. For technical reasons, it is more convenient to work with $\mathcal K$-presheaves rather than presheaves, though at the conceptual level, the reader may safely ignore the difference.} of complexes} (or \emph{complex of $\mathcal K$-presheaves}) on $M$, which just means that we have natural maps $\mathcal F^\bullet(K)\to\mathcal F^\bullet(K')$ for $K\supseteq K'$, which are suitably compatible with each other. Now $\mathcal F^\bullet$ satisfies the following key properties: \begin{rlist} \item(``$\mathcal F^\bullet$ is a homotopy $\mathcal K$-sheaf'') The total complex of the following double complex is acyclic: \begin{equation} \mathcal F^\bullet(K_1\cup K_2)\to\mathcal F^\bullet(K_1)\oplus\mathcal F^\bullet(K_2)\to\mathcal F^\bullet(K_1\cap K_2) \end{equation} This is essentially just a restatement of the Mayer--Vietoris exact sequence. \item(``$\mathcal F^\bullet$ is pure and $H^0\mathcal F^\bullet=\mathfrak o_M$'') The homology of $\mathcal F^\bullet(\{p\})$ (namely $H_{n-\bullet}(M,M\setminus p)$) is concentrated in degree zero, where it can be canonically identified with the fiber of $\mathfrak o_M$ (the orientation sheaf of $M$) at $p\in M$. \end{rlist} (the precise notions of a homotopy $\mathcal K$-sheaf and of purity are given in Definitions \ref{homotopyKsheaf} and \ref{purehomotopyKsheaf}; in the above statements they have been simplified for sake of exposition). A formal consequence (Proposition \ref{cechcohomologypurehomotopysheaf}) of the fact that $\mathcal F^\bullet$ is a pure homotopy $\mathcal K$-sheaf with $H^0\mathcal F^\bullet=\mathfrak o_M$ is that there is a canonical isomorphism: \begin{equation} H_{n-i}(M,M\setminus K)=H^i\mathcal F^\bullet(K)=\check H^i(K;\mathfrak o_M) \end{equation} Specializing to $K=M$, we have derived the Poincar\'e duality isomorphism $H_{n-i}(M)=\check H^i(M;\mathfrak o_M)$.
nodes.name: Poincare duality via homotopy K-sheaves (sketch)
nodes.statement_short: K -> C_{n-*}(M, M minus K) is a pure homotopy K-sheaf with H^0 the orientation sheaf, giving H_{n-i}(M,M-K)=H^i(K;o_M).
nodes.section: 2.3.5 Homotopy \texorpdfstring{$\mathcal K$}{K}-sheaves in the theory of virtual fundamental cycles

nodes.name: Mayer--Vietoris double complex
nodes.statement: \mathcal F^\bullet(K_1\cup K_2)\to\mathcal F^\bullet(K_1)\oplus\mathcal F^\bullet(K_2)\to\mathcal F^\bullet(K_1\cap K_2)
nodes.section: 2.3.5 Homotopy \texorpdfstring{$\mathcal K$}{K}-sheaves in the theory of virtual fundamental cycles

nodes.name: Poincar\'e duality via a pure homotopy K-sheaf
nodes.statement: H_{n-i}(M,M\setminus K)=H^i\mathcal F^\bullet(K)=\check H^i(K;\mathfrak o_M)
nodes.section: 2.3.5 Homotopy \texorpdfstring{$\mathcal K$}{K}-sheaves in the theory of virtual fundamental cycles
nodes.label: PDintropurehomotopysheafex

nodes.statement: This argument generalizes as follows to prove the isomorphism \eqref{homotopyisogoal}. For sake of concreteness, let us take $C^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(X;A)$ to be the mapping cone of \eqref{multichartcomplex}, though the general case is not much different. First of all, we observe that there is a natural complex of $\mathcal K$-presheaves $\mathcal F^\bullet$ on $X$ whose complex of global sections is $C^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(X;A)$. Namely, to get $\mathcal F^\bullet(K)$ we simply replace every occurence of $U_\alpha$, $U_\beta$, or $U_{\alpha\beta}$ in \eqref{multichartcomplex} by its intersection with $K$. Now $\mathcal F^\bullet$ is a homotopy $\mathcal K$-sheaf (extensions of homotopy $\mathcal K$-sheaves are homotopy $\mathcal K$-sheaves by Lemma \ref{associatedgradedhomotopysheaf}, and each of the individual complexes appearing in \eqref{multichartcomplex} gives a homotopy $\mathcal K$-sheaf by Mayer--Vietoris). To prove that $\mathcal F^\bullet$ is pure and to identify its $H^0$, we can calculate $H^i\mathcal F^\bullet(\{p\})$ using a spectral sequence which degenerates at the $E_2$ term (this is the argument in Lemma \ref{gluingcechsimple}). It is this second step where it matters that we glued the complexes together ``correctly''. Since $\mathcal F^\bullet$ is a pure homotopy $\mathcal K$-sheaf and we have identified its $H^0$, this gives the desired isomorphism.
nodes.name: Strategy for the isomorphism $H^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}=\check H^\bullet$ (two charts)
nodes.statement_short: The two-chart virtual cochain complex is global sections of a homotopy K-sheaf; a degenerating spectral sequence shows purity, giving the isomorphism.
nodes.section: 2.3.5 Homotopy \texorpdfstring{$\mathcal K$}{K}-sheaves in the theory of virtual fundamental cycles

nodes.name: Concatenation map of Floer moduli spaces
nodes.statement: \overline{\mathcal M}(p,q)\times\overline{\mathcal M}(q,r)\to\overline{\mathcal M}(p,r)
nodes.label: concatintro

nodes.name: Combined atlases $A\sqcup B$ arise naturally in practice
nodes.statement: In theory, there is no way to go from a pair of implicit atlases $A$ and $B$ on a space $X$ to an implicit atlas $A\sqcup B$ on $X$ whose subatlases $A$ and $B$ coincide with the given atlases (and there is no uniqueness for atlases $A\sqcup B$ with this property). However in practice, there is often a natural choice of such an atlas, which moreover is essentially the only reasonable choice. The atlas (\ref{IAPQR}) is a good example of this.
nodes.statement_short: There is no general way to combine two atlases, but in practice a natural choice exists.

nodes.statement: We fix a finite set $\mathcal P$ (the ``set of generators'') equipped with partial order $\prec$ and a grading $\operatorname{gr}:\mathcal P\to\mathbb Z$. For all pairs $p\prec q$ in $\mathcal P$, we fix a compact Hausdorff space $\mathcal X(p,q)$ (the ``space of broken trajectories from $p$ to $q$''). These spaces $\mathcal X(p,q)$ are also equipped with ``concatenation maps'': \begin{equation} \mathcal X(p,q)\times\mathcal X(q,r)\to\mathcal X(p,r) \end{equation} which satisfy some natural properties, in particular associativity. We call such a pair $(\mathcal P,\mathcal X)$ (when defined precisely) a \emph{flow category}.
nodes.name: Flow category (introduction)
nodes.statement_short: A poset of graded generators with compact spaces of broken trajectories X(p,q) and associative concatenation maps.

nodes.name: Concatenation maps of a flow category
nodes.statement: \mathcal X(p,q)\times\mathcal X(q,r)\to\mathcal X(p,r)
nodes.label: productmapexample

nodes.statement: This terminology is due to Cohen--Jones--Segal \cite{cohenjonessegal}, who used it to mean something closer to what we prefer to call a \emph{Morse--Smale flow category}, namely a flow category in which every $\mathcal X(p,q)$ is a manifold with corners of dimension $\operatorname{gr}(q)-\operatorname{gr}(p)-1$ in a manner compatible with the concatenation maps \eqref{productmapexample}.
nodes.name: Morse--Smale flow category
differentia: every $\mathcal X(p,q)$ is a manifold with corners of dimension $\operatorname{gr}(q)-\operatorname{gr}(p)-1$

nodes.statement: The basic example of a flow category is the flow category of a Morse function: $\mathcal P$ is the set of critical points, and $\mathcal X(p,q)$ is the space of (broken) Morse trajectories from $p$ to $q$; if the Morse function is Morse--Smale, then this flow category is Morse--Smale.
nodes.name: Flow category of a Morse function

nodes.statement: Given a Morse--Smale flow category $(\mathcal P,\mathcal X)$, one can construct a map $d:\mathbb Z[\mathcal P]\to\mathbb Z[\mathcal P]$ by counting those $\mathcal X$ of dimension $0$, and one can prove that $d^2=0$ by considering those $\mathcal X$ of dimension $1$.
nodes.name: Morse differential from a Morse--Smale flow category
assumptions: Given a Morse--Smale flow category $(\mathcal P,\mathcal X)$
conclusions: one can construct a map $d:\mathbb Z[\mathcal P]\to\mathbb Z[\mathcal P]$ by counting those $\mathcal X$ of dimension $0$
one can prove that $d^2=0$ by considering those $\mathcal X$ of dimension $1$

nodes.name: Choice of compatible system of implicit atlases
nodes.statement: There are many different choices for what one could mean by a ``compatible system of implicit atlases'' $\mathcal A(p,q)$ on the spaces $\mathcal X(p,q)$. For sake of exposition, we have chosen here the structure for which it is \emph{easiest to apply the VFC package}. In the actual construction in \S\ref{homologygroupssection}, we use the structure which is the \emph{easiest to construct in practice} (via the natural generalization of \S\ref{floerintroIA}). As a result, various complexes that here \emph{coincide} are only \emph{canonically quasi-isomorphic} in \S\ref{homologygroupssection}. Basically, this means that in \S\ref{homologygroupssection}, we will have to take lots of homotopy colimits to make certain maps well-defined on the chain level. A systematic use of $\infty$-categories of complexes would tame the resulting explosion of notation, at the cost of relying on that more abstract language/machinery.
nodes.statement_short: The exposition uses the structure easiest for the VFC package; the actual construction uses the easiest to build, requiring homotopy colimits.

nodes.statement: We now review what the VFC package gives to us for a flow category $(\mathcal P,\mathcal X)$ equipped with a compatible system of implicit atlases. For a space $X$ equipped with an implicit atlas with boundary, the VFC package provides \emph{virtual cochain complexes} $C^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(X\operatorname{rel}\partial)$ and $C^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(X)$ (defined using the ideas from \S\ref{vfcintrosec}). Moreover, giving $\partial X$ the ``restriction to the boundary'' implicit atlas, there is a natural map: \begin{equation} C_\mathrm{vir}^{\bullet-1}(\partial X)\to C_\mathrm{vir}^\bullet(X\operatorname{rel}\partial) \end{equation} whose mapping cone is $C^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(X)$ (by definition). There are canonical isomorphisms: \begin{align} H^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(X)&\xrightarrow\sim\check H^\bullet(X;\mathfrak o_X)\\ H^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(X\operatorname{rel}\partial)&\xrightarrow\sim\check H^\bullet(X;\mathfrak o_{X\operatorname{rel}\partial}) \end{align} where $\mathfrak o_X$ is the ``virtual orientation sheaf'' of $X$. There is also a map: \begin{equation} C^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(X\operatorname{rel}\partial)\xrightarrow{s_\ast}C_{\dim E_A-\bullet}(E_A,E_A\setminus 0) \end{equation} (which, when combined with \eqref{HXrelisointro}, can be thought of as pairing against the virtual fundamental cycle of $X$). Now, there are also product maps: \begin{equation} C_\mathrm{vir}^\bullet(\mathcal X(p,q)\operatorname{rel}\partial)\otimes C_\mathrm{vir}^\bullet(\mathcal X(q,r)\operatorname{rel}\partial)\to C_\mathrm{vir}^\bullet([\mathcal X(p,q)\times\mathcal X(q,r)]\operatorname{rel}\partial) \end{equation} which, when combined with the concatenation maps \eqref{productmapexample} induce maps: \begin{equation} C_\mathrm{vir}^\bullet(\mathcal X(p,q)\operatorname{rel}\partial)\otimes C_\mathrm{vir}^\bullet(\mathcal X(q,r)\operatorname{rel}\partial)\to C_\mathrm{vir}^\bullet(\partial\mathcal X(p,r)) \end{equation} From construction, it is clear that the following diagram commutes: \begin{equation} \begin{tikzcd} C_\mathrm{vir}^\bullet(\mathcal X(p,q)\operatorname{rel}\partial)\otimes C_\mathrm{vir}^\bullet(\mathcal X(q,r)\operatorname{rel}\partial)\ar{r}{\eqref{productmapfromIA}}\ar{d}{s_\ast\otimes s_\ast}&C_\mathrm{vir}^\bullet(\partial\mathcal X(p,r))\ar{d}{s_\ast}\\ C_\bullet(E_{\mathcal A(p,q)},E_{\mathcal A(p,q)}\setminus 0)\otimes C_\bullet(E_{\mathcal A(q,r)},E_{\mathcal A(q,r)}\setminus 0)\ar{r}&C_\bullet(E_{\mathcal A(p,r)},E_{\mathcal A(p,r)}\setminus 0) \end{tikzcd} \end{equation} where the bottom map is simply the cartesian product on chains (recall that $\mathcal A(p,r)=\mathcal A(p,q)\sqcup\mathcal A(q,r)$).
nodes.name: VFC package for flow categories (overview)
nodes.statement_short: Virtual cochain complexes rel boundary, the coboundary map, isomorphisms with Cech cohomology, Thom pushforward and product maps compatible with s_*.

nodes.name: Coboundary map on virtual cochain complexes (introduction)
nodes.statement: C_\mathrm{vir}^{\bullet-1}(\partial X)\to C_\mathrm{vir}^\bullet(X\operatorname{rel}\partial)
nodes.label: introcoboundary

nodes.name: Isomorphisms $H^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}=\check H^\bullet$ (introduction)
nodes.statement: H^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(X)&\xrightarrow\sim\check H^\bullet(X;\mathfrak o_X)\\ H^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(X\operatorname{rel}\partial)&\xrightarrow\sim\check H^\bullet(X;\mathfrak o_{X\operatorname{rel}\partial})
nodes.statement_short: Canonical isomorphisms of virtual cohomology with Cech cohomology twisted by orientation sheaves.
nodes.label: HXisointro

nodes.name: Thom pushforward $s_\ast$ (introduction)
nodes.statement: C^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(X\operatorname{rel}\partial)\xrightarrow{s_\ast}C_{\dim E_A-\bullet}(E_A,E_A\setminus 0)
nodes.label: thomintro

nodes.name: Product maps on virtual cochain complexes
nodes.statement: C_\mathrm{vir}^\bullet(\mathcal X(p,q)\operatorname{rel}\partial)\otimes C_\mathrm{vir}^\bullet(\mathcal X(q,r)\operatorname{rel}\partial)\to C_\mathrm{vir}^\bullet([\mathcal X(p,q)\times\mathcal X(q,r)]\operatorname{rel}\partial)

nodes.name: Product maps to the boundary
nodes.statement: C_\mathrm{vir}^\bullet(\mathcal X(p,q)\operatorname{rel}\partial)\otimes C_\mathrm{vir}^\bullet(\mathcal X(q,r)\operatorname{rel}\partial)\to C_\mathrm{vir}^\bullet(\partial\mathcal X(p,r))
nodes.label: productmapfromIA

nodes.name: Compatibility of product maps with $s_\ast$
nodes.statement: \begin{tikzcd} C_\mathrm{vir}^\bullet(\mathcal X(p,q)\operatorname{rel}\partial)\otimes C_\mathrm{vir}^\bullet(\mathcal X(q,r)\operatorname{rel}\partial)\ar{r}{\eqref{productmapfromIA}}\ar{d}{s_\ast\otimes s_\ast}&C_\mathrm{vir}^\bullet(\partial\mathcal X(p,r))\ar{d}{s_\ast}\\ C_\bullet(E_{\mathcal A(p,q)},E_{\mathcal A(p,q)}\setminus 0)\otimes C_\bullet(E_{\mathcal A(q,r)},E_{\mathcal A(q,r)}\setminus 0)\ar{r}&C_\bullet(E_{\mathcal A(p,r)},E_{\mathcal A(p,r)}\setminus 0) \end{tikzcd}
nodes.label: productofVCandonEcompare

nodes.statement: To define $d$, we need to choose:\footnote{That these should be contractible choices is suggested by the Dold--Thom--Almgren theorem \cite{almgren} \cite[p430]{gromovI}.} \begin{rlist} \item(``Chain level coherent orientations'') Cochains $\lambda(p,q)\in C^0_\mathrm{vir}(\mathcal X(p,q)\operatorname{rel}\partial)$ satisfying the following property. Define: \begin{equation} \mu(p,r):=\sum_{p\prec q\prec r}\lambda(p,q)\cdot\lambda(q,r)\in C_\mathrm{vir}^0(\partial\mathcal X(p,r)) \end{equation} (where we implicitly use \eqref{productmapfromIA} on the right hand side). We require that $d\lambda(p,r)$ equal (the image under \eqref{introcoboundary}) of $\mu(p,r)$. Thus $(\mu(p,r),\lambda(p,r))$ defines a cycle in the mapping cone of \eqref{introcoboundary}, and thus a homology class in $H^0_\mathrm{vir}(\mathcal X(p,r))=\check H^0(\mathcal X(p,r),\mathfrak o_{\mathcal X(p,r)})$ (by \eqref{HXisointro}). We require that this homology class coincide with the (given) orientation on $\mathcal X(p,r)$. \item(``Thom cocycles'') Cocycles $[[E_{\mathcal A(p,q)}]]\in C^{\dim E_{\mathcal A(p,q)}}(E_{\mathcal A(p,q)},E_{\mathcal A(p,q)}\setminus 0)$ whose pairing with $[E_{\mathcal A(p,q)}]$ is $1$ and which are compatible in the sense that the following diagram commutes: \begin{equation} \hspace{-1.5cm} \begin{tikzcd} C_\bullet(E_{\mathcal A(p,q)},E_{\mathcal A(p,q)}\setminus 0)\otimes C_\bullet(E_{\mathcal A(q,r)},E_{\mathcal A(q,r)}\setminus 0)\ar{r}\ar{d}[swap]{[[E_{\mathcal A(p,q)}]]\otimes[[E_{\mathcal A(q,r)}]]}&C_\bullet(E_{\mathcal A(p,r)},E_{\mathcal A(p,r)}\setminus 0)\ar{ld}{[[E_{\mathcal A(p,r)}]]}\\ \mathbb Z \end{tikzcd} \hspace{-1.5cm} \end{equation} \end{rlist} Given such choices, we define the boundary operator $d:\mathbb Z[\mathcal P]\to\mathbb Z[\mathcal P]$ to have ``matrix coefficients'' $[[E_{\mathcal A(p,q)}]](s_\ast\lambda(p,q))$.
nodes.name: Floer boundary operator from coherent chain-level choices
nodes.definiendum: boundary operator $d:\mathbb Z[\mathcal P]\to\mathbb Z[\mathcal P]$
nodes.statement_short: Choose chain-level coherent orientations lambda(p,q) and compatible Thom cocycles [[E]]; d has matrix coefficients [[E]](s_* lambda(p,q)).

nodes.name: Definition of $\mu(p,r)$
nodes.statement: \mu(p,r):=\sum_{p\prec q\prec r}\lambda(p,q)\cdot\lambda(q,r)\in C_\mathrm{vir}^0(\partial\mathcal X(p,r))
nodes.label: boundarychainlevelcoherent

nodes.name: Coherent Thom cocycles
nodes.statement: \hspace{-1.5cm} \begin{tikzcd} C_\bullet(E_{\mathcal A(p,q)},E_{\mathcal A(p,q)}\setminus 0)\otimes C_\bullet(E_{\mathcal A(q,r)},E_{\mathcal A(q,r)}\setminus 0)\ar{r}\ar{d}[swap]{[[E_{\mathcal A(p,q)}]]\otimes[[E_{\mathcal A(q,r)}]]}&C_\bullet(E_{\mathcal A(p,r)},E_{\mathcal A(p,r)}\setminus 0)\ar{ld}{[[E_{\mathcal A(p,r)}]]}\\ \mathbb Z \end{tikzcd} \hspace{-1.5cm}
nodes.label: coherentcofundamentalcocycles

nodes.statement: One can show that $d^2=0$ by using $d\lambda(p,q)=\mu(p,q)$ and the compatibilities \eqref{productofVCandonEcompare} and \eqref{coherentcofundamentalcocycles}.
nodes.name: $d^2=0$ for the boundary operator

nodes.statement: Let us now sketch the proof of the existence of $\lambda$ and $[[E]]$ as above. We will work by induction on $(p,q)$; that is, we show that valid $\lambda(p,q)$ and $[[E_{\mathcal A(p,q)}]]$ exist given that we have fixed valid $\lambda(p',q')$ and $[[E_{\mathcal A(p',q')}]]$ for all $p\preceq p'\prec q'\preceq q$ (other than $(p',q')=(p,q)$). To construct $\lambda(p,q)$, argue as follows. Notice that $\mu(p,q)$ is automatically a cycle (apply \eqref{boundarychainlevelcoherent} to expand its boundary and everything cancels). Now from a general statement about cycles in mapping cones, the existence of $\lambda(p,q)$ inducing the correct homology class in $H_\mathrm{vir}^0(\mathcal X(p,q))=\check H^0(\mathcal X(p,q);\mathfrak o_{\mathcal X(p,q)})$ reduces to showing that the homology class $[\mu(p,q)]\in H^0_\mathrm{vir}(\partial\mathcal X(p,q))=\check H^0(\partial\mathcal X(p,q),\mathfrak o_{\partial\mathcal X(p,q)})$ is correct (namely, that it coincides with the image of the desired class under the coboundary map $\check H^0(\mathcal X(p,q);\mathfrak o_{\mathcal X(p,q)})\to\check H^0(\partial\mathcal X(p,q),\mathfrak o_{\partial\mathcal X(p,q)})$). The key observation is that \emph{this can be checked locally} since $\mathfrak o_{\partial\mathcal X(p,q)}$ is a sheaf. Over the top strata of $\partial\mathcal X(p,q)$ (that is, those trajectories that split only once), the agreement is clear by the induction hypothesis on $\lambda$ and the compatibility of the given coherent orientations. Unfortunately, the top strata may not be dense in $\partial\mathcal X(p,q)$, so we need to work harder (see Proposition \ref{stratifiedispurehomotopysheaf}). In the end, we must use the induction hypothesis for \emph{all} $\lambda(p',q')$. To construct $[[E_{\mathcal A(p,r)}]]$, argue as follows. First, observe that the ``homology diagram'' trivially commutes: \begin{equation} \begin{tikzcd} H_\bullet(E_{\mathcal A(p,q)},E_{\mathcal A(p,q)}\setminus 0)\otimes H_\bullet(E_{\mathcal A(q,r)},E_{\mathcal A(q,r)}\setminus 0)\ar{r}\ar{d}[swap]{[E_{\mathcal A(p,q)}]\otimes[E_{\mathcal A(q,r)}]\mapsto 1}&H_\bullet(E_{\mathcal A(p,r)},E_{\mathcal A(p,r)}\setminus 0)\ar{ld}{[E_{\mathcal A(p,r)}]\mapsto 1}\\ \mathbb Z \end{tikzcd} \end{equation} If the horizontal map in \eqref{coherentcofundamentalcocycles} were a cofibration (think ``injective'') in a suitable sense, then the commutativity of \eqref{coherentcofundamentalcocycleshomology} would be sufficient to imply the existence of $[[E_{\mathcal A(p,r)}]]$. Unfortunately, it is far from clear that this map is a cofibration; moreover, its failure to be a cofibration is a genuine obstruction to defining $[[E_{\mathcal A(p,r)}]]$ inductively. For the correct inductive construction, we must use ``cofibrant replacements'' for the system of complexes $C_\bullet(E_{\mathcal A(p,q)},E_{\mathcal A(p,q)}\setminus 0)$ (the details of which we leave for \S\ref{homologygroupssection}).
nodes.name: Existence of coherent choices (sketch)
nodes.statement_short: Induction on (p,q): lambda exists since the boundary class can be checked locally (orientation sheaf); Thom cocycles need cofibrant replacements.

nodes.name: Homology-level compatibility of Thom classes
nodes.statement: \begin{tikzcd} H_\bullet(E_{\mathcal A(p,q)},E_{\mathcal A(p,q)}\setminus 0)\otimes H_\bullet(E_{\mathcal A(q,r)},E_{\mathcal A(q,r)}\setminus 0)\ar{r}\ar{d}[swap]{[E_{\mathcal A(p,q)}]\otimes[E_{\mathcal A(q,r)}]\mapsto 1}&H_\bullet(E_{\mathcal A(p,r)},E_{\mathcal A(p,r)}\setminus 0)\ar{ld}{[E_{\mathcal A(p,r)}]\mapsto 1}\\ \mathbb Z \end{tikzcd}
nodes.label: coherentcofundamentalcocycleshomology

nodes.statement: Finally, we should argue that the homology groups defined via a choice of $(\lambda,[[E]])$ are in fact independent of that choice. For this, we use the usual strategy of constructing a chain map between $(\mathbb Z[\mathcal P],d)$ and $(\mathbb Z[\mathcal P],d')$ for any $d$ and $d'$ arising from $(\lambda,[[E]])$ and $(\lambda',[[E]]')$ respectively (plus appropriate chain homotopies). To construct such a chain map, we use a similar inductive procedure, starting from the base choices $(\lambda,[[E]])$ and $(\lambda',[[E]]')$. Note that for this argument for independence of choice to work, the inductive nature of our construction is crucial.
nodes.name: Independence of choices (sketch)
nodes.statement_short: Inductively construct chain maps and homotopies between complexes from two sets of choices.

nodes.name: Quotient implicit atlas on $X/S^1$ does not exist in general
nodes.statement: A natural strategy for proving $S^1$-localization results is to consider $X_I/S^1$ as forming an atlas on $X/S^1$ of virtual dimension one less, and then ``pulling back'' to $X$ the virtual fundamental cycle on $X/S^1$ (this is the approach taken by Fukaya--Oh--Ohta--Ono \cite{fukayaono,foootechnicaldetails}). In the general setting where the $S^1$-action is merely continuous, the implicit atlas on $X$ does not induce an implicit atlas on $X/S^1$ because of the existence of free $S^1$-actions on topological manifolds whose quotients are not manifolds\footnote{Such an action may be constructed out of any non-manifold $X$ for which $X\times\mathbb R$ is a manfold (namely the obvious action on $X\times S^1$). Many examples of such spaces are known, the first being due to Bing \cite{bingstablemanifoldexample}; see also Cannon \cite{cannon}.}, though we still consider this ``quotient implicit atlas'' in spirit. This extra generality is convenient, since it means we do not need to construct an $S^1$-equivariant gluing map (providing the local slice necessary to show that the ``quotient implicit atlas'' exists).
nodes.statement_short: Free S^1-actions on topological manifolds may have non-manifold quotients, so no quotient atlas exists; this avoids needing equivariant gluing.
nodes.label: cannotquotientbySS

nodes.statement: Let us now prove our assertion $\pi_\ast[X]^\mathrm{vir}=0$ in the simple case of a single chart (for which we defined $[X]^\mathrm{vir}$ in \S\ref{vfcsinglechart}).
nodes.name: $S^1$-localization for a single chart
conclusions: $\pi_\ast[X]^\mathrm{vir}=0$
assumptions: in the simple case of a single chart
nodes.statement_short: For a free S^1-space with a single-chart S^1-equivariant atlas, the pushforward of the VFC to X/S^1 vanishes.

nodes.statement: In this case, the implicit atlas $A=\{\alpha\}$ consists of a topological manifold $X_\alpha$, a function $s_\alpha:X_\alpha\to E_\alpha$, and an identification $X=s_\alpha^{-1}(0)$. This atlas being $S^1$-equivariant means that $X_\alpha$ is equipped with an $S^1$-action for which $s_\alpha$ is $S^1$-invariant and which induces the given action on $X$. The desired statement follows from the following diagram, as we explain below: \begin{equation*} \begin{CD} \check H^d(X/S^1)@=H_{\dim E_\alpha-1}^{S^1}(X_\alpha,X_\alpha\setminus X)@>(s_\alpha)_\ast>>H_{\dim E_\alpha-1}^{S^1}(E_\alpha,E_\alpha\setminus 0)\cr @V\pi^\ast VV@VV\pi^!V@VV\pi^!V\cr \check H^d(X)@=H_{\dim E_\alpha}(X_\alpha,X_\alpha\setminus X)@>(s_\alpha)_\ast>>H_{\dim E_\alpha}(E_\alpha,E_\alpha\setminus 0)@>[E_\alpha]\mapsto 1>>\mathbb Z \end{CD} \end{equation*} The map $\pi^\ast$ is pullback under $\pi:X\to X/S^1$. The maps $\pi^!$ are the maps from the Gysin long exact sequence for an $S^1$-space: \begin{equation} \cdots\xrightarrow{\cap e}H_{\bullet-1}^{S^1}(Z)\xrightarrow{\pi^!}H_\bullet(Z)\xrightarrow{\pi_\ast}H_\bullet^{S^1}(Z)\xrightarrow{\cap e}H_{\bullet-2}^{S^1}(Z)\xrightarrow{\pi^!}\cdots \end{equation} The two leftmost horizontal identifications are a form of Poincar\'e duality (which can be proven, along with the commutativity of the square, with homotopy $\mathcal K$-sheaves as in \S\ref{homotopysheavesintrosec}); it is at this step where we use the fact that $S^1$ acts freely on $X$. Now $[X]^\mathrm{vir}$ is by definition the composition of the bottom row. Hence $\pi_\ast[X]^\mathrm{vir}$ is the map from the upper left corner to the bottom right. On the other hand, the rightmost vertical map $\pi^!:H_{\dim E_\alpha-1}^{S^1}(E_\alpha,E_\alpha\setminus 0)\to H_{\dim E_\alpha}(E_\alpha,E_\alpha\setminus 0)$ vanishes since $S^1$ acts trivially on $E_\alpha$. It follows that $\pi_\ast[X]^\mathrm{vir}=0$ as desired.
nodes.name: Proof of $S^1$-localization for a single chart
nodes.statement_short: Compare equivariant and ordinary Poincare duality diagrams via Gysin maps; the Gysin map on (E, E minus 0) vanishes since S^1 acts trivially on E.

nodes.name: Gysin sequence for an $S^1$-space
nodes.statement: \cdots\xrightarrow{\cap e}H_{\bullet-1}^{S^1}(Z)\xrightarrow{\pi^!}H_\bullet(Z)\xrightarrow{\pi_\ast}H_\bullet^{S^1}(Z)\xrightarrow{\cap e}H_{\bullet-2}^{S^1}(Z)\xrightarrow{\pi^!}\cdots

nodes.name: Scope of the $S^1$-localization results
nodes.statement: We do not construct an $S^1$-equivariant virtual fundamental class, nor do we address $S^1$-localization for actions which are not free or almost free (having finite stabilizer at every point). However, the machinery we develop could potentially be used for these purposes, see Remark \ref{SSequivariantvfcmaybe}.
nodes.statement_short: No S^1-equivariant VFC or non-free localization is constructed, though the machinery may apply.

nodes.name: Implicit atlas
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a compact Hausdorff space.
