nodes.section: 7.5 Resolution \texorpdfstring{$\tilde Z_\bullet\to Z_\bullet$}{tilde Z to Z}

nodes.name: Choose lifts $\tilde\lambda$
nodes.statement: \textbf{Choosing $\tilde\lambda_{\sigma,p,q}$.}\ We must find $\tilde\lambda_{\sigma,p,q}$ lifting $s_\ast\lambda_{\sigma,p,q}$ and satisfying $d\tilde\lambda_{\sigma,p,q}=\tilde\mu_{\sigma,p,q}$. Now we know that $\tilde\mu_{\sigma,p,q}$ is a cycle (see Definition \ref{systemofcycles}); furthermore its image in $C_\bullet(E;\mathcal B)^+$ is $s_\ast\mu_{\sigma,p,q}=d(s_\ast\lambda_{\sigma,p,q})$ which is null-homologous. Since $Q\mathcal W_\bullet\overset\sim\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal W_\bullet$ is always a quasi-isomorphism, it follows that $\tilde\mu_{\sigma,p,q}$ is null-homologous. Hence there exists $\tilde\lambda_{\sigma,p,q}'$ with $d\tilde\lambda_{\sigma,p,q}'=\tilde\mu_{\sigma,p,q}$; now we must modify $\tilde\lambda_{\sigma,p,q}'$ so that it lifts $s_\ast\lambda_{\sigma,p,q}$. The difference of $s_\ast\lambda_{\sigma,p,q}$ and the image of $\tilde\lambda_{\sigma,p,q}'$ is a cycle in $C_\bullet(E;\mathcal B)^+$. It can be lifted to a cycle in $QC_\bullet(E;\mathcal B)^+$ using Lemma \ref{cycleliftinglemma} (again using that $Q\mathcal W_\bullet\overset\sim\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal W_\bullet$ is a quasi-isomorphism), which is enough.
nodes.statement_short: Since $Q\mathcal W\to\mathcal W$ is a surjective quasi-isomorphism, find $\tilde\lambda$ and correct it by Lemma 7.4.27.
nodes.section: 7.5 Resolution \texorpdfstring{$\tilde Z_\bullet\to Z_\bullet$}{tilde Z to Z}

nodes.name: Write the map as $1-\epsilon$
nodes.statement: Let $d:R[[\mathcal P]]\to R[[\mathcal P]]$ denote the boundary operator associated to the vertex of $\sigma$, and let $1-\epsilon:R[[\mathcal P]]\to R[[\mathcal P]]$ denote the chain map associated to $\sigma$. We must show that $\epsilon$ is chain homotopic to the zero map.
nodes.statement_short: Denote the differential and write the map as $1-\epsilon$; show $\epsilon\simeq 0$.

nodes.name: Lift a degenerate 2-simplex
nodes.statement: Since $\tilde Z_\bullet\to Z_\bullet$ is a trivial Kan fibration (Proposition \ref{trivialKanfibration}), there exists a $2$-simplex in $\tilde Z_\bullet$ all of whose edges are $\sigma$. Associated to this $2$-simplex is a chain homotopy $h:R[[\mathcal P]]\to R[[\mathcal P]]$ between $(1-\epsilon)$ and $(1-\epsilon)\circ(1-\epsilon)$; in other words: \begin{equation} \epsilon=dh+hd+\epsilon^2 \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: By the trivial Kan fibration property, a 2-simplex with all edges $\sigma$ gives $\epsilon=dh+hd+\epsilon^2$.

nodes.name: Claim: support of matrix coefficients
nodes.statement:
Now we claim that the only nonzero ``matrix coefficients'' $c_{p,q}$ of $d,\epsilon,h$ are those for which $\mathcal X(\sigma^0,p,q)
e\varnothing$. By definition, $f_\sigma$ can have nonzero matrix coefficients $c_{p,q}$ only for $\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)
e\varnothing$. Hence hypothesis (ef{highernonemptyissameaszero}) gives the desired claim as long as $p
e q$. For the diagonal matrix coefficients $c_{p,p}$, we argue separately as follows. By degree considerations, only $\epsilon$ can have nonzero $c_{p,p}$. It thus suffices to show that the matrix coefficient $c_{p,p}=[[E]]_{\sigma^1,p,p}(	ilde\lambda_{\sigma^1,p,p})$ of $f_{\sigma^1}=1-\epsilon$ equals $1$. Note that no product/face maps have target $(\sigma^1,p,p)$, so $\lambda_{\sigma^1,p,p}$ is a cycle representing $\omega(\sigma^1,p,p)=1$. Hence $	ilde\lambda_{\sigma^1,p,p}$ is a cycle representing $[E]$, and so $[[E]]_{\sigma^1,p,p}(	ilde\lambda_{\sigma,p,p})=1$ as needed. Hence the claim is valid.
nodes.statement_short: Nonzero matrix coefficients of $d,\epsilon,h$ occur only where $\mathcal X(\sigma^0,p,q)\ne\varnothing$.

nodes.name: Off-diagonal coefficients
nodes.statement: By definition, $f_\sigma$ can have nonzero matrix coefficients $c_{p,q}$ only for $\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)\ne\varnothing$. Hence hypothesis (\ref{highernonemptyissameaszero}) gives the desired claim as long as $p\ne q$.
nodes.statement_short: Off-diagonal case follows from hypothesis (2).

nodes.name: Diagonal coefficients equal 1
nodes.statement: For the diagonal matrix coefficients $c_{p,p}$, we argue separately as follows. By degree considerations, only $\epsilon$ can have nonzero $c_{p,p}$. It thus suffices to show that the matrix coefficient $c_{p,p}=[[E]]_{\sigma^1,p,p}(\tilde\lambda_{\sigma^1,p,p})$ of $f_{\sigma^1}=1-\epsilon$ equals $1$. Note that no product/face maps have target $(\sigma^1,p,p)$, so $\lambda_{\sigma^1,p,p}$ is a cycle representing $\omega(\sigma^1,p,p)=1$. Hence $\tilde\lambda_{\sigma^1,p,p}$ is a cycle representing $[E]$, and so $[[E]]_{\sigma^1,p,p}(\tilde\lambda_{\sigma,p,p})=1$ as needed. Hence the claim is valid.
nodes.statement_short: Only $\epsilon$ has diagonal terms; the coefficient of $f_{\sigma^1}$ is $[[E]](\tilde\lambda)=1$.

nodes.name: Norm observations
nodes.statement: From the claim, we make the following two observations: \begin{rlist} \item We have $\left|d(p)\right|_a,\left|\epsilon(p)\right|_a,\left|h(p)\right|_a\leq\left|p\right|_a$. \item For all $M<\infty$ and $p\in\mathcal P$, there exists $N<\infty$ such that any length $N$ composition of $d,\epsilon,h$ applied to $p$ has $a$-adic norm $\leq e^{-M}$. \end{rlist} (the second observation also uses Definition \ref{semisimplicialfcdef}(\ref{novikovfiniteness})).
nodes.statement_short: The operators are $a$-adically non-expanding and long compositions become small.

nodes.name: Catalan series
nodes.statement: Now iterating the identity $\epsilon=dh+hd+\epsilon^2$, we are led to the following infinite series:\footnote{The coefficients $\frac 1n\binom{2n-2}{n-1}$ are integers (Catalan numbers $C_{n-1}$), so writing this expression does not make any implicit assumptions on the ring $R$.} \begin{equation} \epsilon=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac 1n\binom{2n-2}{n-1}(hd+dh)^n \end{equation} which by observations (\ref{firstO})--(\ref{secondO}) converges in the $a$-adic topology when applied to any element of $R[[\mathcal P]]$.
nodes.statement_short: Iterate the identity to express $\epsilon$ as a convergent Catalan series in $hd+dh$.

nodes.name: Explicit null-homotopy
nodes.statement: Now we have $(hd+dh)^n=\sum_{k=0}^n(dh)^k(hd)^{n-k}=H_nd+dH_n$ where $H_n=\sum_{k=1}^nh(dh)^{k-1}(hd)^{n-k}$. This gives the desired chain homotopy between $\epsilon$ and zero (again using observations (\ref{firstO})--(\ref{secondO}) to justify convergence of infinite sums).
nodes.statement_short: Each $(hd+dh)^n=H_nd+dH_n$, giving a convergent null-homotopy of $\epsilon$.

nodes.name: Descent via sections
nodes.statement: The proof below shows that we may define $\mathbb H:=\widetilde\mathbb H\circ s$ for any section $s:Z_\bullet\to\tilde Z_\bullet$.
nodes.statement_short: The descent can be taken as $\widetilde\mathbb H\circ s$ for any section.

nodes.name: Over $0$-simplices
nodes.statement: \textbf{Defining $\mathbb H$ over $0$-simplices.}\ Fix some $0$-simplex $v$ of $Z_\bullet$. For every lift $\tilde v$, we have an object $\widetilde\mathbb H(\tilde v)$. Furthermore, for every lift $\tilde e$ of the degenerate $1$-simplex $e$ over $v$, we get a map $\widetilde\mathbb H(\tilde v_1)\xrightarrow{\widetilde\mathbb H(\tilde e)}\widetilde\mathbb H(\tilde v_2)$, which is the identity map if $\tilde v_1=\tilde v_2$. Finally, for every lift $\tilde f$ of the degenerate $2$-simplex $f$ over $v$, the following diagram commutes: \begin{equation} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep = small] &\widetilde\mathbb H(\tilde v_2)\ar{rd}{\widetilde\mathbb H(\tilde e_{23})}&{}\cr \widetilde\mathbb H(\tilde v_1)\ar{ur}{\widetilde\mathbb H(\tilde e_{12})}\ar{rr}[swap]{\widetilde\mathbb H(\tilde e_{13})}&&{\widetilde\mathbb H(\tilde v_3)} \end{tikzcd} \end{equation} where $\tilde e_{12},\tilde e_{23},\tilde e_{13}$ are the edges of $\tilde f$. Using that $\tilde Z_\bullet\to Z_\bullet$ is a trivial Kan fibration to conclude that we can always find lifts with specified boundary conditions, it follows that all $\widetilde\mathbb H(\tilde v)$ are canonically isomorphic. Thus there exists a unique choice for $\mathbb H(v)$.
nodes.statement_short: Lifts of degenerate simplices identify all $\widetilde\mathbb H(\tilde v)$ canonically.

nodes.name: Over $1$-simplices
nodes.statement: \textbf{Defining $\mathbb H$ over $1$-simplices.}\ Fix some $1$-simplex $e$ of $Z_\bullet$ with vertices $v_1,v_2$. If $\tilde e$ is any lift of $e$, then we get a map $\mathbb H(v_1)=\widetilde\mathbb H(\tilde v_1)\xrightarrow{\widetilde\mathbb H(\tilde e)}\widetilde\mathbb H(\tilde v_2)=\mathbb H(v_2)$. Furthermore, this map $\mathbb H(v_1)\to\mathbb H(v_2)$ is seen to be independent of the choice of lift $\tilde e$ by lifting degenerate $2$-simplices over $e$. Thus there exists a unique choice for $\mathbb H(e)$.
nodes.statement_short: The map over an edge is independent of the lift, by lifting degenerate 2-simplices.

nodes.name: Over $2$-simplices
nodes.statement: \textbf{Defining $\mathbb H$ over $n$-simplices for $n\geq 2$.}\ We just need to check that the following diagram commutes for all $2$-simplices $f$ in $Z_\bullet$: \begin{equation} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep = small] &\mathbb H(v_2)\ar{rd}{\mathbb H(e_{23})}&{}\cr \mathbb H(v_1)\ar{ur}{\mathbb H(e_{12})}\ar{rr}[swap]{\mathbb H(e_{13})}&&{\mathbb H(v_3)} \end{tikzcd} \end{equation} where $e_{12},e_{23},e_{13}$ are the edges of $f$. This follows from lifting $f$ and the commutativity of \eqref{liftedF}.
nodes.statement_short: Commutativity over 2-simplices follows by lifting.

nodes.name: Reduce to matrix coefficients
nodes.statement: We will show an equality of ``matrix coefficients'': \begin{equation} ([[E]]_{\sigma,p,q}\otimes\operatorname{id}_R)(\tilde\lambda_{\sigma,p,q})=\langle\omega(\sigma,p,q),[\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)]\rangle \end{equation} for $(\sigma,p,q)\in\tilde Z_\bullet$ with $\operatorname{vdim}\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)=0$.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to show equality of matrix coefficients in virtual dimension $0$.

nodes.name: Diagrams coincide
nodes.statement: Thus comparing \eqref{diagramndgformula} and \eqref{diagramndgformulaMS}, it follows that the two diagrams $\tilde Z_\bullet\to\mathsf{N}_{\mathsf{dg}}(\mathsf{Ch}_{R[[H]]})$ in question, namely $\widetilde\mathbb H(\mathcal X)$ and $\mathbb H'(\mathcal X)\circ\pi$, coincide. The desired isomorphism thus follows from the definition of $\mathbb H(\mathcal X)$ as the descent of $\widetilde\mathbb H(\mathcal X)$.
nodes.statement_short: Then $\widetilde\mathbb H(\mathcal X)=\mathbb H'(\mathcal X)\circ\pi$, so the descents agree.

nodes.name: Vanishing and cycles
nodes.statement: To prove \eqref{matrixcoeffsame}, argue as follows. Since $\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)=\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^\mathrm{reg}$, we know that if $\operatorname{vdim}\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)<0$ then $\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)=\varnothing$ and hence $\lambda_{\sigma,p,q}=0$ and $\tilde\lambda_{\sigma,p,q}=0$. Now when $\operatorname{vdim}\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)=0$, we see that $\mu_{\sigma,p,q}=0$ and $\tilde\mu_{\sigma,p,q}=0$ (because all of the terms defining them involve a triple with negative dimension), so $\lambda_{\sigma,p,q}$ and $\tilde\lambda_{\sigma,p,q}$ are cycles.
nodes.statement_short: Negative virtual dimension spaces are empty; in dimension $0$, $\lambda,\tilde\lambda$ are cycles.

nodes.name: Evaluate on the fundamental class
nodes.statement: Since the homology class of $\lambda_{\sigma,p,q}$ coincides with $\omega(\sigma,p,q)$, the left hand side of \eqref{matrixcoeffsame} coincides with the evaluation of $\omega(\sigma,p,q)$ on $[\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)]^\mathrm{vir}\in\check H^0(\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q);\mathfrak o_{\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)})^\vee$. Now we are done since $[\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)]^\mathrm{vir}=[\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)]$ by Lemma \ref{fclasstransverse}.
nodes.statement_short: The coefficient is $\omega$ evaluated on $[\mathcal X]^\mathrm{vir}=[\mathcal X]$.

nodes.statement: The composition $H_\bullet(X)\to H_\bullet(X\times BS^1)\to H_\bullet(X)$ is the identity map, and so the first map is injective.
nodes.name: Injectivity of first map
nodes.statement_short: Composition through $X\times BS^1$ is the identity, so the first map is injective.

nodes.statement: On the other hand, this map is precisely $\pi_\ast:H_\bullet(X)\to H_\bullet^{S^1}(X)$ since the $S^1$-action is trivial, so $\pi_\ast$ is injective which is sufficient. The same argument applies in the relative setting as well.
nodes.name: Identify with $\pi_\ast$
nodes.statement_short: This map is $\pi_\ast$, so $\pi_\ast$ injective, hence $\pi^!=0$; same relatively.

nodes.statement: Apply the Tietze extension theorem to the identity map $S^1p\to S^1p$ to obtain an $S^1$-invariant neighborhood $K$ of $S^1p$ and a retraction $r:K\to S^1p$. By averaging and passing to a smaller neighborhood, we may assume without loss of generality that $r$ is $S^1$-equivariant.
nodes.name: Equivariant retraction
nodes.statement_short: Construct an invariant neighborhood $K$ with equivariant retraction onto the orbit (Tietze, averaging).

nodes.statement: Now by the naturality of the Euler class, we have $e(K)=r^\ast e(S^1p)$. Thus it suffices to show that $e(S^1p)\in H^2_{S^1}(S^1p)$ vanishes.
nodes.name: Reduce to the orbit
nodes.statement_short: By naturality $e(K)=r^\ast e(S^1p)$, reducing to the orbit.

nodes.statement: Now we have $H^2_{S^1}(S^1p)=H^2_{(S^1)_p}(p)=H^2((S^1)_p)$, where the latter is the group cohomology of the finite stabilizer group $(S^1)_p$. It is a standard fact that the group cohomology of a finite group is annihilated by the order of the group. Hence our assumption that $\#(S^1)_p$ is invertible in $R$ guarantees that this cohomology group vanishes.
nodes.name: Finite group cohomology vanishes
nodes.statement_short: $H^2_{S^1}(S^1p)$ is group cohomology of the finite stabilizer, killed by its invertible order.

nodes.statement: By Poincar\'e duality, we have canonical isomorphisms: \begin{equation} H_\bullet(M,M\setminus S^1p)=\begin{cases}H^0(S^1p;\mathfrak o_M)&\bullet=d\cr H^1(S^1p;\mathfrak o_M)&\bullet=d-1\cr 0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} \end{equation}
nodes.name: Poincaré duality
nodes.statement_short: Local homology at the orbit via Poincaré duality.

nodes.statement: By excision and Lemma \ref{freeactionislocallytrivial}, the Gysin sequence reduces to a short exact sequence: \begin{equation} 0\to H_{\bullet-1}^{S^1}(M,M\setminus S^1p)\xrightarrow{\pi^!}H_\bullet(M,M\setminus S^1p)\xrightarrow{\pi_\ast}H_\bullet^{S^1}(M,M\setminus S^1p)\to 0 \end{equation}
nodes.name: Gysin sequence becomes short exact
nodes.statement_short: Euler class vanishes locally, so the Gysin sequence is short exact.

nodes.statement: Combining this with \eqref{PDforSSPD}, we see that $H_\bullet^{S^1}(M,M\setminus S^1p)=0$ for $\bullet\ne d-1$, and that the following are both isomorphisms: \begin{equation} H_{d-1}(M,M\setminus S^1p)\xrightarrow{\pi_\ast}H_{d-1}^{S^1}(M,M\setminus S^1p)\xrightarrow{\pi^!}H_d(M,M\setminus S^1p) \end{equation} which yields the desired result.
nodes.name: Combine
nodes.statement_short: Combining gives vanishing off degree $d-1$ and the isomorphism.

nodes.statement: As in the proof of Lemma \ref{CSTpure}, we use Lemmas \ref{singularchainshomotopyKsheaf} and \ref{associatedgradedhomotopysheaf} to see that $C^\bullet_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(-;A)_{IJ}$ and $C^\bullet_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(-\operatorname{rel}\partial;A)_{IJ}$ are homotopy $\mathcal K$-sheaves. More precisely, in the present context we need the statement of Lemma \ref{singularchainshomotopyKsheaf} for $C_\bullet^{S^1}$ in place of $C_\bullet$. The proof of this lemma applies equally well to $C_\bullet^{S^1}$, noting that since $C_\bullet^{S^1}$ is a model of $S^1$-equivariant chains, it in particular satisfies Mayer--Vietoris in that following (total complex) is acyclic: \begin{equation} C_\bullet^{S^1}(U\cap U')\to C_\bullet^{S^1}(U)\oplus C_\bullet^{S^1}(U')\to C_\bullet^{S^1}(U\cup U') \end{equation}
nodes.name: Homotopy $\mathcal K$-sheaf property
nodes.statement_short: Homotopy $\mathcal K$-sheaf property as for $C_\mathrm{vir}$, via Mayer--Vietoris for $C^{S^1}_\bullet$.

nodes.statement: Now let us show purity. By Lemma \ref{openclosedpurity}, it suffices to show that the restrictions of $C^\bullet_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(-;A)_{IJ}$ and $C^\bullet_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(-\operatorname{rel}\partial;A)_{IJ}$ to $(V_I\cap V_J)/S^1$ and to $X/S^1\setminus(V_I\cap V_J)/S^1$ are pure. The latter restriction is trivially pure, since both complexes are simply zero for $K\cap V_I\cap V_J=\varnothing$. Hence it suffices to show that the restrictions of both complexes to $(V_I\cap V_J)/S^1$ are pure.
nodes.name: Reduce purity to $(V_I\cap V_J)/S^1$
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma openclosedpurity reduce purity to the locus $(V_I\cap V_J)/S^1$.

nodes.statement: We consider the comparison maps: \begin{align} H^\bullet_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(K;A)_{IJ}&\to H^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(K;A)_{IJ}\\ H^\bullet_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(K\operatorname{rel}\partial;A)_{IJ}&\to H^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(K\operatorname{rel}\partial;A)_{IJ} \end{align} These are Gysin maps $\pi^!$, and hence by the Gysin sequence, their kernels coincide (respectively) with the images of: \begin{align} H^{\bullet-2}_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(K;A)_{IJ}&\xrightarrow{\cap e}H^\bullet_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(K;A)_{IJ}\\ H^{\bullet-2}_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(K\operatorname{rel}\partial;A)_{IJ}&\xrightarrow{\cap e}H^\bullet_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(K\operatorname{rel}\partial;A)_{IJ} \end{align} where $e$ is (the pullback of) $e\in H^2_{S^1}(X_J^\mathrm{reg}/\Gamma_J)$.
nodes.name: Gysin kernels
nodes.statement_short: Comparison maps are Gysin maps; their kernels are images of cap with the Euler class.

nodes.statement: Pick any $p\in V_J\subseteq X$. By Lemma \ref{freeactionislocallytrivial}, this $e$ vanishes when restricted to small $S^1$-invariant compact neighborhoods of $S^1p\subseteq V_J=(s_J|X_J^\mathrm{reg})^{-1}(0)/\Gamma_J\subseteq X_J^\mathrm{reg}/\Gamma_J$. It follows that \eqref{HSTzero}--\eqref{HSTzerorel} vanish for small $S^1$-invariant compact neighborhoods $K$ of $S^1p\subseteq V_J$. Hence \eqref{HSTinjective}--\eqref{HSTinjectiverel} are injective for such $K$. Now, using this injectivity and the fact that $C^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(-;A)_{IJ}$ and $C^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(-\operatorname{rel}\partial;A)_{IJ}$ are pure homotopy $\mathcal K$-sheaves (Lemma \ref{CSTpure}), it follows that $C^\bullet_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(-;A)_{IJ}$ and $C^\bullet_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(-\operatorname{rel}\partial;A)_{IJ}$ are pure on $V_J/S^1$, and hence on all of $X/S^1$.
nodes.name: Local injectivity gives purity
nodes.statement_short: Euler class vanishes near orbits (Lemma freeactionislocallytrivial), so comparison maps are injective and purity follows from Lemma CSTpure.

nodes.statement: It remains to identify $H^0_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(-;A)_{IJ}$ and $H^0_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(-\operatorname{rel}\partial;A)_{IJ}$. Consider the comparison maps: \begin{align} H^0_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(-;A)_{IJ}&\to\pi_\ast H^0_\mathrm{vir}(-;A)_{IJ}\\ H^0_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(-\operatorname{rel}\partial;A)_{IJ}&\to\pi_\ast H^0_\mathrm{vir}(-\operatorname{rel}\partial;A)_{IJ} \end{align} which are maps of sheaves on $X/S^1$.
nodes.name: Comparison maps on $H^0$
nodes.statement_short: Remaining: identify $H^0$ via comparison maps of sheaves.

nodes.statement: It suffices (by Lemma \ref{CSTpure}) to show that these are isomorphisms (which we will check on stalks, i.e.\ for $K=S^1p$). Now this is just a calculation, similar to that in the proof of Lemma \ref{CSTpure}, except using an $S^1$-equivariant version of Poincar\'e--Lefschetz duality based on Lemma \ref{SSmanifoldPDbase} in place of Lemma \ref{poincareduality} (and it is in this calculation where we use the local $S^1$-orientability of $A$).
nodes.name: Stalk calculation
nodes.statement_short: Check on stalks via equivariant Poincaré--Lefschetz duality (Lemma SSmanifoldPDbase).

nodes.statement: Consider the following diagram: \begin{equation*} \begin{tikzcd} H^\bullet_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(X;A)\ar{d}{\sim}\ar{rr}{\eqref{CSStimesSS}}&&H^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(X;A)\ar{d}{\sim}\\ \check H^\bullet(X/S^1;C^\bullet_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(-;A))\ar{r}{\eqref{CSStimesSS}}\ar{d}{\sim}&\check H^\bullet(X/S^1,\pi_\ast C^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(-;A))\ar{r}{\pi^\ast}\ar{d}{\sim}&\check H^\bullet(X;C^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(-;A))\ar{d}{\sim}\\ \check H^\bullet(X/S^1;\tau_{\geq 0}C^\bullet_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(-;A))\ar{r}{\eqref{CSStimesSS}}&\check H^\bullet(X/S^1,\pi_\ast\tau_{\geq 0}C^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(-;A))\ar{r}{\pi^\ast}&\check H^\bullet(X;\tau_{\geq 0}C^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(-;A))\\ \check H^\bullet(X/S^1;H^0_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(-;A))\ar{u}[swap]{\sim}\ar{r}{\eqref{CSStimesSS}}\ar{d}{\sim}&\check H^\bullet(X/S^1,\pi_\ast H^0_\mathrm{vir}(-;A))\ar{r}{\pi^\ast}\ar{u}\ar{d}{\sim}&\check H^\bullet(X;H^0_\mathrm{vir}(-;A))\ar{u}[swap]{\sim}\ar{d}{\sim}\\ \check H^\bullet(X/S^1;\pi_\ast\mathfrak o_X)\ar[equal]{r}&\check H^\bullet(X/S^1,\pi_\ast\mathfrak o_X)\ar{r}{\pi^\ast}&\check H^\bullet(X;\mathfrak o_X) \end{tikzcd} \end{equation*} where the vertical isomorphisms are by Propositions \ref{CpureSS} and \ref{Cpure} (see also \eqref{isosforpurehtpysheafcech}).
nodes.name: Ladder diagram
nodes.statement_short: Diagram whose vertical isomorphisms come from purity (Propositions CpureSS, Cpure).

nodes.statement: Now each small square of this diagram above commutes (only the bottom left requires an argument; one shows that the corresponding diagram of sheaves commutes by checking it locally, where it is just a calculation). Now the first square in Theorem \ref{Slocalfundamentaliso} is the same as the big square above, which commutes by a diagram chase (for which one should be careful of the fact that one of the vertical arrows is not an isomorphism).
nodes.name: Diagram chase
nodes.statement_short: Small squares commute (local check), so the big square commutes by diagram chase.

nodes.statement: An identical argument applies to the second square in Theorem \ref{Slocalfundamentaliso}.
nodes.name: Relative case
nodes.statement_short: Same argument for the rel $\partial$ square.

nodes.statement: We may assume that $A$ is finite. Now by Theorem \ref{Slocalfundamentaliso}, we have a commutative diagram: \begin{equation*} \begin{tikzcd} \check H^{d+\bullet}(X/S^1;\pi_\ast\mathfrak o_{X\operatorname{rel}\partial})\ar{d}{\pi^\ast}\ar[equal]{r}{\text{Thm \ref{Slocalfundamentaliso}}}&H^{d+\bullet}_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(X\operatorname{rel}\partial;A)\ar{d}{\eqref{CSStimesSS}}\ar{r}{\eqref{CSSpushforward}}&H_{-\bullet-1}^{S^1}(E;A)\ar{d}{\pi^!}\\ \check H^{d+\bullet}(X;\mathfrak o_{X\operatorname{rel}\partial})\ar[equal]{r}{\text{Thm \ref{Fsheaffundamentaliso}}}&H^{d+\bullet}_\mathrm{vir}(X\operatorname{rel}\partial;A)\ar{r}{\eqref{Fpushforward}}&H_{-\bullet}(E;A)\ar{r}{[E_A]\mapsto 1}&R \end{tikzcd} \end{equation*}
nodes.name: Commutative diagram
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to finite $A$ and use Theorem Slocalfundamentaliso to build a commutative diagram.

nodes.statement: By definition, $[X]^\mathrm{vir}$ is the total composition of the bottom row for $\bullet=0$. Now the desired statement follows since the rightmost vertical map is zero (by Lemma \ref{trivialactiongysin}, because $S^1$ acts trivially on $E_A$).
nodes.name: Gysin map vanishes
nodes.statement_short: $[X]^\mathrm{vir}$ is the bottom row; the right vertical Gysin map vanishes by Lemma trivialactiongysin.

nodes.statement: Since $\mathcal Y$ is saturated, there exists a morphism of MF-sets $\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0}\to\{M_i\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}$ (where $\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0}$ is as in Example \ref{standardsimplicialMFset}). Since $C_\bullet(X)=C^{\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0}}_\bullet(X)$ by definition, we obtain a chain map $C_\bullet(X)\to C_\bullet^\mathcal Y(X)$.
nodes.name: Simplices into $\mathcal Y$
nodes.statement_short: Saturation gives a morphism from the standard simplicial MF-set, hence a chain map.

nodes.statement: The resulting map: \begin{equation} H_\bullet(X)\to H_\bullet^\mathcal Y(X) \end{equation} is independent of the choice of morphism $\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0}\to\{M_i\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}$, as can be seen as follows. There is an MF-set $\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0}\sqcup\{\Delta^n\times[0,1]\}_{n\geq 0}\sqcup\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0}$ where each $\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0}$ is as in Example \ref{standardsimplicialMFset}, where $\Delta^n\times[0,1]$ is given the product stratification ($[0,1]$ stratified by $\{\{0\},\{1\},(0,1)\}$), and $\Delta^n\times\{0\}$ (resp.\ $\Delta^n\times\{1\}$) is identified with the first (resp.\ second) copy of $\Delta^n$. Since $\mathcal Y$ is saturated, it follows that for any pair of morphisms $\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0}\to\{M_i\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}$ there is a morphism $\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0}\sqcup\{\Delta^n\times[0,1]\}_{n\geq 0}\sqcup\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0}\to\{M_i\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}$ whose restriction to the two copies of $\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0}$ are the two given morphisms. From this data one easily constructs a chain homotopy between the two maps $C_\bullet(X)\to C_\bullet^\mathcal Y(X)$. Hence the map \eqref{homologyYcomparison} is canonical.
nodes.name: Independence of choice
nodes.statement_short: Cylinder MF-set and saturation give a chain homotopy between choices, so the map is canonical.

nodes.statement: Now let us show that \eqref{homologyYcomparison} is an isomorphism. Fix a map $\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0}\to\{M_i\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}$. Fix triangulations $T_i$ of $M_i$ for which each $M_i^{\leq\mathfrak s}$ is a union of simplices, which are compatible with the face identifications, and which restrict to the tautological triangulation of $\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0}$. Such triangulations may be constructed by induction. By triangulation, we mean a triangulation in which each simplex is equipped with a total order on its set of vertices, compatible with its faces (i.e.\ a semisimplicial set rather than a simplicial complex). Such triangluations induce a map of complexes $C_\bullet^\mathcal Y(X)\to C_\bullet(X)$, and the composition $C_\bullet(X)\to C_\bullet^\mathcal Y(X)\to C_\bullet(X)$ is clearly the identity map. It suffices to show that the other composition is chain homotopic to the identity map.
nodes.name: Triangulations give a left inverse
nodes.statement_short: Compatible triangulations give a map back whose composite with the forward map is the identity.

nodes.statement: Now let us define a new MF-set in terms of the map $\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0}\to\{M_i\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}$ and the triangulations $T_i$. Note that the stratification of $M_i$ by the face poset $\mathcal F(T_i)$ of $T_i$ refines the stratification by $\mathcal S_i$; in other words we have maps $M_i\to\mathcal F(T_i)\to\mathcal S_i$. The objects of the new MF-set are $\{M_i\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}\sqcup\{M_i\times[0,1]\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}$, where $M_i\times[0,1]$ is stratified by the following strata: \begin{align} M_i^\mathfrak s\times\{0\}&\quad\mathfrak s\in\mathcal S_i\\ M_i^\mathfrak s\times(0,1)&\quad\mathfrak s\in\mathcal S_i\\ M_i^\mathfrak t\times\{1\}&\quad\mathfrak t\in\mathcal F(T_i) \end{align} Thus the poset of strata of $M_i\times[0,1]$ is $\mathcal S_i\sqcup\mathcal S_i\sqcup\mathcal F(T_i)$. For the face identifications, $M_i\times\{0\}$ is identified tautologically with $M_i$, and each of the closed strata $M_i^{\leq\mathfrak t}\times\{1\}$ ($\mathfrak t\in\mathcal F(T_i)$) is identified with the corresponding $\Delta^n$ (considered as an object of $\{M_i\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}$ via the inclusion $\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0}\to\{M_i\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}$).
nodes.name: Cylinder MF-set
nodes.statement_short: Define the MF-set of $M_i$ and $M_i\times[0,1]$ with top end stratified by the triangulation.

nodes.statement: Now we have a chain of inclusions $\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0}\hookrightarrow\{M_i\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}\hookrightarrow\{M_i\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}\sqcup\{M_i\times[0,1]\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}$. Since $\mathcal Y$ is saturated, there in fact exists a map backwards $\{M_i\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}\sqcup\{M_i\times[0,1]\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}\to\{M_i\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}$ (acting identically on $\{M_i\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}$). Using this map, we obtain a chain map $C_\bullet^\mathcal Y(X)\to C_{\bullet+1}^\mathcal Y(X)$ (precompose chains with the projection $M_i\times[0,1]\to M_i$). This map is a chain homotopy between the identity map and the composition $C_\bullet^\mathcal Y(X)\to C_\bullet(X)\to C_\bullet^\mathcal Y(X)$, so we are done.
nodes.name: Chain homotopy
nodes.statement_short: Saturation gives a map back from the cylinder MF-set, yielding the needed chain homotopy.

nodes.statement: All $S^1$-MF-sets in this proof will share the same $(ES^1)_\mathcal Y\to(BS^1)_\mathcal Y$, so we will omit the subscript $_\mathcal Y$ from the notation.
nodes.name: Notation
nodes.statement_short: Fix a common $ES^1\to BS^1$.

nodes.statement: Let $\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0,f:\Delta^n\to BS^1}$ denote the $S^1$-MF-set indexed by pairs $(n,f)$ consisting of an integer $n\geq 0$ and a PL map $f:\Delta^n\to BS^1$, where the stratifications and face identifications are as in Example \ref{standardsimplicialMFset}. Now the complex $C^{S^1,\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0,f:\Delta^n\to BS^1}}_\bullet(X)$ is freely generated by maps $\Delta^n\to(X\times ES^1)/S^1$ whose composition with the projection $(X\times ES^1)/S^1\to BS^1$ is PL. A straightforward approximation argument shows that the inclusion of this complex into the complex generated by all maps $\Delta^n\to(X\times ES^1)/S^1$ is a quasi-isomorphism. Hence there is a canonical isomorphism: \begin{equation} H^{S^1,\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0,f:\Delta^n\to BS^1}}_\bullet(X)\xrightarrow\sim H_\bullet((X\times ES^1)/S^1)=H_\bullet^{S^1}(X) \end{equation}
nodes.name: Simplicial $S^1$-MF-set
nodes.statement_short: The simplicial $S^1$-MF-set over $BS^1$ computes equivariant homology by PL approximation.

nodes.statement: As in the proof of Lemma \ref{saturatedcalculatesH} there exists a morphism of $S^1$-MF-sets $\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0,f:\Delta^n\to BS^1}\to\mathcal Y$ since $\mathcal Y$ is saturated. This induces a chain map $C^{S^1,\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0,f:\Delta^n\to BS^1}}_\bullet(X)\to C^{S^1,\mathcal Y}_\bullet(X)$, which as before induces a canonical map on homology: \begin{equation} H^{S^1,\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0,f:\Delta^n\to BS^1}}_\bullet(X)\to H^{S^1,\mathcal Y}_\bullet(X) \end{equation} which is independent of the choice of morphism $\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0,f:\Delta^n\to BS^1}\to\mathcal Y$. It suffices to show that this map is an isomorphism.
nodes.name: Canonical comparison map
nodes.statement_short: Saturation gives a canonical comparison map; reduce to showing it is an isomorphism.

nodes.statement: Fix a map $\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0,f:\Delta^n\to BS^1}\to\mathcal Y$, which we observe is necessarily injective. Fix triangulations $T_i$ of $M_i$ as in the proof of Lemma \ref{saturatedcalculatesH}. Such triangulations induce a map of complexes $C^{S^1,\mathcal Y}_\bullet(X)\to C^{S^1,\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0,f:\Delta^n\to BS^1}}_\bullet(X)$. The composition $C^{S^1,\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0,f:\Delta^n\to BS^1}}_\bullet(X)\to C^{S^1,\mathcal Y}_\bullet(X)\to C^{S^1,\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0,f:\Delta^n\to BS^1}}_\bullet(X)$ is clearly the identity map. It thus suffices to show that the reverse composition is chain homotopic to the identity.
nodes.name: Triangulations give a left inverse
nodes.statement_short: Triangulations give a map back; one composite is the identity.

nodes.statement: As in the proof of Lemma \ref{saturatedcalculatesH}, we construct a new $S^1$-MF-set, namely $\{M_i\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}\sqcup\{M_i\times[0,1]\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}$, from the inclusion $\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0,f:\Delta^n\to BS^1}\hookrightarrow\{M_i\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}$ and the triangulations $T_i$. There are inclusions $\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0,f:\Delta^n\to BS^1}\hookrightarrow\{M_i\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}\hookrightarrow\{M_i\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}\sqcup\{M_i\times[0,1]\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}$. The desired chain homotopy may then be constructed as in the proof of Lemma \ref{saturatedcalculatesH}. The fact that the induced map $H^{S^1}_\bullet(X)\to H_{\bullet+1}(X)$ is the Gysin map is left to the reader.
nodes.name: Chain homotopy via cylinders
nodes.statement_short: Cylinder $S^1$-MF-set gives the chain homotopy; the Gysin statement is left to the reader.

nodes.statement: It suffices to perform the inductive step for a given $(\sigma,p,q)$.
nodes.name: Reduce to inductive step
nodes.statement_short: Only the inductive step at $(\sigma,p,q)$ is needed.

nodes.statement: First, we show that the colimits \eqref{colimitYone}--\eqref{colimitYtwo} exist, essentially by rewriting the proofs of Lemmas \ref{cofibrantinjectivelemma} and \ref{cofibranthaslotsofcofibrations} in the present context. We actually show the more general statement that the colimits: \begin{equation} \operatornamewithlimits{colim}_{\mathfrak t\in\mathcal T}\mathcal Y(\sigma,p,q,\mathfrak t)\qquad\operatornamewithlimits{colim}_{\mathfrak t\in\mathcal T}\mathcal Y_{S^1}(\sigma,p,q,\mathfrak t) \end{equation} exist for any $\mathcal T\subseteq\partial\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)$ which is downward closed. We show this by induction on the cardinality of $\mathcal T$. If $\mathcal T=\varnothing$, existence is trivial. For $\mathcal T$ nonempty, let $\mathfrak t_0\in\mathcal T$ be any maximal element, and observe that \eqref{Tcolimit} can be written as the colimit of the diagram: \begin{equation} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep = tiny] &\mathcal Y(\sigma,p,q,\mathfrak t_0)\\ \smash{\displaystyle\operatornamewithlimits{colim}_{\begin{smallmatrix}\mathfrak t\in\mathcal T\cr\mathfrak t\prec\mathfrak t_0\end{smallmatrix}}}\mathcal Y(\sigma,p,q,\mathfrak t)\ar[hook]{ur}\ar{rd}\\ &\displaystyle\operatornamewithlimits{colim}_{\mathfrak t\in\mathcal T\setminus\mathfrak t_0}\mathcal Y(\sigma,p,q,\mathfrak t) \end{tikzcd} \end{equation} Let us show that the top arrow is injective. Write $\mathfrak t_0$ in the form \eqref{SdataA}--\eqref{SdataB}. Then we have: \begin{equation} \mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^{\leq\mathfrak t_0}=\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma|[j_{a_0}\ldots j_{a_1}],p_0,p_1)\times\cdots\times\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma|[j_{a_{m-1}}\ldots j_{a_m}],p_{m-1},p_m) \end{equation} Now we consider the $m$-cubical diagram: \begin{equation} \prod_{i=1}^m\left[\operatornamewithlimits{colim}_{\mathfrak s\in\partial\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma|[j_{a_{i-1}}\ldots j_{a_i}],p_{i-1},p_i)}\mathcal Y(\sigma|[j_{a_{i-1}}\ldots j_{a_i}],p_{i-1},p_i,\mathfrak s)\hookrightarrow\mathcal Y(\sigma|[j_{a_{i-1}}\ldots j_{a_i}],p_{i-1},p_i)\right] \end{equation} Now the top arrow of \eqref{colimitdiagramnice} is simply the map to the maximal vertex of this $m$-cube from the colimit over the $m$-cube minus the maximal vertex (this is where we use the fact that $\mathcal T$ is downward closed). This is injective for any cubical diagram of the form $\prod_{i=1}^m[A_i\hookrightarrow B_i]$ where each $A_i\hookrightarrow B_i$ is injective. Now that the top arrow in \eqref{colimitdiagramnice} is injective, the existence of the colimit is clear (first take the colimit of underlying sets and then the rest of the structure extends in an obvious way), and hence the colimit in \eqref{Tcolimit} exists. This reasoning applies equally well to $\mathcal Y_{S^1}$ (including $(ES^1)_\mathcal Y\to(BS^1)_\mathcal Y$).
nodes.name: Existence of the boundary colimits
nodes.statement_short: The colimits over the boundary poset exist.

nodes.statement: First, we show that the colimits \eqref{colimitYone}--\eqref{colimitYtwo} exist, essentially by rewriting the proofs of Lemmas \ref{cofibrantinjectivelemma} and \ref{cofibranthaslotsofcofibrations} in the present context. We actually show the more general statement that the colimits: \begin{equation} \operatornamewithlimits{colim}_{\mathfrak t\in\mathcal T}\mathcal Y(\sigma,p,q,\mathfrak t)\qquad\operatornamewithlimits{colim}_{\mathfrak t\in\mathcal T}\mathcal Y_{S^1}(\sigma,p,q,\mathfrak t) \end{equation} exist for any $\mathcal T\subseteq\partial\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)$ which is downward closed.
nodes.name: Generalize to downward closed $\mathcal T$
nodes.statement_short: Prove existence of colimits over every downward closed $\mathcal T$.

nodes.statement: We show this by induction on the cardinality of $\mathcal T$. If $\mathcal T=\varnothing$, existence is trivial. For $\mathcal T$ nonempty, let $\mathfrak t_0\in\mathcal T$ be any maximal element, and observe that \eqref{Tcolimit} can be written as the colimit of the diagram: \begin{equation} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep = tiny] &\mathcal Y(\sigma,p,q,\mathfrak t_0)\\ \smash{\displaystyle\operatornamewithlimits{colim}_{\begin{smallmatrix}\mathfrak t\in\mathcal T\cr\mathfrak t\prec\mathfrak t_0\end{smallmatrix}}}\mathcal Y(\sigma,p,q,\mathfrak t)\ar[hook]{ur}\ar{rd}\\ &\displaystyle\operatornamewithlimits{colim}_{\mathfrak t\in\mathcal T\setminus\mathfrak t_0}\mathcal Y(\sigma,p,q,\mathfrak t) \end{tikzcd} \end{equation} Let us show that the top arrow is injective. Write $\mathfrak t_0$ in the form \eqref{SdataA}--\eqref{SdataB}. Then we have: \begin{equation} \mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^{\leq\mathfrak t_0}=\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma|[j_{a_0}\ldots j_{a_1}],p_0,p_1)\times\cdots\times\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma|[j_{a_{m-1}}\ldots j_{a_m}],p_{m-1},p_m) \end{equation} Now we consider the $m$-cubical diagram: \begin{equation} \prod_{i=1}^m\left[\operatornamewithlimits{colim}_{\mathfrak s\in\partial\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma|[j_{a_{i-1}}\ldots j_{a_i}],p_{i-1},p_i)}\mathcal Y(\sigma|[j_{a_{i-1}}\ldots j_{a_i}],p_{i-1},p_i,\mathfrak s)\hookrightarrow\mathcal Y(\sigma|[j_{a_{i-1}}\ldots j_{a_i}],p_{i-1},p_i)\right] \end{equation} Now the top arrow of \eqref{colimitdiagramnice} is simply the map to the maximal vertex of this $m$-cube from the colimit over the $m$-cube minus the maximal vertex (this is where we use the fact that $\mathcal T$ is downward closed). This is injective for any cubical diagram of the form $\prod_{i=1}^m[A_i\hookrightarrow B_i]$ where each $A_i\hookrightarrow B_i$ is injective. Now that the top arrow in \eqref{colimitdiagramnice} is injective, the existence of the colimit is clear (first take the colimit of underlying sets and then the rest of the structure extends in an obvious way), and hence the colimit in \eqref{Tcolimit} exists.
nodes.name: Induction on $\#\mathcal T$
nodes.statement_short: Induction on the size of $\mathcal T$.

nodes.statement: If $\mathcal T=\varnothing$, existence is trivial.
nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement_short: Empty $\mathcal T$ is trivial.

nodes.statement: For $\mathcal T$ nonempty, let $\mathfrak t_0\in\mathcal T$ be any maximal element, and observe that \eqref{Tcolimit} can be written as the colimit of the diagram: \begin{equation} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep = tiny] &\mathcal Y(\sigma,p,q,\mathfrak t_0)\\ \smash{\displaystyle\operatornamewithlimits{colim}_{\begin{smallmatrix}\mathfrak t\in\mathcal T\cr\mathfrak t\prec\mathfrak t_0\end{smallmatrix}}}\mathcal Y(\sigma,p,q,\mathfrak t)\ar[hook]{ur}\ar{rd}\\ &\displaystyle\operatornamewithlimits{colim}_{\mathfrak t\in\mathcal T\setminus\mathfrak t_0}\mathcal Y(\sigma,p,q,\mathfrak t) \end{tikzcd} \end{equation}
nodes.name: Pushout decomposition
nodes.statement_short: Remove a maximal $\mathfrak t_0$: the colimit is a pushout.

nodes.statement: Let us show that the top arrow is injective. Write $\mathfrak t_0$ in the form \eqref{SdataA}--\eqref{SdataB}. Then we have: \begin{equation} \mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^{\leq\mathfrak t_0}=\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma|[j_{a_0}\ldots j_{a_1}],p_0,p_1)\times\cdots\times\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma|[j_{a_{m-1}}\ldots j_{a_m}],p_{m-1},p_m) \end{equation} Now we consider the $m$-cubical diagram: \begin{equation} \prod_{i=1}^m\left[\operatornamewithlimits{colim}_{\mathfrak s\in\partial\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma|[j_{a_{i-1}}\ldots j_{a_i}],p_{i-1},p_i)}\mathcal Y(\sigma|[j_{a_{i-1}}\ldots j_{a_i}],p_{i-1},p_i,\mathfrak s)\hookrightarrow\mathcal Y(\sigma|[j_{a_{i-1}}\ldots j_{a_i}],p_{i-1},p_i)\right] \end{equation} Now the top arrow of \eqref{colimitdiagramnice} is simply the map to the maximal vertex of this $m$-cube from the colimit over the $m$-cube minus the maximal vertex (this is where we use the fact that $\mathcal T$ is downward closed). This is injective for any cubical diagram of the form $\prod_{i=1}^m[A_i\hookrightarrow B_i]$ where each $A_i\hookrightarrow B_i$ is injective.
nodes.name: Top arrow is injective
nodes.statement_short: Injectivity via an $m$-cube of injections.

nodes.statement: Write $\mathfrak t_0$ in the form \eqref{SdataA}--\eqref{SdataB}. Then we have: \begin{equation} \mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^{\leq\mathfrak t_0}=\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma|[j_{a_0}\ldots j_{a_1}],p_0,p_1)\times\cdots\times\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma|[j_{a_{m-1}}\ldots j_{a_m}],p_{m-1},p_m) \end{equation}
nodes.name: Face poset decomposition
nodes.statement_short: Below $\mathfrak t_0$ the poset is a product.

nodes.statement: Now we consider the $m$-cubical diagram: \begin{equation} \prod_{i=1}^m\left[\operatornamewithlimits{colim}_{\mathfrak s\in\partial\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma|[j_{a_{i-1}}\ldots j_{a_i}],p_{i-1},p_i)}\mathcal Y(\sigma|[j_{a_{i-1}}\ldots j_{a_i}],p_{i-1},p_i,\mathfrak s)\hookrightarrow\mathcal Y(\sigma|[j_{a_{i-1}}\ldots j_{a_i}],p_{i-1},p_i)\right] \end{equation}
nodes.name: Cubical diagram
nodes.statement_short: Consider the cube of boundary inclusions.

nodes.statement: Now the top arrow of \eqref{colimitdiagramnice} is simply the map to the maximal vertex of this $m$-cube from the colimit over the $m$-cube minus the maximal vertex (this is where we use the fact that $\mathcal T$ is downward closed). This is injective for any cubical diagram of the form $\prod_{i=1}^m[A_i\hookrightarrow B_i]$ where each $A_i\hookrightarrow B_i$ is injective.
nodes.name: Cube injectivity
nodes.statement_short: The top arrow is the map from the punctured cube colimit, injective for cubes of injections.

nodes.statement: Now that the top arrow in \eqref{colimitdiagramnice} is injective, the existence of the colimit is clear (first take the colimit of underlying sets and then the rest of the structure extends in an obvious way), and hence the colimit in \eqref{Tcolimit} exists.
nodes.name: Colimit exists
nodes.statement_short: With injective top arrow, the pushout exists.

nodes.statement: This reasoning applies equally well to $\mathcal Y_{S^1}$ (including $(ES^1)_\mathcal Y\to(BS^1)_\mathcal Y$).
nodes.name: Equivariant case
nodes.statement_short: Same for $\mathcal Y_{S^1}$.

nodes.statement: Now that we have shown that the colimits on the left hand side of \eqref{colimitYone}--\eqref{colimitYtwo} exist, it remains to define $\mathcal Y(\sigma,p,q)$ and $\mathcal Y_{S^1}(\sigma,p,q)$.
nodes.name: Remaining definitions
nodes.statement_short: It remains to define $\mathcal Y(\sigma,p,q)$ and $\mathcal Y_{S^1}(\sigma,p,q)$.

nodes.statement: We observed earlier that any $S^1$-MF-set injects into a saturated $S^1$-MF-set. Let $\mathcal Y_{S^1}(\sigma,p,q)$ be any saturated $S^1$-MF-set with an injection \eqref{colimitYtwo}. Note that with this definition, the product/face maps with target $\mathcal Y_{S^1}(\sigma,p,q)$ are obvious, as is their compatibility.
nodes.name: Define $\mathcal Y_{S^1}(\sigma,p,q)$
nodes.statement_short: Take a saturated $S^1$-MF-set containing the boundary colimit.

nodes.statement: To define $\mathcal Y(\sigma,p,q)$, consider the following diagram: \begin{equation} \begin{tikzcd} \displaystyle\operatornamewithlimits{colim}_{\mathfrak s\in\partial\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)}\mathcal Y(\sigma,p,q,\mathfrak s)\\ \displaystyle\operatornamewithlimits{colim}_{\mathfrak s\in\partial\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)}\mathcal Y_{S^1}(\sigma,p,q,\mathfrak s)\ar{u}\ar[hook]{r}&\mathcal Y_{S^1}(\sigma,p,q) \end{tikzcd} \end{equation} The lower colimit is in the category of $S^1$-MF-sets. It is clear from the inductive proof of its existence that this particular colimit commutes with the forgetful functor to MF-sets. Hence we may equally well think of this colimit as taking place in the category of MF-sets, and with this perspective the definition of the vertical map is clear. Now since the horizontal map is injective, the colimit of this diagram (in the category of MF-sets) clearly exists (first take the colimit in sets and then the rest of the structure is obvious). We pick any saturated MF-set into which the colimit of \eqref{biggluingcolimit} embeds, and we call this saturated MF-set $\mathcal Y(\sigma,p,q)$. Via the embedding of the upper colimit into $\mathcal Y(\sigma,p,q)$, it is tautological that the face/product maps with target $\mathcal Y(\sigma,p,q)$ exist and are compatible. The map $\mathcal Y_{S^1}(\sigma,p,q)\to\mathcal Y(\sigma,p,q)$ is similarly tautological, as is the fact that it is compatible with the product/face maps.
nodes.name: Define $\mathcal Y(\sigma,p,q)$
nodes.statement_short: Embed the pushout of the boundary colimit and $\mathcal Y_{S^1}(\sigma,p,q)$ into a saturated MF-set.

nodes.statement: We show that our model of chains (generated by diagrams \eqref{bigcomplex}) calculates singular homology as follows. Let us abbreviate $\mathcal Y=\mathcal Y(\sigma,p,q)$. Our complex generated by maps \eqref{bigcomplex} is in fact a double complex with bigrading $p=\sum_\alpha i_\alpha$ and $q=\dim M_i$. Now let us consider the associated spectral sequence. We calculate the $E^1_{p,q}$ term as follows. By definition $E^1_{p,q}$ is simply the homology of the complex with only the differentials decreasing $q$. Clearly this breaks up as a direct sum over tuples $\{i_\alpha\in\mathbb Z_{\geq 0}\}$. For a given tuple $\{i_\alpha\in\mathbb Z_{\geq 0}\}$, we must calculate the homology of the complex:
nodes.name: Spectral sequence of the double complex
nodes.statement_short: Bigrade by $\sum i_\alpha$ and $\dim M_i$; compute $E^1$ tuple by tuple.
nodes.section: 8.7.3 Augmented virtual cochain complexes from $\mathsf{F}$-module MF-sets and $S^1$-MF-sets

nodes.statement: We claim that this is the same as the homology of the complex: \begin{equation} \bigoplus_{\begin{smallmatrix}i\in\mathcal Y\cr M_i\to X\end{smallmatrix}}\mathbb Z \end{equation} There is a clearly a map $\eqref{withoutDelta}\to\eqref{withDelta}$ (precompose with the projection $M_i\times\prod_\alpha\Delta^{i_\alpha}\to M_i$), and picking a point $x\in\prod_\alpha\Delta^{i_\alpha}$ gives a map in the opposite direction. The composition $\eqref{withoutDelta}\to\eqref{withDelta}\to\eqref{withoutDelta}$ is clearly the identity. The other composition is chain homotopic to the identity by the following argument. Since $\mathcal Y$ is saturated, we can choose a map $I:\mathcal Y\to\mathcal Y$ and isomorphisms $(M_{I(i)},\mathcal S_{I(i)})\xrightarrow\sim(M_i\times[0,1],\mathcal S_i\times\mathcal S)$ compatible with the face identifications, where $([0,1],\mathcal S)$ is the PL manifold $[0,1]$ with strata $\{\{0\},\{1\},(0,1)\}$, and $M_i\times\{0\}$, $M_i\times\{1\}$ have the obvious face identifications with $M_i$ (construct $I$ and the isomorphisms by induction on dimension). Using this coherent choice of ``cylinder objects'', it is easy to define a chain homotopy between the identity map and the composition $\eqref{withDelta}\to\eqref{withoutDelta}\to\eqref{withDelta}$ (using the fact that $\prod_\alpha\Delta^{i_\alpha}$ is contractible). It follows that the canonical map $\eqref{withoutDelta}\to\eqref{withDelta}$ is a quasi-isomorphism. By Lemma \ref{saturatedcalculatesH}, the complex $\eqref{withoutDelta}$ calculates singular homology.
nodes.name: Drop the simplex factors
nodes.statement_short: The complexes with and without simplex factors are quasi-isomorphic via cylinder objects; Lemma saturatedcalculatesH.
nodes.section: 8.7.3 Augmented virtual cochain complexes from $\mathsf{F}$-module MF-sets and $S^1$-MF-sets

nodes.statement: Hence we conclude that the $E^1$ term is: \begin{equation} E^1_{p,q}=\bigoplus_{\sum_\alpha i_\alpha=p}H_q(X) \end{equation} The differentials on the $E^1$ page are easy to understand (essentially we have $H_q(X)$ tensored with the restricted tensor product $\bigotimes_\alpha C_\bullet(\mathrm{pt})$). We conclude that: \begin{equation} E^2_{p,q}=\begin{cases}H_q(X)&p=0\cr 0&p\ne 0\end{cases} \end{equation} Hence there are no further differentials and we are done.
nodes.name: Degeneration
nodes.statement_short: $E^1$ is a sum of $H_q(X)$; $E^2$ is concentrated in $p=0$.
nodes.section: 8.7.3 Augmented virtual cochain complexes from $\mathsf{F}$-module MF-sets and $S^1$-MF-sets

nodes.statement: We now use a similar argument to show that our model of $S^1$-equivariant chains calculates $S^1$-equivariant singular homology. Let us abbreviate $\mathcal Y_{S^1}=\mathcal Y_{S^1}(\sigma,p,q)$. Our complex generated by maps \eqref{bigcomplexSS} is a double complex as before, and we consider the associated spectral sequence. As before, $E^1_{p,q}$ splits up as a direct sum over tuples $\{i_\alpha\in\mathbb Z_{\geq 0}\}$. For a given tuple $\{i_\alpha\in\mathbb Z_{\geq 0}\}$, the corresponding direct summand is the homology of the complex:
nodes.name: Equivariant spectral sequence
nodes.statement_short: Same double complex spectral sequence for the equivariant model.
nodes.section: 8.7.3 Augmented virtual cochain complexes from $\mathsf{F}$-module MF-sets and $S^1$-MF-sets

nodes.statement: As in the non-equivariant case, this is canonically quasi-isomorphic to: \begin{equation} \bigoplus_{\begin{smallmatrix}&i\in\mathcal Y_{S^1}\cr M_i&\to&X\times(ES^1)_{\mathcal Y_{S^1}}\cr\downarrow&&\downarrow\cr M_i&\to&(ES^1)_{\mathcal Y_{S^1}}\end{smallmatrix}}\mathbb Z \end{equation} Thus by Lemma \ref{saturatedcalculatesHSS} the $E^1$ term is: \begin{equation} E^1_{p,q}=\bigoplus_{\sum_\alpha i_\alpha=p}H_q^{S^1}(X) \end{equation}
nodes.name: Equivariant $E^1$ page
nodes.statement_short: Drop simplex factors; Lemma saturatedcalculatesHSS identifies $E^1$.
nodes.section: 8.7.3 Augmented virtual cochain complexes from $\mathsf{F}$-module MF-sets and $S^1$-MF-sets

nodes.statement: The differentials on the $E^1$ page are as before, and thus: \begin{equation} E^2_{p,q}=\begin{cases}H_q^{S^1}(X)&p=0\cr 0&p\ne 0\end{cases} \end{equation} so we are done.
nodes.name: Degeneration
nodes.statement_short: $E^2$ concentrated in $p=0$.
nodes.section: 8.7.3 Augmented virtual cochain complexes from $\mathsf{F}$-module MF-sets and $S^1$-MF-sets

nodes.statement: \textbf{Part I.}\ We begin by reducing to a situation in which the partition \eqref{partitionsfreefixedII} is extended to every thickened moduli space, so that the product/face maps on thickened moduli spaces also take the form \eqref{PFfirst}--\eqref{PFlast}. Precisely, consider a new implicit atlas $\tilde\mathcal A$ (on the same index set $\mathcal A$) in which the thickened moduli spaces are: \begin{equation} \mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)_{\tilde I}^{\leq\mathfrak s}:=[\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)_I^{\leq\mathfrak s}\setminus\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^1]\sqcup[\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)_I^{\leq\mathfrak s}\setminus\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^0] \end{equation} Now these thickened moduli spaces are by definition equipped with a partition $\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)_{\tilde I}^{\leq\mathfrak s}=(\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)_{\tilde I}^{\leq\mathfrak s})^0\sqcup(\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)_{\tilde I}^{\leq\mathfrak s})^1$ (namely the partition \eqref{newatlastrickSS}), and the natural product/face maps for the implicit atlas $\tilde\mathcal A$ take the form \eqref{PFfirst}--\eqref{PFlast}. The thickened moduli spaces of $\tilde\mathcal A$ are equipped with natural maps to those of $\mathcal A$ (compatibile with the product/face maps); these maps are not open embeddings, but nevertheless the proof of Lemma \ref{homologyopenreduction} applies to give a canonical isomorphism $\mathbb H(\mathcal X)_\mathcal A=\mathbb H(\mathcal X)_{\tilde\mathcal A}$. Thus it suffices to produce an isomorphism $\mathbb H(\mathcal X)_{\tilde\mathcal A}=\mathbb H(\mathcal X^0)_{\tilde\mathcal A^0}$, where $\tilde\mathcal A^0$ is the implicit atlas on $\mathcal X^0$ with thickened moduli spaces $(\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)_{\tilde I}^{\leq\mathfrak s})^0$. From now on, we will work exclusively with the atlas $\tilde\mathcal A$, which we now rather abusively rename as $\mathcal A$.
nodes.name: Part I: partitioned atlas
nodes.statement_short: Replace $\mathcal A$ by an atlas whose thickenings are partitioned compatibly with products/faces.

nodes.statement: \textbf{Part II.}\ We will define an isomorphism $\mathbb H(\mathcal X)_\mathcal A=\mathbb H(\mathcal X^0)_{\mathcal A^0}$, where $\mathcal A^0$ is the implicit atlas on $\mathcal X^0$ with thickened moduli spaces $(\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)_I^{\leq\mathfrak s})^0$. Note that since we have coherent orientations $\omega$ and $S^1$ is connected, it follows that all the flow spaces are locally $S^1$-orientable (see Remark \ref{orientedthenSSoriented}), so we may use the $S^1$-localization machinery freely. Let $\tilde Z_\bullet\to Z_\bullet$ denote the resolution (as in \S\ref{floerhomologyfromMFsets}) associated to $\mathcal X/Z_\bullet$ with the implicit atlas $\mathcal A$, and let $\tilde Z_\bullet^0\to Z_\bullet$ denote the resolution associated to $\mathcal X^0/Z_\bullet$ with the implicit atlas $\mathcal A^0$. We will construct a diagram of the following shape: \begin{equation} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep = large, column sep = tiny] \tilde Z_\bullet\ar{drr}&\tilde Z_\bullet^a\ar{l}\ar{r}\ar{dr}&\tilde Z_\bullet^b\ar{d}&\tilde Z_\bullet^c\ar{l}\ar{r}\ar{dl}&\tilde Z_\bullet^0\ar{dll}\\ &&Z_\bullet \end{tikzcd} \end{equation} and natural diagrams $\widetilde\mathbb H,\widetilde\mathbb H^a,\widetilde\mathbb H^b,\widetilde\mathbb H^c,\widetilde\mathbb H^0$ from $\tilde Z_\bullet,\tilde Z_\bullet^a,\tilde Z_\bullet^b,\tilde Z_\bullet^c,\tilde Z_\bullet^0$ to $\mathsf{N}_{\mathsf{dg}}(\mathsf{Ch}_{R[[H]]})$ (respectively). We will also construct natural isomorphisms relating these and their pullbacks under the horizontal maps in \eqref{differentresolutions}. Finally, we will show that each of the vertical maps \eqref{differentresolutions} satisfies the conclusions of Propositions \ref{trivialKanfibration} and \ref{degenerateID}. The desired result follows easily from these statements; let us now start on the proof. We may consider $\mathcal A(\sigma,p,q)$ as a system of implicit atlases on $\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^0$ and on $\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^1$ separately. Now consider the following maps (where the complexes on the left are defined analogously to those on the right as in \S\ref{SSaugmentedsec}): \begin{align} C^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(\partial\mathcal X^0,\mathcal A)^+&\oplus C^\bullet_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(\partial\mathcal X^1,\mathcal A)^+&&\to C^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(\partial\mathcal X;\mathcal A)^+\\ C^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(\mathcal X^0\operatorname{rel}\partial,\mathcal A)^+&\oplus C^\bullet_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(\mathcal X^1\operatorname{rel}\partial,\mathcal A)^+&&\to C^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(\mathcal X\operatorname{rel}\partial;\mathcal A)^+ \end{align} We give $C^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(\mathcal X^0\operatorname{rel}\partial,\mathcal A)^+\oplus C^\bullet_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(\mathcal X^1\operatorname{rel}\partial,\mathcal A)^+$ the structure of an $\mathsf{F}$-module with product/face maps: \begin{align} C^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(\mathcal X^0\operatorname{rel}\partial;\mathcal A)^+(\cdots)\otimes C^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(\mathcal X^0\operatorname{rel}\partial;\mathcal A)^+(\cdots)&\to C^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(\partial\mathcal X^0;\mathcal A)^+(\cdots)\\ C^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(\mathcal X^0\operatorname{rel}\partial;\mathcal A)^+(\cdots)\otimes C^\bullet_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(\mathcal X^1\operatorname{rel}\partial;\mathcal A)^+(\cdots)&\to C^\bullet_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(\partial\mathcal X^1;\mathcal A)^+(\cdots)\\ C^\bullet_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(\mathcal X^1\operatorname{rel}\partial;\mathcal A)^+(\cdots)\otimes C^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(\mathcal X^0\operatorname{rel}\partial;\mathcal A)^+(\cdots)&\to C^\bullet_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(\partial\mathcal X^1;\mathcal A)^+(\cdots)\\ C^\bullet_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(\mathcal X^1\operatorname{rel}\partial;\mathcal A)^+(\cdots)\otimes C^\bullet_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(\mathcal X^1\operatorname{rel}\partial;\mathcal A)^+(\cdots)&\to C^\bullet_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(\partial\mathcal X^1;\mathcal A)^+(\cdots)\\ C^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(\mathcal X^0\operatorname{rel}\partial;\mathcal A)^+(\cdots)&\to C^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(\partial\mathcal X^0;\mathcal A)^+(\cdots)\\ C^\bullet_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(\mathcal X^1\operatorname{rel}\partial;\mathcal A)^+(\cdots)&\to C^\bullet_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(\partial\mathcal X^1;\mathcal A)^+(\cdots) \end{align} just as in Definition \ref{Cproductface} (and using the chain models from \S\ref{SSaugmentedsec}). These are compatible with \eqref{partialSSpushforwardbigcomplex}--\eqref{relpartialSSpushforwardbigcomplex} and \eqref{Ccomposition}--\eqref{Csimplexextension}. Next, we consider $C_\bullet(E;\mathcal A)^+\oplus C_{\bullet-1}^{S^1}(E;\mathcal A)^+$ (as in \S\ref{SSaugmentedsec}). Now, there are \emph{two} natural maps: \begin{equation} \begin{tikzcd} C_\bullet(E;\mathcal A)^+\oplus C_{\bullet-1}^{S^1}(E;\mathcal A)^+\ar[yshift=0.5ex]{r}{\operatorname{id}\oplus{\pi^!}}\ar[yshift=-0.5ex]{r}[swap]{\operatorname{id}\oplus 0}&C_\bullet(E;\mathcal A)^+ \end{tikzcd} \end{equation} We give $C_\bullet(E;\mathcal A)^+\oplus C_{\bullet-1}^{S^1}(E;\mathcal A)^+$ the structure of an $\mathsf{F}$-module with product/face maps of the shape \eqref{CSSproductfacesplitfirst}--\eqref{CSSproductfacesplitlast} just as in Definition \ref{CEcomplexaugmented}. Then both maps \eqref{CESSpushforward} are maps of $\mathsf{F}$-modules. There is also a pushforward map: \begin{equation*} C^{\operatorname{vdim}\mathcal X+\bullet}_\mathrm{vir}(\mathcal X^0\operatorname{rel}\partial,\mathcal A)^+\oplus C^{\operatorname{vdim}\mathcal X+\bullet}_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(\mathcal X^1\operatorname{rel}\partial,\mathcal A)^+\to C_{-\bullet}(E;\mathcal A)^+\oplus C_{-\bullet-1}^{S^1}(E;\mathcal A)^+ \end{equation*} which is a map of $\mathsf{F}$-modules. Now let us define $\tilde Z_\bullet^a$, $\tilde Z_\bullet^b$, and $\tilde Z_\bullet^c$. We modify the definition of $\tilde Z_\bullet\to Z_\bullet$ (i.e.\ Definition \ref{Lambdadef} as amended in \S\ref{floerhomologyfromMFsets}) as follows. For $\tilde Z_\bullet^a=\tilde Z_\bullet^c$ we replace Definition \ref{Lambdadef}(\ref{lambdachoice},\ref{liftschoice}) with (\ref{lambdachoiceSS},\ref{liftschoiceSS}) below, and for $\tilde Z_\bullet^b$ we replace Definition \ref{Lambdadef}(\ref{lambdachoice},\ref{liftschoice},\ref{augmentationschoice}) with (\ref{lambdachoiceSS},\ref{liftschoiceSS},\ref{augmentationschoiceSS}) below. \begin{rlist} \item An $H$-invariant system of chains: \begin{equation*} \lambda=\lambda^0\oplus\lambda^1\in C^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(\mathcal X^0\operatorname{rel}\partial,\mathcal B)^+\oplus C^\bullet_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(\mathcal X^1\operatorname{rel}\partial,\mathcal B)^+ \end{equation*} (degree $0$ and supported inside $\operatorname{supp}\mathcal X$) with the following property. Note that $(\mu,\lambda)$ is a cycle in the mapping cone: \begin{equation*} \begin{matrix} C^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(\partial f^\ast\mathcal X^0;\mathcal B)^+\cr\oplus\cr C^\bullet_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(\partial f^\ast\mathcal X^1;\mathcal B)^+ \end{matrix} \longrightarrow \begin{matrix} C^\bullet_{\mathrm{vir}}(f^\ast\mathcal X^0\operatorname{rel}\partial;\mathcal B)^+\cr\oplus\cr C^\bullet_{S^1,\mathrm{vir}}(f^\ast\mathcal X^1\operatorname{rel}\partial;\mathcal B)^+ \end{matrix} \end{equation*} whose homology is identified with $\check H^\bullet(f^\ast\mathcal X^0;\mathfrak o_{f^\ast\mathcal X^0})\oplus\check H^\bullet((f^\ast\mathcal X^1)/S^1;\pi_\ast\mathfrak o_{f^\ast\mathcal X^1})$, which in degree zero simply equals $\check H^0(f^\ast\mathcal X;\mathfrak o_{f^\ast\mathcal X})$. We require that the homology class of $(\mu,\lambda)$ equal $f^\ast\omega\in\check H^0(f^\ast\mathcal X;\mathfrak o_{f^\ast\mathcal X})$. \item An $H$-invariant system of chains $\tilde\lambda$ for $Q[C_\bullet(E;\mathcal A)^+\oplus C_{\bullet-1}^{S^1}(E;\mathcal A)^+]$ (degree $\operatorname{gr}(q)-\operatorname{gr}(p)+\dim\sigma-1$ and supported inside $\operatorname{supp}\mathcal X$) whose image in $C_\bullet(E;\mathcal A)^+\oplus C_{\bullet-1}^{S^1}(E;\mathcal A)^+$ coincides with the image of $\lambda$. \item An $H$-invariant map of $\mathsf{F}$-modules $[[E]]:Q[C_\bullet(E;\mathcal A)^+_\mathbb Z\oplus C_{\bullet-1}^{S^1}(E;\mathcal A)^+_\mathbb Z]\to\mathbb Z$ which sends the fundamental class in $H_\bullet(E;\mathcal A)^+_\mathbb Z$ to $1$ and is zero on $H_{\bullet-1}^{S^1}(E;\mathcal A)^+_\mathbb Z$. \end{rlist} The maps $\tilde Z_\bullet\leftarrow\tilde Z_\bullet^a\to\tilde Z_\bullet^b\leftarrow\tilde Z_\bullet^c\to\tilde Z_\bullet^0$ are defined as follows: \begin{equation} \begin{tikzcd} \tilde Z_\bullet&\ar{l}\tilde Z_\bullet^a\ar{r}&\tilde Z_\bullet^b&\ar{l}\tilde Z_\bullet^c\ar{r}&\tilde Z_\bullet^0\cr \lambda&\ar[mapsto]{l}[swap]{\eqref{relpartialSSpushforwardbigcomplex}}\lambda&&\lambda\ar[mapsto]{r}{\lambda=\lambda^0\oplus\lambda^1}&\lambda^0\cr \tilde\lambda&\ar[mapsto]{l}[swap]{Q[\operatorname{id}\oplus\pi^!]}\tilde\lambda&&\tilde\lambda\ar[mapsto]{r}{Q[\operatorname{id}\oplus 0]}&\tilde\lambda^0\cr &{}[[E]]\ar[mapsto]{r}{\circ Q[\operatorname{id}\oplus\pi^!]}&{}[[E]]&\ar[mapsto]{l}[swap]{\circ Q[\operatorname{id}\oplus 0]}\null[[E]] \end{tikzcd} \end{equation} Note that Lemma \ref{trivialactiongysin} shows that the map $\tilde Z^a\to\tilde Z^b$ above produces an $[[E]]$ satisfying (\ref{augmentationschoiceSS}). Now $\widetilde\mathbb H,\widetilde\mathbb H^a,\widetilde\mathbb H^b,\widetilde\mathbb H^c,\widetilde\mathbb H^0$ are defined via the matrix coefficients $c_{\sigma,p,q}$ defined as follows: \begin{align*} \text{for $\widetilde\mathbb H$:}\quad c_{\sigma,p,q}&:=([[E]]_{\sigma,p,q}\otimes\operatorname{id}_R)(\tilde\lambda_{\sigma,p,q})\\ \text{for $\widetilde\mathbb H^a$:}\quad c_{\sigma,p,q}&:=([[E]]_{\sigma,p,q}\otimes\operatorname{id}_R)(\operatorname{id}\oplus\pi^!)(\tilde\lambda_{\sigma,p,q})\\ \text{for $\widetilde\mathbb H^b$:}\quad c_{\sigma,p,q}&:=([[E]]_{\sigma,p,q}\otimes\operatorname{id}_R)(\tilde\lambda_{\sigma,p,q})\\ \text{for $\widetilde\mathbb H^c$:}\quad c_{\sigma,p,q}&:=([[E]]_{\sigma,p,q}\otimes\operatorname{id}_R)(\operatorname{id}\oplus 0)(\tilde\lambda_{\sigma,p,q})\\ \text{for $\widetilde\mathbb H^0$:}\quad c_{\sigma,p,q}&:=([[E]]_{\sigma,p,q}\otimes\operatorname{id}_R)(\tilde\lambda_{\sigma,p,q}) \end{align*} These matrix coefficients give rise to diagrams in $\mathsf{N}_{\mathsf{dg}}(\mathsf{Ch}_{R[[H]]})$ since $[[E]]$ is a map of $\mathsf{F}$-modules. The isomorphisms between these diagrams and their pullbacks under the maps \eqref{defofZabcmaps} are evident. It now remains to show that each of the maps $\tilde Z_\bullet^a,\tilde Z_\bullet^b,\tilde Z_\bullet^c\to\tilde Z_\bullet$ satisfies the conclusions of Propositions \ref{trivialKanfibration} and \ref{degenerateID}. The proof of Proposition \ref{trivialKanfibration} applies to $\tilde Z_\bullet^a,\tilde Z_\bullet^b,\tilde Z_\bullet^c\to\tilde Z_\bullet$ as written (for $\tilde Z_\bullet^b$, the extension of $[[E]]$ step uses the fact that $H_\bullet(E;\mathcal A)\oplus H_{\bullet-1}^{S^1}(E;\mathcal A)$ is concentrated in degrees $\geq 0$ so that Lemma \ref{Hzeroofcofibrantcolimit} still applies). The proof of Proposition \ref{degenerateID} also applies to $\tilde Z_\bullet^a,\tilde Z_\bullet^b,\tilde Z_\bullet^c\to\tilde Z_\bullet$ as written. Now the uniqueness of descent from Lemma \ref{descentofdiagram} shows that there are canonical isomorphisms of the descents $\mathbb H=\mathbb H^a=\mathbb H^b=\mathbb H^c=\mathbb H^0$.
nodes.name: Part II: zigzag of resolutions
nodes.statement_short: Construct the zigzag of resolutions and diagrams and conclude by uniqueness of descent.

nodes.name: Modified resolutions
nodes.statement_short: Define $\tilde Z^a,\tilde Z^b,\tilde Z^c$ by modified choices of $\lambda$, lifts, augmentations.

nodes.statement: The maps $\tilde Z_\bullet\leftarrow\tilde Z_\bullet^a\to\tilde Z_\bullet^b\leftarrow\tilde Z_\bullet^c\to\tilde Z_\bullet^0$ are defined as follows: \begin{equation} \begin{tikzcd} \tilde Z_\bullet&\ar{l}\tilde Z_\bullet^a\ar{r}&\tilde Z_\bullet^b&\ar{l}\tilde Z_\bullet^c\ar{r}&\tilde Z_\bullet^0\cr \lambda&\ar[mapsto]{l}[swap]{\eqref{relpartialSSpushforwardbigcomplex}}\lambda&&\lambda\ar[mapsto]{r}{\lambda=\lambda^0\oplus\lambda^1}&\lambda^0\cr \tilde\lambda&\ar[mapsto]{l}[swap]{Q[\operatorname{id}\oplus\pi^!]}\tilde\lambda&&\tilde\lambda\ar[mapsto]{r}{Q[\operatorname{id}\oplus 0]}&\tilde\lambda^0\cr &{}[[E]]\ar[mapsto]{r}{\circ Q[\operatorname{id}\oplus\pi^!]}&{}[[E]]&\ar[mapsto]{l}[swap]{\circ Q[\operatorname{id}\oplus 0]}\null[[E]] \end{tikzcd} \end{equation} Note that Lemma \ref{trivialactiongysin} shows that the map $\tilde Z^a\to\tilde Z^b$ above produces an $[[E]]$ satisfying (\ref{augmentationschoiceSS}).
nodes.name: Zigzag maps
nodes.statement_short: Define the zigzag maps; Lemma trivialactiongysin ensures the augmentation condition.

nodes.statement: Now $\widetilde\mathbb H,\widetilde\mathbb H^a,\widetilde\mathbb H^b,\widetilde\mathbb H^c,\widetilde\mathbb H^0$ are defined via the matrix coefficients $c_{\sigma,p,q}$ defined as follows: \begin{align*} \text{for $\widetilde\mathbb H$:}\quad c_{\sigma,p,q}&:=([[E]]_{\sigma,p,q}\otimes\operatorname{id}_R)(\tilde\lambda_{\sigma,p,q})\\ \text{for $\widetilde\mathbb H^a$:}\quad c_{\sigma,p,q}&:=([[E]]_{\sigma,p,q}\otimes\operatorname{id}_R)(\operatorname{id}\oplus\pi^!)(\tilde\lambda_{\sigma,p,q})\\ \text{for $\widetilde\mathbb H^b$:}\quad c_{\sigma,p,q}&:=([[E]]_{\sigma,p,q}\otimes\operatorname{id}_R)(\tilde\lambda_{\sigma,p,q})\\ \text{for $\widetilde\mathbb H^c$:}\quad c_{\sigma,p,q}&:=([[E]]_{\sigma,p,q}\otimes\operatorname{id}_R)(\operatorname{id}\oplus 0)(\tilde\lambda_{\sigma,p,q})\\ \text{for $\widetilde\mathbb H^0$:}\quad c_{\sigma,p,q}&:=([[E]]_{\sigma,p,q}\otimes\operatorname{id}_R)(\tilde\lambda_{\sigma,p,q}) \end{align*} These matrix coefficients give rise to diagrams in $\mathsf{N}_{\mathsf{dg}}(\mathsf{Ch}_{R[[H]]})$ since $[[E]]$ is a map of $\mathsf{F}$-modules. The isomorphisms between these diagrams and their pullbacks under the maps \eqref{defofZabcmaps} are evident.
nodes.name: Diagrams from matrix coefficients
nodes.statement_short: Define the diagrams via matrix coefficients; pullback isomorphisms are evident.

nodes.statement: It now remains to show that each of the maps $\tilde Z_\bullet^a,\tilde Z_\bullet^b,\tilde Z_\bullet^c\to\tilde Z_\bullet$ satisfies the conclusions of Propositions \ref{trivialKanfibration} and \ref{degenerateID}. The proof of Proposition \ref{trivialKanfibration} applies to $\tilde Z_\bullet^a,\tilde Z_\bullet^b,\tilde Z_\bullet^c\to\tilde Z_\bullet$ as written (for $\tilde Z_\bullet^b$, the extension of $[[E]]$ step uses the fact that $H_\bullet(E;\mathcal A)\oplus H_{\bullet-1}^{S^1}(E;\mathcal A)$ is concentrated in degrees $\geq 0$ so that Lemma \ref{Hzeroofcofibrantcolimit} still applies). The proof of Proposition \ref{degenerateID} also applies to $\tilde Z_\bullet^a,\tilde Z_\bullet^b,\tilde Z_\bullet^c\to\tilde Z_\bullet$ as written. Now the uniqueness of descent from Lemma \ref{descentofdiagram} shows that there are canonical isomorphisms of the descents $\mathbb H=\mathbb H^a=\mathbb H^b=\mathbb H^c=\mathbb H^0$.
nodes.name: Trivial Kan fibrations and descent
nodes.statement_short: Proofs of Propositions trivialKanfibration and degenerateID apply; uniqueness of descent gives the isomorphisms.

nodes.statement: Let us observe that if $C_0\subseteq C$ is any unstable irreducible component, we must have $u:C_0\to X$ is nonconstant. Hence since $u$ is $J$-holomorphic, it follows that there is a point on $C_0$ (which is not a node or marked point) where $du$ is injective.
nodes.name: Injectivity point on unstable component
nodes.statement_short: Unstable components are nonconstant, so du is injective somewhere.

nodes.statement: It follows using Lemma \ref{sortofsard} that there exists $D\subseteq X$ such that $u\pitchfork D$ and adding $u^{-1}(D)$ to $C$ as marked points makes $C$ stable.
nodes.name: Apply Sard-type lemma
nodes.statement_short: Conclude via the Sard-type divisor lemma.

nodes.statement: Fix a point in $\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}^\beta(X)$ (that is, a curve $u:C\to X$). We will construct $\alpha\in A^\mathrm{GW}$ so that this point is contained in $\psi_{\varnothing\{\alpha\}}((s_\alpha|\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}^\beta(X)_{\{\alpha\}}^\mathrm{reg})^{-1}(0))$.
nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement_short: Fix a stable map; aim to construct a single covering thickening datum.

nodes.statement: First, pick $D_\alpha\subseteq X$ satisfying the conclusion of Lemma \ref{stabilizationlemma}.
nodes.name: Choose stabilizing divisor
nodes.statement_short: Pick D_alpha by domain stabilization.

nodes.statement: Now let $r_\alpha=\#u^{-1}(D_\alpha)$. Adding $u^{-1}(D_\alpha)$ as extra marked points to $C$ gives a point in $\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n+r_\alpha}/S_{r_\alpha}$, and we pick some local orbifold chart $\overline{\mathcal M}_\alpha/\Gamma_\alpha\to\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n+r_\alpha}/S_{r_\alpha}$ covering this point.
nodes.name: Choose orbifold chart
nodes.statement_short: Set r_alpha and choose a local orbifold chart of the stabilized curve.

nodes.statement: Now let us consider the linearized $\bar\partial$ operator: \begin{equation} D\bar\partial(u,\cdot):C^\infty(C,u^\ast TX)\to C^\infty(\tilde C,\Omega^{0,1}_{\tilde C}\otimes_\mathbb C u^\ast TX) \end{equation} ($\tilde C$ being the normalization of $C$) where $C^\infty(C,u^\ast TX)\subseteq C^\infty(\tilde C,u^\ast TX)$ is the subspace of functions descending continuously to $C$. If $(k,p)\in\mathbb Z_{\geq 1}\times(1,\infty)$ with $kp>2$, then we get a corresponding $D\bar\partial(u,\cdot)$ map $W^{k,p}\to W^{k-1,p}$ (the restriction on $(k,p)$ comes from the need to define $W^{k,p}(C,u^\ast TX)\subseteq W^{k,p}(\tilde C,u^\ast TX)$). This operator is Fredholm; in particular its cokernel is finite-dimensional.
nodes.name: Linearized operator is Fredholm
nodes.statement_short: Consider the linearized dbar-operator, Fredholm with finite-dimensional cokernel.

nodes.statement: Suppose we have a finite-dimensional vector space $E_0$ equipped with a linear map: \begin{equation} \tilde\lambda_0:E_0\to C^\infty(\tilde C,\Omega^{0,1}_{\tilde C}\otimes_\mathbb C u^\ast TX) \end{equation} supported away from (the inverse image in $\tilde C$ of) the nodes and marked points of $C$. Then the following conditions are equivalent (exercise using elliptic regularity): \begin{rlist} \item\eqref{lambdazero} is surjective onto the cokernel of $D\bar\partial(u,\cdot):C^\infty\to C^\infty$. \item\eqref{lambdazero} is surjective onto the cokernel of $D\bar\partial(u,\cdot):W^{k,p}\to W^{k-1,p}$ for some $(k,p)$. \item\eqref{lambdazero} is surjective onto the cokernel of $D\bar\partial(u,\cdot):W^{k,p}\to W^{k-1,p}$ for all $(k,p)$. \end{rlist} There exists such a pair $E_0$ and $\tilde\lambda_0$ satisfying these conditions since we may choose $k=1$ and $p>2$ and then remember that $C^\infty$ functions supported away from the nodes and marked points are dense in $W^{0,p}=L^p$.
nodes.name: Obstruction space covering cokernel
nodes.statement_short: An E_0 with lambda_0 surjecting onto the cokernel exists by density of smooth compactly supported sections.

nodes.statement: Now pick any isomorphism to a fiber $\phi_\alpha:C\to\overline{\mathcal C}_\alpha$ and extend $\tilde\lambda_0$ to a map $\lambda_0:E_0\to C^\infty(\overline{\mathcal C}_\alpha\times X,\Omega^{0,1}_{\overline{\mathcal C}_\alpha/\overline{\mathcal M}_\alpha}\otimes_\mathbb C TX)$ supported away from the nodes and marked points of the fibers. Define $E_\alpha=E_0[\Gamma]$ and define $\lambda_\alpha:E_\alpha\to C^\infty(\overline{\mathcal C}_\alpha\times X,\Omega^{0,1}_{\overline{\mathcal C}_\alpha/\overline{\mathcal M}_\alpha}\otimes_\mathbb C TX)$ by $\Gamma_\alpha$-linear extension from $\lambda_0$. It is now clear by definition that $u:C\to X$ is covered by $\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}^\beta(X)_{\{\alpha\}}^\mathrm{reg}$, where $\alpha\in A^\mathrm{GW}$ is the element just constructed.
nodes.name: Assemble thickening datum
nodes.statement_short: Extend lambda_0 equivariantly to get alpha whose regular locus covers the point.

nodes.statement: Let $J_0$ and $J_1$ be any two smooth $\omega$-tame almost complex structures on $X$. We denote by $\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}^\beta(X,J_0)$ and $\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}^\beta(X,J_1)$ the corresponding moduli spaces of stable maps (denoted earlier by simply $\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}^\beta(X)$ when we considered just a fixed $J$).
nodes.name: Two almost complex structures
nodes.statement_short: Introduce J_0, J_1 and their moduli spaces.

nodes.statement: There exists a smooth path of $\omega$-tame almost complex structures $J_{[0,1]}=\{J_t\}_{t\in[0,1]}$ connecting $J_0$ and $J_1$. Let us consider the corresponding ``parameterized'' moduli space of stable maps $\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}^\beta(X,J_{[0,1]})$. The construction from \S\ref{gromovwittenimplicitatlassubsection} gives an implicit atlas with boundary $A^\mathrm{GW}$ on $\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}^\beta(X,J_{[0,1]})$ whose restriction to $\partial\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}^\beta(X,J_{[0,1]}):=\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}^\beta(X,J_0)\sqcup\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}^\beta(X,J_1)$ agrees with $A^\mathrm{GW}$ on these spaces.
nodes.name: Parameterized moduli space
nodes.statement_short: Join by a path J_t; the parameterized moduli space carries an implicit atlas with boundary restricting to A^GW.

nodes.statement: Hence it follows using Lemmas \ref{disjointunionfc} and \ref{cobordismworks} that $[\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}^\beta(X,J_0)]^\mathrm{vir}=[\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}^\beta(X,J_1)]^\mathrm{vir}$ in $\check H^\bullet(\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}^\beta(X,J_{[0,1]}))^\vee$, which is enough.
nodes.name: Cobordism invariance
nodes.statement_short: Cobordism lemmas give equality of virtual classes.

nodes.statement: As in the proof of Lemma \ref{stabilizationlemma}, we use (an appropriate variant for manifolds with corners of) Lemma \ref{sortofsard} (which we may also use to avoid the periodic orbits in question). It thus suffices to show that for any unstable component $C_0$ of $C$, there exists a point $p\in C_0$ where $d((\operatorname{id}_{M\times S^1}\times\ell)\circ u):TC_0\to TM\times TS^1\times T\Delta^n$ injective. To find such a point, we split into two cases.
nodes.name: Reduction to injectivity points
nodes.statement_short: Reduce via the Sard-type lemma to finding injectivity points on unstable components.

nodes.statement: First, suppose $u:C_0\to S^1\times\mathbb R$ is constant. Then $u:C_0\to M$ is a (nonconstant!) $J$-holomorphic sphere, and thus has a point of injectivity of $du$.
nodes.name: Constant projection case
nodes.statement_short: Then the component is a nonconstant J-holomorphic sphere.

nodes.statement: Second, suppose $u:C_0\to S^1\times\mathbb R$ is not constant. Then $u:C_0\to S^1\times\mathbb R$ is an isomorphism; let us use $(t,s)\in S^1\times\mathbb R$ as coordinates on $C_0$. Now $\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}\in TM\times TS^1$ has nonzero coordinate in the $TS^1$ component (everywhere), and $\frac{\partial u}{\partial s}\in TM\times TS^1$ has zero coordinate in the $TS^1$ coordinate (everywhere). Hence if $du$ is everywhere noninjective, we find that $\frac{\partial u}{\partial s}=0\in TM\times TS^1$ everywhere. It follows that $u:C_0\to M\times S^1$ is independent of the $\mathbb R$ coordinate, and thus is simply a trivial cylinder mapping onto a periodic orbit. Now the stability condition (the automorphism group being finite) implies that the corresponding (piece of a) flow line $\ell:\mathbb R\to\Delta^n$ is nontrivial. It follows that we have the desired injectivity.
nodes.name: Nonconstant projection case
nodes.statement_short: If du is nowhere injective the component is a trivial cylinder, so stability forces a nontrivial flow line on the simplex.

nodes.statement: For the case of the zero simplex $\sigma=\sigma^0$, this is proved by Wehrheim \cite{wehrheimMS}.
nodes.name: Zero simplex case
nodes.statement_short: Wehrheim proves the 0-simplex case.

nodes.statement: In fact, the general case also follows from \cite{wehrheimMS} since $\overline{\mathcal M}_\mathrm{morse}(\sigma,p,q)$ is the space of broken Morse flow lines on $M\times\Delta^n$ from $p\times 0$ to $q\times n$ for the Morse function $H+f$ (and $f$ is defined and smooth on a neighborhood of $\Delta^n\subseteq\mathbb R^n$).
nodes.name: General simplex
nodes.statement_short: Reduce the general case to Morse flow lines of H+f on M x Delta^n.

nodes.statement: Alternatively, one may restrict to $H$ which have a particular normal form near each critical point in which case this result holds by more elementary arguments (see also \cite{wehrheimMS}).
nodes.name: Alternative route
nodes.statement_short: Alternatively use a normal form near critical points.

nodes.statement: Suppose a stable Floer trajectory $(C,\ell,u)$ is $S^1$-invariant. Then each of the components $\{C_1^\circ,\ldots,C_k^\circ\}$ must be smooth (no nodes) and hence isomorphic to $S^1\times\mathbb R$. Using the holomorphic projection $M\times S^1\times\coprod_{i=1}^k\mathbb R\to S^1\times\coprod_{i=1}^k\mathbb R$, we get holomorphic identifications $C_i^\circ=S^1\times\mathbb R$.
nodes.name: Components are cylinders
nodes.statement_short: S^1-invariance forces smooth cylindrical components identified with S^1 x R.

nodes.statement: Since $(C,\ell,u)$ is $S^1$-invariant, the function $u:C_i^\circ\to M$ must be independent of the $S^1$-coordinate, and hence (examining the $\bar\partial$-equation) is simply a Morse flow line of $H$.
nodes.name: Morse flow line
nodes.statement_short: u is S^1-independent hence a Morse flow line.

nodes.statement: Running this argument in reverse, we also see that every stable Morse trajectory gives rise to a stable Floer trajectory which is $S^1$-invariant.
nodes.name: Converse
nodes.statement_short: Morse trajectories give S^1-invariant Floer trajectories.

nodes.statement: Salamon--Zehnder \cite[p1342, Theorem 7.3(1)]{salamonzehnder} show that $\overline{\mathcal M}(\sigma^0,p,q)^{S^1}\subseteq\overline{\mathcal M}(\sigma^0,p,q)^\mathrm{reg}$ for the $0$-simplex $\sigma^0$ and sufficiently small $\epsilon>0$. Since we only consider constant families of $J$ and $H$, the linearized operators for the higher $\sigma^i$ can be written in terms of the linearized operators for $\sigma^0$, and it follows that $\overline{\mathcal M}(\sigma,p,q)^{S^1}\subseteq\overline{\mathcal M}(\sigma,p,q)^\mathrm{reg}$ for all $\sigma$.
nodes.name: Transversality from Salamon--Zehnder
nodes.statement_short: Salamon-Zehnder give transversality for sigma^0; constant families extend it to all simplices.

nodes.statement: Now we have $\overline{\mathcal M}_\mathrm{morse}(\sigma,p,q)=\overline{\mathcal M}(\sigma,p,q)^{S^1}\subseteq\overline{\mathcal M}(\sigma,p,q)^\mathrm{reg}$. It remains to show that this is an open inclusion.
nodes.name: Remaining: openness
nodes.statement_short: It remains to show openness.

nodes.statement: This can likely be seen by following closely the gluing argument used to prove Propositions \ref{HFgluingneeded} and \ref{morseassumptionMS}, however we can argue directly as follows.
