Both $\overline{\mathcal M}_\mathrm{morse}(\sigma,p,q)$ and $\overline{\mathcal M}(\sigma,p,q)^\mathrm{reg}$ are topological manifolds with corners, and the stratification for the former is the pullback of the stratification for the latter. Their dimensions are dictated by the Morse index and the Conley--Zehnder index respectively, which in this case coincide.
nodes.name: Equal-dimensional manifolds with corners
nodes.statement_short: Both are manifolds with corners of equal dimension with compatible stratifications.

nodes.statement: Hence we are done by Lemma \ref{cornersinvarianceofdomain} below.
nodes.name: Invariance of domain
nodes.statement_short: Conclude by invariance of domain with corners.

nodes.statement: The question is local on $M$, so we may assume that $M=\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R_{\geq 0}^m$.
nodes.name: Localize
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the local model.

nodes.statement: Let $\tilde K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m$ be obtained by reflecting $K$ across the last $m$ coordinate hyperplanes. The hypotheses then imply that $\tilde K$ is a manifold of dimension $n+m$.
nodes.name: Reflection
nodes.statement_short: Reflect K to a full-dimensional manifold.

nodes.statement: Now we have $\tilde K\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+m}$ is open by Brouwer's ``invariance of domain''. This is enough.
nodes.name: Brouwer invariance of domain
nodes.statement_short: Apply invariance of domain.

nodes.statement: Instead of finding an $S^1$-invariant $D\subseteq M\times S^1\times\Delta^n$, we find a $D\subseteq M\times\Delta^n$ (which is clearly equivalent) and we ignore the $S^1$ factor in the codomain of $u$. As in Lemma \ref{stabilizationlemmaforHF}, it suffices to show that for any unstable component $C_0\subseteq C$, either $C_0$ is a Morse flow line or there exists a point (other than a node) where $d((\operatorname{id}_M\times\ell)\circ u):TC_0\to TM\times T\Delta^n$ is injective.
nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement_short: Work in M x Delta^n and reduce to injectivity points on non-Morse unstable components.

nodes.statement: If the projection $C_0\to S^1\times\mathbb R$ is constant, then $u:C_0\to M$ is a (nonconstant!) $J$-holomorphic sphere and we are done as in Lemma \ref{stabilizationlemmaforHF}. Hence it suffices to treat the case when $u:C_0\to S^1\times\mathbb R$ is not constant. Thus $u:C_0\to S^1\times\mathbb R$ is an isomorphism, so we can use $(t,s)\in S^1\times\mathbb R$ as coordinates on $C_0$. Now we split into two cases.
nodes.name: Constant projection; reduce to cylinder
nodes.statement_short: The constant projection case is a J-holomorphic sphere; otherwise C_0 is a cylinder.

nodes.statement: First, suppose $\ell:\mathbb R\to\Delta^n$ is not constant. If $u:C_0\to M$ is independent of the $S^1$ coordinate, then it is a Morse flow line, and we do not need to stabilize. Otherwise, there is a point where $\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}\ne 0$, and since $\ell:\mathbb R\to\Delta^n$ has nonvanishing derivative everywhere, it follows that $du$ is injective at this point.
nodes.name: Nonconstant flow line case
nodes.statement_short: Either a Morse flow line or du injective where du/dt is nonzero.

nodes.statement:
Second, suppose $\ell:\mathbb R	o\Delta^n$ is constant. Then our map $u:C_0	o M$ satisfies:  egin{equation}  rac{\partial u}{\partial t}+J\circ rac{\partial u}{\partial s}=
abla H \end{equation} Certainly $u:C_0	o M$ is not constant; otherwise it would be unstable (infinite automorphism group). Thus $du$ is nonzero somewhere. If $du$ has rank two somewhere, then we are done. Thus let us suppose that this is not the case and show that $u|C_0$ is independent of the $t$ coordinate (and thus is a Morse flow line). Thus there exists some open set $U\subseteq C_0=S^1	imes\mathbb R$ where $du$ has rank $1$. Inside $U$, we have $\ker du\subseteq TC_0=T(S^1	imes\mathbb R)$ is an (integrable!) $1$-dimensional distribution, so $U$ is equipped with a $1$-dimensional foliation and $u$ is constant on the leaves. Thus we have (locally) a factorization $u:S^1	imes\mathbb R\xrightarrow r(-\epsilon,\epsilon)\xrightarrow wM$, the leaves of the foliation being given by $r^{-1}(\delta)$ for $\delta\in(-\epsilon,\epsilon)$. Now \eqref{pseudoholoncylinderformorseHamiltonian} becomes:  egin{equation} \Bigl( rac{\partial r}{\partial t}+ rac{\partial r}{\partial s}\cdot J\Bigr)\cdot w'(r(s,t))=(
abla H)(w(r(s,t))) \end{equation} Since $du$ has rank $1$, we know that $w'(r(s,t))
e 0$. Hence the value of $r(s,t)$ determines the value of its derivative uniquely, i.e.\ $dr$ is constant along the leaves $r^{-1}(\delta)$ of the foliation. It follows that the foliation is (locally) linear(!) and that we can follow any leaf infinitely in both directions and it never exits $U$ (since $dr=0$ outside $U$). Now if any leaf had nonzero slope, it would force $u:C_0	o M$ to be constant, a contradiction. Thus all leaves have slope zero; in other words $u$ is independent of the $S^1$-coordinate over $U=S^1	imes U'$. But now we see that $U'=\mathbb R$, since if $U'$ had boundary, it would imply that we have a Morse flow line reaching a critical point in finite time. Thus $u$ is (globally) a Morse flow line.
nodes.name: Constant flow line case
nodes.statement_short: Show via a rank-one foliation argument that u is a Morse flow line if du never has rank two.

nodes.statement: Second, suppose $\ell:\mathbb R\to\Delta^n$ is constant. Then our map $u:C_0\to M$ satisfies: \begin{equation} \frac{\partial u}{\partial t}+J\circ\frac{\partial u}{\partial s}=\nabla H \end{equation}
nodes.name: Floer equation
nodes.statement_short: u satisfies the Floer equation with time-independent H.

nodes.statement: Certainly $u:C_0\to M$ is not constant; otherwise it would be unstable (infinite automorphism group). Thus $du$ is nonzero somewhere. If $du$ has rank two somewhere, then we are done. Thus let us suppose that this is not the case and show that $u|C_0$ is independent of the $t$ coordinate (and thus is a Morse flow line).
nodes.name: Assume rank at most one
nodes.statement_short: u is nonconstant; suppose du never has rank two.

nodes.statement: Thus there exists some open set $U\subseteq C_0=S^1\times\mathbb R$ where $du$ has rank $1$. Inside $U$, we have $\ker du\subseteq TC_0=T(S^1\times\mathbb R)$ is an (integrable!) $1$-dimensional distribution, so $U$ is equipped with a $1$-dimensional foliation and $u$ is constant on the leaves. Thus we have (locally) a factorization $u:S^1\times\mathbb R\xrightarrow r(-\epsilon,\epsilon)\xrightarrow wM$, the leaves of the foliation being given by $r^{-1}(\delta)$ for $\delta\in(-\epsilon,\epsilon)$. Now \eqref{pseudoholoncylinderformorseHamiltonian} becomes: \begin{equation} \Bigl(\frac{\partial r}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial r}{\partial s}\cdot J\Bigr)\cdot w'(r(s,t))=(\nabla H)(w(r(s,t))) \end{equation}
nodes.name: Foliation factorization
nodes.statement_short: On a rank-one region u factors through a function r constant on leaves of a foliation.

nodes.statement: Since $du$ has rank $1$, we know that $w'(r(s,t))\ne 0$. Hence the value of $r(s,t)$ determines the value of its derivative uniquely, i.e.\ $dr$ is constant along the leaves $r^{-1}(\delta)$ of the foliation. It follows that the foliation is (locally) linear(!) and that we can follow any leaf infinitely in both directions and it never exits $U$ (since $dr=0$ outside $U$). Now if any leaf had nonzero slope, it would force $u:C_0\to M$ to be constant, a contradiction. Thus all leaves have slope zero; in other words $u$ is independent of the $S^1$-coordinate over $U=S^1\times U'$. But now we see that $U'=\mathbb R$, since if $U'$ had boundary, it would imply that we have a Morse flow line reaching a critical point in finite time. Thus $u$ is (globally) a Morse flow line.
nodes.name: Linear foliation
nodes.statement_short: The foliation is linear with slope zero and fills the cylinder, so u is a Morse flow line.

nodes.statement: The homology groups associated to the flow category diagram $\overline{\mathcal M}/\ast$ and the implicit atlas $\mathcal A$ are by definition $F\mathbb H^\bullet(M)$. Now, as we observed previously, the thickened moduli spaces of $\mathcal A$ are open subsets of those of $\mathcal B$, so by Lemma \ref{homologyopenreduction}, $F\mathbb H^\bullet(M)$ may also be defined using the implicit atlas $\mathcal B$ on $\overline{\mathcal M}/\ast$. Now $\mathcal B^{S^1}\subseteq\mathcal B$ is a subatlas, so by Lemma \ref{homologysameassubatlas} it may also be used to define $F\mathbb H^\bullet(M)$.
nodes.name: Change of atlas
nodes.statement_short: We use the setup of the S^1 sections; by open-reduction and subatlas lemmas FH may be computed with B^{S^1}.
nodes.section: 10.7 Calculation of Hamiltonian Floer homology and the Arnold conjecture

nodes.statement: Thus let us restrict attention to the atlas $\mathcal B^{S^1}$ on $\overline{\mathcal M}/\ast$. Recall that by Lemma \ref{morseistransverse}, there is a partition into closed subsets: \begin{equation} \overline{\mathcal M}(\sigma,p,q)=\overline{\mathcal M}(\sigma,p,q)^{S^1}\sqcup[\overline{\mathcal M}(\sigma,p,q)\setminus\overline{\mathcal M}(\sigma,p,q)^{S^1}] \end{equation} Now we apply $S^1$-localization to $\mathcal B^{S^1}$ on $\overline{\mathcal M}/\ast$ in the form of Theorem \ref{circlelocalizationhomology}, which applies since $S^1$ acts with finite stabilizers on $\overline{\mathcal M}(\sigma,p,q)\setminus\overline{\mathcal M}(\sigma,p,q)^{S^1}$ and our coefficient group is $\mathbb Q$. It follows that $F\mathbb H^\bullet(M)$ may be defined using the flow category diagram $\overline{\mathcal M}^{S^1}/\ast$ with the implicit atlas obtained from $\mathcal B^{S^1}$ by removing $\overline{\mathcal M}\setminus\overline{\mathcal M}^{S^1}$ from every thickening.
nodes.name: S^1-localization
nodes.statement_short: Apply S^1-localization to reduce to the fixed-locus flow category diagram.
nodes.section: 10.7 Calculation of Hamiltonian Floer homology and the Arnold conjecture

nodes.statement: All the flow spaces of $\overline{\mathcal M}^{S^1}/\ast$ are cut out transversally by Lemma \ref{morseistransverse}, so by Proposition \ref{iftransversejustcountzero}, the homology groups of $\overline{\mathcal M}^{S^1}/\ast$ can be defined by simply counting the $0$-dimensional flow spaces according to the orientations $\omega$. Now $\overline{\mathcal M}^{S^1}$ coincides with the Morse flow category diagram $\overline{\mathcal M}_\mathrm{morse}/\ast$ of $H$ by Lemma \ref{fixedismorse} (with the same orientations by Proposition \ref{HFgluingSS}), and this gives the desired isomorphism.
nodes.name: Count Morse trajectories
nodes.statement_short: The fixed locus is transversally cut out and equals the Morse flow category, giving Morse homology.
nodes.section: 10.7 Calculation of Hamiltonian Floer homology and the Arnold conjecture

nodes.statement: Pick any $\omega$-compatible almost complex structure $J$ and consider the vertex $(J,H)\in J\!H_\bullet(M)$. Over this vertex, pick any complex $F\mathbb C^\bullet(M)$ which calculates $F\mathbb H^\bullet(M)$. Then $F\mathbb C^\bullet(M)$ is a free $\mathbb Q[[\pi]]$-module of rank: \begin{equation} \operatorname{rk}_{\mathbb Q[[\pi]]}F\mathbb C^\bullet(M)\leq\#\operatorname{Fix}\phi_H \end{equation} (its rank equals the number of null-homotopic periodic orbits).
nodes.name: Floer complex
nodes.statement_short: Pick (J,H) and a complex computing FH; its rank is at most #Fix phi_H.
nodes.section: 10.7 Calculation of Hamiltonian Floer homology and the Arnold conjecture

nodes.statement: By Theorem \ref{HFcalculation}, the homology $F\mathbb H^\bullet(M)$ is free of rank: \begin{equation} \operatorname{rk}_{\mathbb Q[[\pi]]}F\mathbb H^\bullet(M)=\dim H_\bullet(M;\mathbb Q) \end{equation}
nodes.name: Rank of homology
nodes.statement_short: By the calculation, FH has rank dim H_*(M;Q).
nodes.section: 10.7 Calculation of Hamiltonian Floer homology and the Arnold conjecture

nodes.statement: Now by definition, there is a $\mathbb Q[[\pi]]$-linear boundary map $d:F\mathbb C^\bullet(M)\to F\mathbb C^{\bullet+1}(M)$ and by definition $\operatorname{rk}_{\mathbb Q[[\pi]]}F\mathbb H^\bullet(M)=\ker d/\operatorname{im} d$. Now apply Lemma \ref{homologyhassmallerrank} to conclude that: \begin{equation} \operatorname{rk}_{\mathbb Q[[\pi]]}F\mathbb H^\bullet(M)\leq\operatorname{rk}_{\mathbb Q[[\pi]]}F\mathbb C^\bullet(M) \end{equation} Thus we are done.
nodes.name: Compare ranks
nodes.statement_short: Homology rank is at most chain rank.
nodes.section: 10.7 Calculation of Hamiltonian Floer homology and the Arnold conjecture

nodes.statement: Since $H$ is free, it is projective, so the surjection $\ker d\twoheadrightarrow H$ has a section $H\hookrightarrow\ker d\subseteq M$. Hence there is an injection $H\hookrightarrow M$.
nodes.name: Section of kernel
nodes.statement_short: Projectivity gives an injection H into M.

nodes.statement: Now use Lemma \ref{freesubhassmallerrank}.
nodes.name: Apply rank lemma
nodes.statement_short: Apply the free submodule rank lemma.

nodes.statement: This is a standard yet tricky exercise. We recall one of the (many) standard proofs.
nodes.name: Standard proof
nodes.statement_short: Recall a standard proof.

nodes.statement: The map $\phi$ is described by some matrix of $A\times B$ elements of $R$. Certainly the kernel of this matrix remains zero over the subring of $R$ generated by its entries. Thus we may assume without loss of generality that $R$ is a finitely generated $\mathbb Z$-algebra.
nodes.name: Reduce to f.g. Z-algebra
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the subring generated by matrix entries.

nodes.statement: Now localize at a prime ideal $\mathfrak p\subset R$ of height zero. Localization is exact, so again $\phi$ remains injective. Thus we may assume without loss of generality that $R$ is a local Noetherian ring of dimension zero, and thus $R$ is an Artin local ring \cite[p90, Theorem 8.5]{atiyahmacdonald}.
nodes.name: Localize to Artin local ring
nodes.statement_short: Localize at a minimal prime to get an Artin local ring.

nodes.statement: Since $R$ is Artinian, all finitely generated modules have finite length \cite[pp76--77, Propositions 6.5 and 6.8]{atiyahmacdonald}, and hence there is a length homomorphism $K_0(R)\to\mathbb Z$ \cite[p77, Proposition 6.9]{atiyahmacdonald} (which is clearly an isomorphism since $R$ is local). It thus follows from the short exact sequence $0\to R^{\oplus A}\xrightarrow\phi R^{\oplus B}\to\operatorname{coker}\phi\to 0$ that $A\leq B$.
nodes.name: Length argument
nodes.statement_short: Additivity of length on the short exact sequence gives A <= B.

nodes.name: Reductions
nodes.statement: We may assume without loss of generality that $X$ is compact. By induction, it suffices to treat the case $n=2$.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG X compact; induction reduces to n=2.

nodes.name: Exercise via normality
nodes.statement: The rest is an exercise (use the fact that a compact Hausdorff space is normal).
nodes.statement_short: Conclude using normality of compact Hausdorff spaces.

nodes.name: alpha^* of a sheaf is a K-sheaf
nodes.statement: Suppose $\mathcal F$ is a sheaf, and let us verify $\alpha^\ast\mathcal F$ is a $\mathcal K$-sheaf. Axiom \eqref{sheafvanishing} is clear (take $A=\varnothing$ in \eqref{opensheafproperty}). Axiom \eqref{sheafproperty} follows from \eqref{opensheafproperty} and Lemma \ref{intersectioncofinal} since direct limits are exact. Axiom \eqref{sheafcontinuity} is clear from the definition also.
nodes.statement_short: Verify the K-sheaf axioms for alpha^*F using Lemma (cofinal intersections) and exactness of direct limits.

nodes.name: alpha_* of a K-sheaf is a sheaf
nodes.statement: Suppose $\mathcal F$ is a $\mathcal K$-sheaf, and let us verify that $\alpha_\ast\mathcal F$ is a sheaf. Let us first observe that (by induction using \eqref{sheafvanishing} and \eqref{sheafproperty}) if $\{K_\alpha\subseteq X\}_{\alpha\in A}$ is any collection of compact sets, all but finitely many of which are empty, then the following is exact: \begin{equation} 0\to\mathcal F\Bigl(\bigcup_{\alpha\in A}K_\alpha\Bigr)\to\prod_{\alpha\in A}\mathcal F(K_\alpha)\to\prod_{\alpha,\beta\in A}\mathcal F(K_\alpha\cap K_\beta) \end{equation} Let us now verify axiom \eqref{opensheafproperty} for $\alpha_\ast\mathcal F$ for open sets $\{U_\alpha\subseteq X\}_{\alpha\in A}$. Certainly \eqref{opensheafproperty} is the inverse limit of \eqref{compactfiniteexact} over all collections of compact subsets $\{K_\alpha\subseteq U_\alpha\}_{\alpha\in A}$ for which $K_\alpha=\varnothing$ except for finitely many $\alpha\in A$. This is sufficient since inverse limit is left exact.
nodes.statement_short: Finite compact exactness plus left exactness of inverse limits gives the sheaf axiom for alpha_*F.

nodes.name: Reduce to unit/counit
nodes.statement: Now to see that the adjoint pair $\alpha^\ast\dashv\alpha_\ast$ is actually an equivalence of categories, it suffices to show that the natural morphisms $\mathcal F\to\alpha_\ast\alpha^\ast\mathcal F$ and $\alpha^\ast\alpha_\ast\mathcal G\to\mathcal G$ are isomorphisms. In other words, we must show that following natural maps are isomorphisms: \begin{align} \mathcal F(U)&\to\varprojlim_{\begin{smallmatrix}K\subseteq U\cr K\textrm{ compact}\end{smallmatrix}}\varinjlim_{\begin{smallmatrix}K\subseteq U'\cr U'\textrm{ open}\end{smallmatrix}}\mathcal F(U')\\
nodes.statement_short: Equivalence reduces to unit and counit maps being isomorphisms.

nodes.name: Unit and counit are isomorphisms
nodes.statement: The right hand side of \eqref{Funit} can be thought of as the inverse limit of $\mathcal F(U')$ over all open $U'\subseteq U$ with $\overline{U'}\subseteq U$ and $\overline{U'}$ compact. It is easy to see that the map from $\mathcal F(U)$ to this inverse limit is an isomorphism if $\mathcal F$ is a sheaf. The left hand side of \eqref{Gunit} can be identified with the left hand side of \eqref{sheafcontinuity}, and thus the map to $\mathcal G(K)$ is an isomorphism if $\mathcal F$ is a $\mathcal K$-sheaf.
nodes.statement_short: Identify both sides using the sheaf axiom and (Sh_K3).

nodes.name: Comparison diagram
nodes.statement: Write $K:=\bigcap_{\alpha\in A}K_\alpha$. Now consider the diagram: \begin{equation} \begin{tikzcd} \varinjlim\limits_{\alpha\in A}\varinjlim\limits_{\begin{smallmatrix}K_\alpha\subseteq U\cr U\textrm{ open}\end{smallmatrix}}\mathcal F(\overline U)\ar{r}\ar{d}& \varinjlim\limits_{\begin{smallmatrix}\exists\alpha\in A:K_\alpha\subseteq U\cr U\textrm{ open}\end{smallmatrix}}\mathcal F(\overline U)\ar{r}& \varinjlim\limits_{\begin{smallmatrix}K\subseteq U\cr U\textrm{ open}\end{smallmatrix}}\mathcal F(\overline U)\ar{d}\\ \varinjlim\limits_{\alpha\in A}\mathcal F(K_\alpha)\ar{rr}&&\mathcal F(K) \end{tikzcd}
nodes.statement_short: Set K the intersection and compare limits via a diagram.

nodes.name: Vertical and first horizontal isomorphisms
nodes.statement: The vertical maps are both isomorphisms by \eqref{sheafcontinuity}. The first horizontal map is an isomorphism since $\{K_\alpha\}_{\alpha\in A}$ is filtered.
nodes.statement_short: Vertical maps isomorphic by (Sh_K3); first horizontal by filteredness.

nodes.name: Remaining cofinality
nodes.statement: It thus remains to show that if $K\subseteq U$ and $U$ is open, then there exists $\alpha\in A$ such that $K_\alpha\subseteq U$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to: every open neighborhood of K contains some K_alpha.

nodes.name: Compactness argument
nodes.statement: Since $K\subseteq U$, we have $(X\setminus U)\cap K=\varnothing$, so $\bigcap_{\alpha\in A}(X\setminus U)\cap K_\alpha=\varnothing$. This is a filtered directed system of compact sets, and so the intersection being empty implies that one of the terms $(X\setminus U)\cap K_\alpha$ is empty, so $K_\alpha\subseteq U$ as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Empty filtered intersection of compacts forces some term empty.

nodes.name: Trivial axioms
nodes.statement: For \eqref{homotopysheafacyclic} and \eqref{homotopysheafcontinuity} this is trivial.
nodes.statement_short: Axioms (hSh_K1) and (hSh_K3) are immediate.

nodes.name: Mapping cone acyclic
nodes.statement: For \eqref{homotopysheafproperty}, suppose $\mathcal F^\bullet\xrightarrow\sim\mathcal G^\bullet$ is a quasi-isomorphism. Now the sequence \eqref{homotopysheafproperty} applied to the mapping cone $[\mathcal F^\bullet\to\mathcal G^{\bullet-1}]$ is certainly acyclic (since it has a finite filtration whose associated graded is acyclic).
nodes.statement_short: The (hSh_K2) sequence of the mapping cone is acyclic by a finite filtration.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Thus \eqref{homotopysheafproperty} holds for $\mathcal F^\bullet$ iff it holds for $\mathcal G^\bullet$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence (hSh_K2) holds for F iff for G.

nodes.name: Maps f^* and f_! with supports in K
nodes.statement: For $K\subseteq X$, there are natural maps: \begin{equation} \begin{tikzcd} \check H^\bullet_K(Y;f_!\mathcal F)\ar[yshift=0.5ex]{r}{f^\ast}&\ar[yshift=-0.5ex]{l}{f_!}\check H^\bullet_K(X;\mathcal F) \end{tikzcd} \end{equation} (for $f^\ast$: pull back the open cover) (for $f_!$: add $Y\setminus K$ to the open cover and extend by zero). It is easy to see that $f_!$ and $f^\ast$ are inverses.
nodes.statement_short: For compact K in X, f^* and f_! on supports-in-K Čech cohomology are inverse.

nodes.name: Define f_! on compact supports
nodes.statement: The desired map $f_!:\check H^\bullet_c(X;\mathcal F)\to\check H^\bullet_c(Y;f_!\mathcal F)$ is defined as the composition: \begin{equation} \varinjlim_{K\subseteq X}\check H^\bullet_K(X;\mathcal F)\overset{\eqref{trivialKequivalence}}=\varinjlim_{K\subseteq X}\check H^\bullet_K(Y;f_!\mathcal F)\to\varinjlim_{K\subseteq Y}\check H^\bullet_K(Y;f_!\mathcal F)
nodes.statement_short: Define f_! as a composition of direct limits.

nodes.name: Reduce to supports
nodes.statement: We must show that the second map is an isomorphism; to see this, it suffices to show that the following is an isomorphism for all $K\subseteq Y$: \begin{equation} \varinjlim_{K'\subseteq X\cap K}\check H^\bullet_{K'}(Y;f_!\mathcal F)\to\check H^\bullet_K(Y;f_!\mathcal F)
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to an isomorphism for each compact K in Y.

nodes.name: Claim: cochains can be refined to compact support in X
nodes.statement: We claim that for any \v Cech cochain $\beta$ for $f_!\mathcal F$ with supports in $K$ subordinate to an open cover of $Y$, there is a refinement on which the restriction of $\beta$ has supports in some $K'\subseteq X\cap K$. It follows from the claim (using a cofinality argument) that \eqref{supportcompactinXorY} is an isomorphism. To prove the claim, argue as follows. First, choose a refinement for which only finitely many open sets $U_1,\ldots,U_n$ intersect $K$ and for which the remaining open sets cover $Y\setminus K$. Pick open sets $V_i\subseteq U_i$ which cover $K$ and for which $\overline{V_i}$ is compact and $\overline{V_i}\subseteq U_i$ (this is always possible). Now $\beta$ is a finite collection $\{\beta_I\in(f_!\mathcal F)(\bigcap_{i\in I}U_i)\}_{\varnothing\ne I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}}$. We have: \begin{equation} \operatorname{supp}\Bigl(\beta_I|\bigcap_{i\in I}V_i\Bigr)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\beta_I\cap\bigcap_{i\in I}\overline{V_i} \end{equation} Since $\operatorname{supp}\beta_I\subseteq\bigcap_{i\in I}U_i$ is (relatively) closed and $\bigcap_{i\in I}\overline{V_i}\subseteq\bigcap_{i\in I}U_i$ is compact, it follows that the right hand side is compact. Also, we have $\operatorname{supp}\beta_I\subseteq X$ (by definition of $f_!\mathcal F$). Hence the right hand side of \eqref{restrictionsupport} is a compact subset of $X$. It follows that the restriction of $\beta$ to the refinement obtained by replacing $U_i$ with $V_i$ for $i=1,\ldots,n$ has support in a compact subset of $X$.
nodes.statement_short: Claim that refinements make supports compact in X, which gives the isomorphism by cofinality.

nodes.name: Claim suffices
nodes.statement: It follows from the claim (using a cofinality argument) that \eqref{supportcompactinXorY} is an isomorphism. To prove the claim, argue as follows.
nodes.statement_short: The claim implies the isomorphism by cofinality.

nodes.name: Choose refinement and shrinkings
nodes.statement: First, choose a refinement for which only finitely many open sets $U_1,\ldots,U_n$ intersect $K$ and for which the remaining open sets cover $Y\setminus K$. Pick open sets $V_i\subseteq U_i$ which cover $K$ and for which $\overline{V_i}$ is compact and $\overline{V_i}\subseteq U_i$ (this is always possible).
nodes.statement_short: Refine so finitely many U_i meet K and pick V_i with compact closures.

nodes.name: Supports are compact in X
nodes.statement: Now $\beta$ is a finite collection $\{\beta_I\in(f_!\mathcal F)(\bigcap_{i\in I}U_i)\}_{\varnothing\ne I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}}$. We have: \begin{equation} \operatorname{supp}\Bigl(\beta_I|\bigcap_{i\in I}V_i\Bigr)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\beta_I\cap\bigcap_{i\in I}\overline{V_i} \end{equation} Since $\operatorname{supp}\beta_I\subseteq\bigcap_{i\in I}U_i$ is (relatively) closed and $\bigcap_{i\in I}\overline{V_i}\subseteq\bigcap_{i\in I}U_i$ is compact, it follows that the right hand side is compact. Also, we have $\operatorname{supp}\beta_I\subseteq X$ (by definition of $f_!\mathcal F$). Hence the right hand side of \eqref{restrictionsupport} is a compact subset of $X$.
nodes.statement_short: The supports of restrictions to the V_i are compact subsets of X.

nodes.name: Conclude claim
nodes.statement: It follows that the restriction of $\beta$ to the refinement obtained by replacing $U_i$ with $V_i$ for $i=1,\ldots,n$ has support in a compact subset of $X$.
nodes.statement_short: Restricting to the shrunken refinement gives compact support in X.

nodes.name: Partitions of covers
nodes.statement: Given an open cover containing $U=U_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup U_n$ (finite disjoint union), we get a refinement by replacing $U$ with $\{U_1,\ldots,U_n\}$. A \emph{partition} of an open cover is a refinement obtained by doing such a replacement on some (possibly infinitely many) open sets of the cover. Note that a partition induces an isomorphism on \v Cech cochains since $\mathcal F$ is a sheaf.
nodes.statement_short: Define partitions; they induce isomorphisms on Čech cochains.

nodes.name: Cofinality claim
nodes.statement: We claim that partitions of pullbacks of open covers of $Y$ form a cofinal system of open covers of $X$. This is clear using Lemma \ref{properpullbackfinalneighborhood} and the fact that $f$ has finite fibers.
nodes.statement_short: Partitions of pullback covers are cofinal, by Lemma on proper preimages and finite fibers.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: It follows from this cofinality that $f^\ast$ is an isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Cofinality gives that f^* is an isomorphism.

nodes.name: Isomorphisms one and two
nodes.statement: Isomorphism one: the natural map $\mathcal F\to(\pi_\ast\pi^\ast)^\Gamma$ is in fact an isomorphism of sheaves (check on stalks). Isomorphism two: obvious since taking $\Gamma$-invariants is exact on $\mathbb Z[\frac 1{\#\Gamma}]$-modules.
nodes.statement_short: First via stalks; second since invariants are exact after inverting #Gamma.

nodes.name: Isomorphism three
nodes.statement: Isomorphism three: use Lemma \ref{finitemap}, which applies since $\pi$ is automatically proper.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the finite-fiber pullback lemma to the proper quotient map.

nodes.name: Notation
nodes.statement: Let us denote by $\check H^\bullet(X;\mathcal F;\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha\in A})$ (resp.\ $\check H^\bullet(X;\alpha^\ast\mathcal F;\{K_i\}_{i=1}^n)$) the argument of the direct limit \eqref{cechcomplexI} (resp.\ \eqref{cechcomplexII}).
nodes.statement_short: Name the terms of the two direct limits.

nodes.name: Construct map and reduce
nodes.statement: Since $X$ is compact, every open cover has a finite compact refinement. This gives a map $\check H^\bullet(X;\mathcal F)\to\check H^\bullet(X;\alpha^\ast\mathcal F)$. To show that this map is an isomorphism, it suffices to show that for any fixed finite compact cover $\{K_i\}_{i=1}^n$, the following is an isomorphism: \begin{equation} \varinjlim_{\begin{smallmatrix}X=\bigcup_{\alpha\in A}U_\alpha\cr\text{open cover refined by }\{K_i\}_{i=1}^n\end{smallmatrix}}\check H^\bullet(X;\mathcal F;\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha\in A})\to\check H^\bullet(X;\alpha^\ast\mathcal F;\{K_i\}_{i=1}^n) \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Compact refinement gives the map; reduce to a fixed finite compact cover.

nodes.name: Cofinality reduction
nodes.statement: By a cofinality argument, we can change the directed system on the left side to be open covers $\{U_i\}_{i=1}^n$ with $U_i\supseteq K_i$. Hence it suffices to show that the following is an isomorphism: \begin{equation} \varinjlim_{\{U_i\supseteq K_i\}_{i=1}^n}\check H^\bullet(X;\mathcal F;\{U_i\}_{i=1}^n)\to\check H^\bullet(X;\alpha^\ast\mathcal F;\{K_i\}_{i=1}^n) \end{equation} This
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to covers by open U_i containing K_i.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: This is clear from the definition of $\alpha^\ast$ and from Lemma \ref{intersectioncofinal}.
nodes.statement_short: Follows from the definition of alpha^* and cofinal intersections.

nodes.name: Mapping cone LES
nodes.statement: There is clearly a long exact sequence: \begin{equation} \cdots\to\check H^{\bullet-1}(X;\mathcal G^\bullet)\to\check H^\bullet(X;[\mathcal F^\bullet\to\mathcal G^{\bullet-1}])\to\check H^\bullet(X;\mathcal F^\bullet)\to\check H^\bullet(X;\mathcal G^\bullet)\to\cdots
nodes.statement_short: Write the long exact sequence for the mapping cone.

nodes.name: Reduce to acyclic complexes
nodes.statement: Hence it suffices to show that if $\mathcal F^\bullet$ is acyclic then $\check H^\bullet(X;\mathcal F^\bullet)=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to vanishing for acyclic complexes.

nodes.name: Filtration argument
nodes.statement: This is true because then each \v Cech complex has a finite filtration whose associated graded is acyclic.
nodes.statement_short: Each Čech complex is filtered with acyclic graded pieces.

nodes.name: Set up induction
nodes.statement: We prove that $\mathcal F^\bullet(X)\to\check C^\bullet(X;\mathcal F^\bullet;K_1,\ldots,K_n)$ (the right hand side denotes \v Cech complex for the finite compact cover $X=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_n$) is a quasi-isomorphism by induction on $n$.
nodes.statement_short: Prove the Čech comparison for n-set compact covers by induction on n.

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: The base case $n=1$ is obvious since $\check C^\bullet(X;\mathcal F^\bullet;X)=\mathcal F^\bullet(X)$ by definition.
nodes.statement_short: n=1 is tautological.

nodes.name: Inductive step reduction
nodes.statement: For the inductive step, it suffices to show that the natural map $\check C^\bullet(X;\mathcal F^\bullet;K_1\cup K_2,K_3,\ldots,K_n)\to\check C^\bullet(X;\mathcal F^\bullet;K_1,K_2,K_3,\ldots,K_n)$ is a quasi-isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to merging K_1 and K_2.

nodes.name: Cone is acyclic
nodes.statement: We will show that the mapping cone is acyclic; to see this, let us filter it according to how many of the $K_3,\ldots,K_n$ are chosen among $i_0,\ldots,i_p$. This is a finite filtration, so it suffices to show that the associated graded is acyclic. The associated graded is a direct sum of complexes of the form $[\mathcal F^\bullet(K)\to\mathcal F^{\bullet-1}(K)]$ (which is obviously acyclic) and $[\mathcal F^\bullet(K\cap(K_1\cup K_2))\to\mathcal F^{\bullet-1}(K\cap K_1)\oplus\mathcal F^{\bullet-1}(K\cap K_2)\to\mathcal F^{\bullet-2}(K\cap K_1\cap K_2)]$ (which is acyclic by \eqref{homotopysheafproperty}).
nodes.statement_short: Filter the cone; graded pieces are acyclic, one by (hSh_K2).

nodes.name: Empty case
nodes.statement: The above argument works when $X\ne\varnothing$; if $X=\varnothing$, use \eqref{homotopysheafacyclic}.
nodes.statement_short: If X is empty use (hSh_K1).

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: It suffices to show that for all $\alpha\in\mathcal F(K)$, there exists a finite compact cover $X=\bigcup_{i=1}^nK_i$ such that $\mathcal F(K)\to\bigoplus_{i=1}^n\mathcal F(K\cap K_i)$ annihilates $\alpha$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to killing each section on a finite compact cover.

nodes.name: Stalk diagram
nodes.statement: We consider the commutative diagram: \begin{equation} \begin{CD} \varinjlim_{K\subseteq U}\mathcal F(\overline U)@>>>\prod_{p\in K}\varinjlim_{p\in U}\mathcal F(\overline U)\cr @VVV@VVV\cr \mathcal F(K)@>>>\prod_{p\in K}\mathcal F_p \end{CD} \end{equation} where the vertical maps are both isomorphisms.
nodes.statement_short: Diagram comparing sections with stalks; vertical maps isomorphisms.

nodes.name: Compactness
nodes.statement: Now the vanishing of $\mathcal F_p$ and a compactness argument shows that there are finitely many open sets $U_i\subseteq X$ covering $K$ such that $\alpha$ vanishes in $\mathcal F(K\cap\overline{U_i})$ for all $i$.
nodes.statement_short: Vanishing stalks and compactness give finitely many U_i killing alpha.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Thus the compact cover $X=(X\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^nU_i)\cup\overline{U_1}\cup\cdots\cup\overline{U_n}$ has the desired properties.
nodes.statement_short: The resulting compact cover works.

nodes.name: Set up induction on truncations
nodes.statement: We show that for all $i$, the map $\check H^\bullet(X;\mathcal F^\bullet)\to\check H^\bullet(X;\tau_{\geq i}\mathcal F^\bullet)$ is an isomorphism (this is sufficient since $\check H^j(X;\tau_{\geq i}\mathcal F^\bullet)=0$ for $j<i$). We proceed by induction on $i$.
nodes.statement_short: Show the truncation maps are isomorphisms, by induction on i.

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: Since $H^i\mathcal F^\bullet=0$ for $i<<0$, we have that $\mathcal F^\bullet\to\tau_{\geq i}\mathcal F^\bullet$ is a quasi-isomorphism, so $\check H^\bullet(X;\mathcal F^\bullet)\to\check H^\bullet(X;\tau_{\geq i}\mathcal F^\bullet)$ is an isomorphism for $i<<0$ (Lemma \ref{qicech}). Thus we have the base case of the induction.
nodes.statement_short: Truncation is a quasi-isomorphism for i<<0.

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: For the inductive step, it suffices to show that $\check H^\bullet(X;H^{i-1}\mathcal F^\bullet)=0$. This follows from Lemma \ref{localvanishingcechzero}.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to vanishing for H^{i-1}, given by Lemma I.

nodes.name: Comparison square
nodes.statement: For any $K\subseteq X$, we have a commutative diagram: \begin{equation} \begin{CD} H^\bullet\mathcal F^\bullet(K)@>\sim>>\check H^\bullet(K;\mathcal F^\bullet)\cr @VVV@VVV\cr H^\bullet\mathcal G^\bullet(K)@>\sim>>\check H^\bullet(K;\mathcal G^\bullet) \end{CD}
nodes.statement_short: Square comparing sections and Čech cohomology on K.

nodes.name: Rows are isomorphisms
nodes.statement: The rows are isomorphisms by Proposition \ref{homotopysheafcechquasiisomorphism}.
nodes.statement_short: Homotopy K-sheaves compute their own Čech cohomology.

nodes.name: Right map is iso
nodes.statement: If $\mathcal F^\bullet_p\to\mathcal G^\bullet_p$ is a quasi-isomorphism, then the right vertical map is a quasi-isomorphism by Proposition \ref{cechdeterminedbystalks}.
nodes.statement_short: Stalkwise quasi-isomorphism gives Čech isomorphism.

nodes.name: H^0 is a K-sheaf
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lowervanishingimpliessheaf}, strong vanishing implies that $H^0\mathcal F^\bullet$ is a $\mathcal K$-sheaf.
nodes.statement_short: Strong vanishing plus lowest-homology lemma gives the K-sheaf claim.

nodes.name: Prove strong vanishing
nodes.statement: Now let us prove strong vanishing. By restricting to a compact subset, it suffices to treat the case when the underlying space is compact. Now from \eqref{homotopysheafproperty}, compactness, and weak vanishing, it follows that $H^i\mathcal F^\bullet=0$ for $i<<0$. Now let us prove strong vanishing by induction on $i<0$ (we have just proven the base case). For the inductive step, observe that $H^i\mathcal F^\bullet$ is a sheaf by the induction hypothesis ($H^{i-1}\mathcal F^\bullet=0$) and Lemma \ref{lowervanishingimpliessheaf}, and thus $H^i\mathcal F^\bullet_p=0\implies H^i\mathcal F^\bullet=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Prove strong vanishing by induction on i.

nodes.name: Reduce to compact
nodes.statement: By restricting to a compact subset, it suffices to treat the case when the underlying space is compact.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to compact underlying space.

nodes.name: Uniform vanishing
nodes.statement: Now from \eqref{homotopysheafproperty}, compactness, and weak vanishing, it follows that $H^i\mathcal F^\bullet=0$ for $i<<0$.
nodes.statement_short: Compactness upgrades local weak vanishing to global vanishing for i<<0.

nodes.name: Induction setup
nodes.statement: Now let us prove strong vanishing by induction on $i<0$ (we have just proven the base case).
nodes.statement_short: Induct on i<0 with the base case just shown.

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: For the inductive step, observe that $H^i\mathcal F^\bullet$ is a sheaf by the induction hypothesis ($H^{i-1}\mathcal F^\bullet=0$) and Lemma \ref{lowervanishingimpliessheaf}, and thus $H^i\mathcal F^\bullet_p=0\implies H^i\mathcal F^\bullet=0$.
nodes.statement_short: H^i is a sheaf with zero stalks, hence zero.

nodes.name: Chain of maps
nodes.statement: The isomorphism \eqref{cechsimplecanonicaliso} is defined as the composition of the following isomorphisms: \begin{equation} \begin{matrix} H^\bullet[\mathcal F^\bullet_0(X)\to\cdots\to\mathcal F^{\bullet-n}_n(X)]\cr \downarrow\cr \check H^\bullet(X;[\mathcal F^\bullet_0\to\cdots\to\mathcal F^{\bullet-n}_n])\cr \downarrow\cr \check H^\bullet(X;[\tau_{\geq 0}\mathcal F^\bullet_0\to\cdots\to\tau_{\geq n}\mathcal F^{\bullet-n}_n])\cr \uparrow\cr \check H^\bullet(X;[H^0\mathcal F^\bullet_0\to\cdots\to H^n\mathcal F^{\bullet-n}_n]) \end{matrix}
nodes.statement_short: Define the isomorphism as a composition of three maps.

nodes.name: Map one
nodes.statement: The maps are isomorphisms for the following reasons. Map one: $[\mathcal F^\bullet_0\to\cdots\to\mathcal F^{\bullet-n}_n]$ is a homotopy $\mathcal K$-sheaf (Lemma \ref{associatedgradedhomotopysheaf}), and a homotopy $\mathcal K$-sheaf calculates its own $\check H^\bullet$ (Proposition \ref{homotopysheafcechquasiisomorphism}).
nodes.statement_short: A homotopy K-sheaf computes its own Čech cohomology.

nodes.name: Map two
nodes.statement: Map two: the map of coefficient $\mathcal K$-presheaves is a quasi-isomorphism (Lemma \ref{cechsimplebasic}) and thus induces an isomorphism on $\check H^\bullet$ (Lemma \ref{qicech}).
nodes.statement_short: Truncation is a quasi-isomorphism by strong vanishing.

nodes.name: Map three
nodes.statement: Map three: the map of coefficient $\mathcal K$-presheaves is a quasi-isomorphism on stalks (by purity), and thus induces an isomorphism on $\check H^\bullet$ (Proposition \ref{cechdeterminedbystalks}).
nodes.statement_short: Stalkwise quasi-isomorphism by purity.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: It suffices to show the weak vanishing property for $\mathcal F^\bullet$.
nodes.statement_short: Only weak vanishing needs proof.

nodes.name: Neighborhood limit
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha\in H^i\mathcal F^\bullet(K)$ be arbitrary with $i<0$. By Remark \ref{nbhdintersectiongood} and Lemma \ref{anycompactintersectionworks}, the following is a quasi-isomorphism: \begin{equation} \varinjlim_{\begin{smallmatrix}Z\subseteq V\cr V\textrm{ open}\end{smallmatrix}}\mathcal F^\bullet(K\cap\overline V)\to\mathcal F^\bullet(K\cap Z) \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Take alpha; F(K∩Z) is the limit over closed neighborhoods of Z.

nodes.name: Vanish near Z
nodes.statement: Since $H^i\mathcal F^\bullet(K\cap Z)=0$ by strong vanishing for $i^\ast\mathcal F^\bullet$, we see that the image of $\alpha$ in $H^i\mathcal F^\bullet(K\cap\overline V)$ vanishes for some open $V\supseteq Z$.
nodes.statement_short: Strong vanishing on Z kills alpha near Z.

nodes.name: Mayer-Vietoris
nodes.statement: Now applying \eqref{homotopysheafproperty} to $K=(K\cap\overline V)\cup(K\setminus V)$, we see that the vanishing of the image of $\alpha$ in $H^i\mathcal F^\bullet(K\cap\overline V)$ implies that $\alpha$ ``comes from'' the cohomology of $[\mathcal F^\bullet(K\setminus V)\to\mathcal F^{\bullet-1}(K\cap\overline V\cap(K\setminus V))$].
nodes.statement_short: Alpha comes from the cone over K minus V.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: On the other hand, this latter group vanishes in degrees $i<0$ by strong vanishing for $j^\ast\mathcal F^\bullet$. Thus $\alpha=0$, so we have even shown strong vanishing for $\mathcal F^\bullet$.
nodes.statement_short: Strong vanishing on U kills it, so alpha=0.

nodes.name: Parts (i) and (ii)
nodes.statement: Statement (\ref{scacyc}) is obvious. Statement (\ref{scpatch}) can be deduced from Mayer--Vietoris using a form of the nine lemma as we now explain. Let us write $U:=X\setminus A$ and $V:=X\setminus B$. Now consider the following total complex: \begin{equation} \begin{CD} C_\bullet(U\cap V)@>>>C_{\bullet+1}(U)\oplus C_{\bullet+1}(V)@>>>C_{\bullet+2}(U\cup V)\cr @VVV@VVV@VVV\cr C_{\bullet+1}(X)@>>>C_{\bullet+2}(X)\oplus C_{\bullet+2}(X)@>>>C_{\bullet+3}(X)\cr @VVV@VVV@VVV\cr C_{\bullet+2}(X,U\cap V)@>>>C_{\bullet+3}(X,U)\oplus C_{\bullet+3}(X,V)@>>>C_{\bullet+4}(X,U\cup V)\cr \end{CD} \end{equation} The columns are acyclic (by definition of relative chains), and hence the total complex is acyclic as well. The first row is acyclic by Mayer--Vietoris, and the second row is obviously acyclic. Thus the third row is acyclic, as needed.
nodes.statement_short: (i) is obvious; (ii) by a nine-lemma argument with Mayer-Vietoris.

nodes.name: Strategy
nodes.statement: Statement (\ref{scpatch}) can be deduced from Mayer--Vietoris using a form of the nine lemma as we now explain.
nodes.statement_short: Deduce from Mayer-Vietoris via a nine lemma.

nodes.name: 3x3 total complex
nodes.statement: Let us write $U:=X\setminus A$ and $V:=X\setminus B$. Now consider the following total complex: \begin{equation} \begin{CD} C_\bullet(U\cap V)@>>>C_{\bullet+1}(U)\oplus C_{\bullet+1}(V)@>>>C_{\bullet+2}(U\cup V)\cr @VVV@VVV@VVV\cr C_{\bullet+1}(X)@>>>C_{\bullet+2}(X)\oplus C_{\bullet+2}(X)@>>>C_{\bullet+3}(X)\cr @VVV@VVV@VVV\cr C_{\bullet+2}(X,U\cap V)@>>>C_{\bullet+3}(X,U)\oplus C_{\bullet+3}(X,V)@>>>C_{\bullet+4}(X,U\cup V)\cr \end{CD}
nodes.statement_short: Set U,V complements and form the 3x3 total complex.

nodes.name: Columns and rows
nodes.statement: The columns are acyclic (by definition of relative chains), and hence the total complex is acyclic as well. The first row is acyclic by Mayer--Vietoris, and the second row is obviously acyclic. Thus the third row is acyclic, as needed.
nodes.statement_short: Columns acyclic so total complex acyclic; first two rows acyclic, hence the third.

nodes.name: Part (iii)
nodes.statement: Statement (\ref{sccont}) is true because the map is in fact an isomorphism on the chain level. It is clearly surjective; to show injectivity we must show that a singular chain on $X$ which is disjoint from $K$ is in fact disjoint from $K_\alpha$ for some $\alpha\in A$. This follows because the standard $n$-simplex is compact.
nodes.statement_short: Chain-level isomorphism; injectivity by compactness of the simplex.

nodes.name: Define the K-presheaf
nodes.statement: Let $X^+$ be the one-point compactification of $X$. Define a complex of $\mathcal K$-presheaves $\mathcal F^\bullet$ on $X^+$: \begin{equation} \mathcal F^\bullet(K):=[C_{n-1-\bullet}(N,N\setminus K)\to C_{n-\bullet}(M,M\setminus K)] \end{equation} (where on the right hand side by $K$ we really mean $K\cap X$).
nodes.statement_short: Define F on the one-point compactification X^+ via relative chains.

nodes.name: Homotopy K-sheaf
nodes.statement: Applying Lemmas \ref{singularchainshomotopyKsheaf} and \ref{associatedgradedhomotopysheaf}, we see that $\mathcal F^\bullet$ is a homotopy $\mathcal K$-sheaf.
nodes.statement_short: Singular chain axioms and extension lemma make F a homotopy K-sheaf.

nodes.name: Purity claim
nodes.statement: We claim that $\mathcal F^\bullet$ is a pure homotopy $\mathcal K$-sheaf. Certainly the homology of $\mathcal F^\bullet$ is bounded below, because the singular chain complex of a topological manifold has homology bounded above and $\mathcal F^\bullet$ is built out of these. Now, it is easy to calculate: \begin{equation} H^\bullet\mathcal F^\bullet_p=\begin{cases}\mathbb Z&p\in M^\circ\cup N^\circ\cr 0&p\notin M^\circ\cup N^\circ\end{cases} \end{equation} concentrated in degree zero (see \cite[p231 \S3.3]{hatcher} for the special case $N=\partial M=\varnothing$). Hence $\mathcal F^\bullet$ is a pure homotopy $\mathcal K$-sheaf.
nodes.statement_short: F is pure.

nodes.name: Bounded below
nodes.statement: Certainly the homology of $\mathcal F^\bullet$ is bounded below, because the singular chain complex of a topological manifold has homology bounded above and $\mathcal F^\bullet$ is built out of these.
nodes.statement_short: Homology is bounded below.

nodes.name: Stalk homology
nodes.statement: Now, it is easy to calculate: \begin{equation} H^\bullet\mathcal F^\bullet_p=\begin{cases}\mathbb Z&p\in M^\circ\cup N^\circ\cr 0&p\notin M^\circ\cup N^\circ\end{cases} \end{equation} concentrated in degree zero (see \cite[p231 \S3.3]{hatcher} for the special case $N=\partial M=\varnothing$).
nodes.statement_short: Stalks are Z on the interior and 0 elsewhere, in degree 0.

nodes.name: Purity
nodes.statement: Hence $\mathcal F^\bullet$ is a pure homotopy $\mathcal K$-sheaf.
nodes.statement_short: Hence F is pure.

nodes.name: Identify H^0
nodes.statement: In fact, it is not hard to see (using the adjunction $j_!\dashv j^\ast$) that \eqref{stalkhomologyofPDpure} lifts to an isomorphism of sheaves $f_!i^\ast j_!j^\ast\mathfrak o_M\to H^0\mathcal F^\bullet$ where $f:X\hookrightarrow X^+$.
nodes.statement_short: H^0 F is the pushed-forward orientation sheaf.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Now we conclude: \begin{equation*} H^\bullet\mathcal F^\bullet(X^+)\overset{\text{Prop \ref{cechcohomologypurehomotopysheaf}}}=\check H^\bullet(X^+;f_!i^\ast j_!j^\ast\mathfrak o_M)\overset{\text{Lem \ref{cptcechembeddingproperty}}}=\check H^\bullet_c(X;i^\ast j_!j^\ast\mathfrak o_M) \end{equation*} Now observe that $H^\bullet\mathcal F^\bullet(X^+)$ is the left hand side of \eqref{poincaredualitygoal}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply pure-sheaf Čech computation and compact-support comparison.

nodes.name: Filtration and reduction
nodes.statement: We filter $\operatornamewithlimits{hocolim}_{\mathfrak s\preceq\mathfrak t\in\mathcal S}A^\bullet_{\mathfrak s,\mathfrak t}$ by the number of $\mathfrak s_0,\ldots,\mathfrak s_p$ which are not equal to $\mathfrak s^\mathrm{top}$. The zeroth associated graded piece is the subcomplex $A^\bullet_{\mathfrak s^\mathrm{top},\mathfrak s^\mathrm{top}}$, so it suffices to show that all the other associated graded pieces are acyclic.
nodes.statement_short: Filter by entries not equal to the top; reduce to acyclicity of higher graded pieces.

nodes.name: Graded pieces acyclic
nodes.statement: Each of these is a direct sum of mapping cones $[A^{\bullet+1}_{\mathfrak s,\mathfrak s^\mathrm{top}}\to A^\bullet_{\mathfrak s,\mathfrak t}]$, which are acyclic by assumption.
nodes.statement_short: Graded pieces are sums of acyclic mapping cones.

nodes.name: Homotopy K-sheaf, bounded below
nodes.statement: Certainly $\mathcal F^\bullet$ is a homotopy $\mathcal K$-sheaf by Lemma \ref{pihomotopysheaf}. Since $A$ is finite, it is easy to see that $H^i\mathcal F^\bullet_{IJ}$ being bounded below implies that $H^i\mathcal F^\bullet$ is bounded below.
nodes.statement_short: F is a homotopy K-sheaf with bounded below homology.
nodes.section: A.8 Homotopy colimits of pure homotopy \texorpdfstring{$\mathcal K$}{K}-sheaves

nodes.name: Spectral sequence for stalks
nodes.statement: Now let us calculate $\mathcal F^\bullet_p$ using the spectral sequence associated to the $p$-filtration. The $E_1$ term is concentrated along the $q=0$ row since $(H^q\mathcal F^\bullet_{IJ})_p$ is concentrated in degree zero; thus there are no further differentials after the $E_1$ page. On the $E_1$ page the differentials coincide precisely with the differentials in the definition of $\operatornamewithlimits{hocolim}_{I\subseteq J\subseteq A}(\mathcal G_{IJ})_p$ (regarding $\mathcal G_{IJ}$ as complexes concentrated in degree zero). Hence we have an isomorphism: \begin{equation} H^\bullet\mathcal F^\bullet_p=H^\bullet\operatornamewithlimits{hocolim}_{I\subseteq J\subseteq A}(\mathcal G_{IJ})_p \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The p-filtration spectral sequence degenerates, identifying stalk homology with the stalk hocolim of G_IJ.
nodes.section: A.8 Homotopy colimits of pure homotopy \texorpdfstring{$\mathcal K$}{K}-sheaves

nodes.name: Stalks of G_IJ and the poset (2^A)_p
nodes.statement: To calculate the right hand side of \eqref{FGiso}, let us start with the trivial observation that: \begin{equation} (\mathcal G_{IJ})_p=\begin{cases}\mathcal G_p&p\in U_I\cap U_J\cr 0&p\notin U_I\cap U_J\end{cases} \end{equation} Now consider $(2^A)_p:=\{I\subseteq A:p\in U_I\}$, which satisfies the following properties: \begin{rlist} \item$(2^A)_p$ has a maximal element (restatement of (\ref{nonnestedintersectionbig})). \item$I,K\in(2^A)_p$ implies $J\in(2^A)_p$ for $I\subseteq J\subseteq K$ (restatement of (\ref{nestedintersectionOK})). \end{rlist}
nodes.statement_short: Compute stalks of G_IJ and introduce the subposet (2^A)_p with its two properties.
nodes.section: A.8 Homotopy colimits of pure homotopy \texorpdfstring{$\mathcal K$}{K}-sheaves

nodes.name: Contractible nerve
nodes.statement: These two properties imply that $\operatornamewithlimits{hocolim}_{I\subseteq J\subseteq A}(\mathcal G_{IJ})_p$ is simply $\mathcal G_p$ tensored with the simplicial chain complex of the nerve of $(2^A)_p$ (which is contractible). Hence \eqref{FGiso} gives a canonical isomorphism of stalks $H^0\mathcal F^\bullet_p=\mathcal G_p$ (and thus in particular $\mathcal F^\bullet$ is pure).
nodes.statement_short: Stalk hocolim is G_p tensor chains on a contractible nerve, so F is pure with H^0 stalks G_p.
nodes.section: A.8 Homotopy colimits of pure homotopy \texorpdfstring{$\mathcal K$}{K}-sheaves

nodes.name: Global isomorphism
nodes.statement: Now it remains to construct a canonical isomorphism of sheaves $\mathcal G\xrightarrow\sim H^0\mathcal F^\bullet$. Over the open set $U_I$, we define this isomorphism to be the composition $\mathcal G_{II}\xrightarrow\sim H^0\mathcal F_{II}^\bullet\to H^0\mathcal F^\bullet$ (the second map being the inclusion of a $p=0$ subcomplex in the homotopy colimit). At any point $p\in U_I$, this specializes to the isomorphism of stalks $\mathcal G_p=H^0\mathcal F^\bullet_p$ defined earlier. Hence since $\{U_I\}_{I\subseteq A}$ is an open cover of $X$, these isomorphisms patch together to give the desired global isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Define the map on each U_I and patch.
nodes.section: A.8 Homotopy colimits of pure homotopy \texorpdfstring{$\mathcal K$}{K}-sheaves

nodes.name: Construct the map
nodes.statement: There is a natural correspondence $C\subseteq X\times N(X;\{\overline E_i\})$, whose fiber over $x\in X$ is the complete simplex on $\{i:x\in\overline{E_i}\}$. Now it is not hard to check that the inverse limit of these correspondences maps bijectively (and thus homeomorphically) to $\varprojlim_{X=\bigsqcup_{i=1}^nE_i}N(X;\{\overline{E_i}\})$, thus giving rise to the desired map \eqref{chogoshvilinervecomparison}.
nodes.statement_short: The inverse limit of correspondences gives the map.

nodes.name: Fibers are acyclic
nodes.statement: Now the inverse image of $p\in X$ under \eqref{chogoshvilinervecomparison} is an inverse limit of complete simplices with surjective transition maps (``the complete simplex on a profinite set''), and this has the \v Cech cohomology of a point. Indeed, for any inverse system of compact spaces $\{X_\alpha\}$, the natural map $\varinjlim_\alpha\check H^\bullet(X_\alpha)\to\check H^\bullet(\varprojlim_\alpha X_\alpha)$ is an isomorphism (since open covers of $\varprojlim_\alpha X_\alpha$ pulled back from some $X_\alpha$ are cofinal among all open covers).
nodes.statement_short: Each fiber is a profinite complete simplex with Čech cohomology of a point.

nodes.name: Leray
nodes.statement: Thus it follows from the Leray spectral sequence that \eqref{chogoshvilinervecomparison} induces an isomorphism on \v Cech cohomology.
nodes.statement_short: Leray spectral sequence gives the isomorphism.

nodes.name: Chain of quasi-isomorphisms
nodes.statement: Let us relate $\check C^\bullet(X;\mathcal F)$ as defined using rigid open covers to a version using partitions. Specifically, we consider the following quasi-isomorphisms: \begin{align} \check C^\bullet(X;\mathcal F)=\varinjlim_{\begin{smallmatrix}\{U_x\subseteq X\}_{x\in X}\cr\text{rigid open cover}\end{smallmatrix}}&\bigoplus_{p\geq 0}\prod_{\begin{smallmatrix}S\subseteq X\cr\left|S\right|=p+1\end{smallmatrix}}\mathcal F\Bigl(\bigcap_{x\in S}U_x\Bigr)[-p]\\ &\quad\uparrow\cr \varinjlim_{\begin{smallmatrix}X=\bigsqcup_{i=1}^nE_i\cr\overline{E_i}\subseteq U_i\end{smallmatrix}}&\bigoplus_{p\geq 0}\prod_{\begin{smallmatrix}S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\cr\left|S\right|=p+1\end{smallmatrix}}\mathcal F\Bigl(\bigcap_{i\in S}U_i\Bigr)[-p]\\ &\quad\downarrow\cr \varinjlim_{X=\bigsqcup_{i=1}^nE_i}&\bigoplus_{p\geq 0}\prod_{\begin{smallmatrix}S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\cr\left|S\right|=p+1\end{smallmatrix}}\mathcal F\Bigl(\bigcap_{i\in S}\overline{E_i}\Bigr)[-p]\\ &\quad\uparrow\cr \bigoplus_{q\geq 0}\bigoplus_{\{E_i^{(0)}\}_{i=1}^{n_0}<\cdots<\{E_i^{(q)}\}_{i=1}^{n_q}}&\bigoplus_{p\geq 0}\prod_{\begin{smallmatrix}S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n_0\}\cr\left|S\right|=p+1\end{smallmatrix}}\mathcal F\Bigl(\bigcap_{i\in S}\overline{E_i^{(0)}}\Bigr)[q-p]\\ &\quad\uparrow\downarrow\cr \bigoplus_{q\geq 0}\bigoplus_{\{E_i^{(0)}\}_{i=1}^{n_0}\leq\cdots\leq\{E_i^{(q)}\}_{i=1}^{n_q}}&\bigoplus_{p\geq 0}\prod_{\begin{smallmatrix}S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n_0\}\cr\left|S\right|=p+1\end{smallmatrix}}\mathcal F\Bigl(\bigcap_{i\in S}\overline{E_i^{(0)}}\Bigr)[q-p] \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Relate rigid-cover Čech cochains to partition-based complexes via a zigzag.

nodes.name: Each map is a quasi-isomorphism
nodes.statement: The first map is induced by associating to a partition $\{E_i\}$ and $\overline{E_i}\subseteq U_i$ the rigid open cover assigning $U_i$ to $x\in E_i$, and pulling back along the induced map on nerves; it can be seen to be a quasi-isomorphism by a filtration argument (basically the Leray spectral sequence). The second map is a quasi-isomorphism by Lemma \ref{intersectioncofinal} and the definition of $\alpha^\ast$. The third map is defined as the tautological map on $q=0$ direct summands and zero for $q>0$; it can be seen to be a quasi-isomorphism by expressing the domain (resp.\ codomain) as the direct limit over partitions $\{E_i\}$ of the corresponding complex (resp.\ direct limit) restricted to partitions refined by $\{E_i\}$ and observing that for any fixed $\{E_i\}$ the map is a quasi-isomorphism by Lemma \ref{comboretraction}. Finally, the last pair of maps consists of the natural inclusion ($\downarrow$) and the retraction annihilating any component with $\{E_i^{(j)}\}_{i=1}^{n_j}=\{E_i^{(j+1)}\}_{i=1}^{n_{j+1}}$ for some $j$ ($\uparrow$); one can see that both are quasi-isomorphisms by filtering by $\{E_i\}$ (as before) and then by the number of distinct $\{E_i^{(j)}\}_{i=1}^{n_j}$.
nodes.statement_short: Justify each map of the zigzag.

nodes.name: First map
nodes.statement: The first map is induced by associating to a partition $\{E_i\}$ and $\overline{E_i}\subseteq U_i$ the rigid open cover assigning $U_i$ to $x\in E_i$, and pulling back along the induced map on nerves; it can be seen to be a quasi-isomorphism by a filtration argument (basically the Leray spectral sequence).
nodes.statement_short: Filtration argument.

nodes.name: Second map
nodes.statement: The second map is a quasi-isomorphism by Lemma \ref{intersectioncofinal} and the definition of $\alpha^\ast$.
nodes.statement_short: Cofinal intersections and alpha^*.

nodes.name: Third map
nodes.statement: The third map is defined as the tautological map on $q=0$ direct summands and zero for $q>0$; it can be seen to be a quasi-isomorphism by expressing the domain (resp.\ codomain) as the direct limit over partitions $\{E_i\}$ of the corresponding complex (resp.\ direct limit) restricted to partitions refined by $\{E_i\}$ and observing that for any fixed $\{E_i\}$ the map is a quasi-isomorphism by Lemma \ref{comboretraction}.
nodes.statement_short: Terminal object lemma for hocolim.

nodes.name: Last pair
nodes.statement: Finally, the last pair of maps consists of the natural inclusion ($\downarrow$) and the retraction annihilating any component with $\{E_i^{(j)}\}_{i=1}^{n_j}=\{E_i^{(j+1)}\}_{i=1}^{n_{j+1}}$ for some $j$ ($\uparrow$); one can see that both are quasi-isomorphisms by filtering by $\{E_i\}$ (as before) and then by the number of distinct $\{E_i^{(j)}\}_{i=1}^{n_j}$.
nodes.statement_short: Filtration arguments.

nodes.name: Locally constant subpresheaf
nodes.statement: For any partition $\{E_i\}$ of $X$ and collection of trivializations of $\mathcal F|_{\overline E_i}$, there is a sub-$\mathcal K$-presheaf $\mathcal F^\mathrm{pre}\subseteq\mathcal F$ whose sections over $K$ are those sections of $\mathcal F$ whose restrictions to $K\cap\overline{E_i}$ are constant with respect to the specified trivializations. The complex \eqref{cechbychogoshvili} calculates \v Cech cohomology \eqref{cechcomplexII} by a cofinality argument, and the inclusion $\mathcal F^\mathrm{pre}\to\mathcal F$ induces an isomorphism on stalks and thus on \v Cech cohomology by Lemma \ref{cechdeterminedbystalks}. The third map above remains a quasi-isomorphism for $\mathcal F^\mathrm{pre}$ (for the same reason), and furthermore we may restrict \eqref{almosthomotopycolimitofchogoshvilicoverstodualize} to partitions refining the fixed $\{E_i\}$ by Lemma \ref{cofinalityforRlim}.
nodes.statement_short: Replace F by the subpresheaf of locally constant sections; stalk iso and cofinality preserve quasi-isomorphisms.

nodes.name: Reduce to RHom
nodes.statement: The conclusion of the above discussion is that we have thus constructed a canonical (and functorial) quasi-isomorphism between $\check C^\bullet(X;\mathcal F)$ and: \begin{equation} \bigoplus_{q\geq 0}\bigoplus_{\{E_i\}\leq\{E_i^{(0)}\}_{i=1}^{n_0}\leq\cdots\leq\{E_i^{(q)}\}_{i=1}^{n_q}}\bigoplus_{p\geq 0}\prod_{\begin{smallmatrix}S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n_0\}\cr\left|S\right|=p+1\end{smallmatrix}}\mathcal F^\mathrm{pre}\Bigl(\bigcap_{i\in S}\overline{E_i^{(0)}}\Bigr)[q-p] \end{equation} (for any fixed partition $\{E_i\}$ and trivializations of $\mathcal F|_{\overline{E_i}}$ giving rise to $\mathcal F^\mathrm{pre}\subseteq\mathcal F$). Note that $\overline C_\bullet(X,\operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal F,M))$ is precisely $\operatorname{Hom}(\eqref{homotopycolimitofchogoshvilicoverstodualize},M)$. Thus it suffices to show that this particular $\operatorname{Hom}$ is in fact the $R\operatorname{Hom}$.
nodes.statement_short: Hom of the resulting complex is Steenrod chains; reduce to showing Hom computes RHom.

nodes.name: Reduce to K-projectivity
nodes.statement: Recall that $R\operatorname{Hom}$ in $D(R)$ may be computed using a K-projective resolution of the first argument (see Spaltenstein \cite{spaltenstein}), where a complex $P^\bullet$ is called K-projective iff $\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(P^\bullet,M^\bullet)$ is acyclic for every acyclic complex $M^\bullet$ (note that a bounded above complex of projective modules is K-projective). Thus it suffices to show that \eqref{homotopycolimitofchogoshvilicoverstodualize} is K-projective.
nodes.statement_short: RHom is computed by K-projective resolutions (Spaltenstein); reduce to K-projectivity.

nodes.name: Transfinite filtration
nodes.statement: We consider subsets $\wp$ of the poset of partitions of $X$ with the property that any partition refined by a partition in $\wp$ also lies in $\wp$. Since the poset of partitions is cofinite, we may use Zorn's lemma to choose a directed system $\{\wp_i\}_{i\in I}$ of such collections, indexed by a well-ordered set $I$, with the following properties: \begin{rlist} \item$\wp_0=\varnothing$, where $0\in I$ is the least element. \item$\left|\wp_i\setminus\wp_{i-1}\right|=1$ if $i\in I$ has a predecessor $i-1$. \item$\wp_i=\bigcup_{i'<i}\wp_{i'}$ if $i\in I$ has no predecessor. \end{rlist} Now for $i\in I$, let $\eqref{homotopycolimitofchogoshvilicoverstodualize}_i\subseteq\eqref{homotopycolimitofchogoshvilicoverstodualize}$ denote the subcomplex generated by restricting to partitions in $\wp_i$. It follows that: \begin{rlist} \item$\eqref{homotopycolimitofchogoshvilicoverstodualize}_0=0$, where $0\in I$ is the least element. \item$\eqref{homotopycolimitofchogoshvilicoverstodualize}_{i-1}\to\eqref{homotopycolimitofchogoshvilicoverstodualize}_i$ is injective and component-wise split with K-projective cokernel if $i\in I$ has a predecessor $i-1$ (this holds since the cokernel is a bounded above complex of free modules). \item$\varinjlim_{i'<i}\eqref{homotopycolimitofchogoshvilicoverstodualize}_{i'}\to\eqref{homotopycolimitofchogoshvilicoverstodualize}_i$ is an isomorphism if $i\in I$ has no predecessor. \end{rlist} It follows that $\eqref{homotopycolimitofchogoshvilicoverstodualize}=\varinjlim_i\eqref{homotopycolimitofchogoshvilicoverstodualize}_i$ is K-projective by Spaltenstein \cite[p131, 2.8 Corollary]{spaltenstein}.
nodes.statement_short: Show K-projectivity via a well-ordered filtration.

nodes.name: Choose filtration by Zorn
nodes.statement: We consider subsets $\wp$ of the poset of partitions of $X$ with the property that any partition refined by a partition in $\wp$ also lies in $\wp$. Since the poset of partitions is cofinite, we may use Zorn's lemma to choose a directed system $\{\wp_i\}_{i\in I}$ of such collections, indexed by a well-ordered set $I$, with the following properties: \begin{rlist} \item$\wp_0=\varnothing$, where $0\in I$ is the least element. \item$\left|\wp_i\setminus\wp_{i-1}\right|=1$ if $i\in I$ has a predecessor $i-1$. \item$\wp_i=\bigcup_{i'<i}\wp_{i'}$ if $i\in I$ has no predecessor. \end{rlist}
nodes.statement_short: Choose a well-ordered exhaustion of downward closed sets of partitions.

nodes.name: Subcomplex properties
nodes.statement: Now for $i\in I$, let $\eqref{homotopycolimitofchogoshvilicoverstodualize}_i\subseteq\eqref{homotopycolimitofchogoshvilicoverstodualize}$ denote the subcomplex generated by restricting to partitions in $\wp_i$. It follows that: \begin{rlist} \item$\eqref{homotopycolimitofchogoshvilicoverstodualize}_0=0$, where $0\in I$ is the least element. \item$\eqref{homotopycolimitofchogoshvilicoverstodualize}_{i-1}\to\eqref{homotopycolimitofchogoshvilicoverstodualize}_i$ is injective and component-wise split with K-projective cokernel if $i\in I$ has a predecessor $i-1$ (this holds since the cokernel is a bounded above complex of free modules). \item$\varinjlim_{i'<i}\eqref{homotopycolimitofchogoshvilicoverstodualize}_{i'}\to\eqref{homotopycolimitofchogoshvilicoverstodualize}_i$ is an isomorphism if $i\in I$ has no predecessor. \end{rlist}
nodes.statement_short: Successive subcomplexes have split K-projective cokernels.

nodes.name: Spaltenstein
nodes.statement: It follows that $\eqref{homotopycolimitofchogoshvilicoverstodualize}=\varinjlim_i\eqref{homotopycolimitofchogoshvilicoverstodualize}_i$ is K-projective by Spaltenstein \cite[p131, 2.8 Corollary]{spaltenstein}.
nodes.statement_short: Hence K-projective by Spaltenstein.

nodes.name: Naturality
nodes.statement: Since the construction of the isomorphism \eqref{strongcechdualiso} was given by a functorial chain-level construction, it can be checked that it is natural, applies in the relative case, and is compatibile with exact triangles.
nodes.statement_short: Functorial chain-level construction gives naturality and relative compatibility.

nodes.name: Local reduction
nodes.statement: Let us now explain how Theorem \ref{mainresult} implies Proposition \ref{GWgluingneeded}. Proposition \ref{GWgluingneeded} is a local statement, so let us prove it in a neighborhood of a specific point $(C,u,\{\phi_\alpha\}_{\alpha\in I},\{e_\alpha\}_{\alpha\in I})\in\overline{\mathcal M}^\beta_{g,n}(X)_I^\mathrm{reg}$. We will construct data $(X,J,D,D_1,\ldots,D_r,\overline{\mathcal M},E,\lambda,E')$ as in the above setup and a point $(s,u,\{x_i\},e)\in\overline{\mathcal M}(X)$. It will be clear from the construction that there is a natural homeomorphism between a small neighborhood of this point in $\overline{\mathcal M}(X)$ and a small neighborhood of the given point in $\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}^\beta(X)_I$, and using this we will infer Proposition \ref{GWgluingneeded} from Theorem \ref{mainresult}.
nodes.statement_short: The statement is local; construct setup data and a matching point of M(X).

nodes.name: Injectivity claim on unstable components
nodes.statement: We claim that every unstable irreducible component of $C$ has a point where $du$ is injective. If $I=\varnothing$, this follows from the domain stabilization step Lemma \ref{everythingcanbethickened}, and if $I\ne\varnothing$, then picking any $\alpha\in I$, this follows from the fact that $u\pitchfork D_\alpha$ and adding the intersections as marked points makes $C$ stable.
nodes.statement_short: Each unstable component has a point where du is injective (domain stabilization).

nodes.name: Choose D, marked points, D_i
nodes.statement: It follows from the claim that we may pick $D\subseteq X$ with $u\pitchfork D$ such that adding these intersections as extra marked points makes $C$ stable, and none of these points are nodes or marked points. We take $\ell$ to be the \emph{minimum} number of points in $u^{-1}(D)$ necessary to stabilize $C$, and we fix an ordered $\ell$-tuple of such points, adding them as new marked points $p_{n+1},\ldots,p_{n+\ell}\in C$, so now $C$ is a curve of type $(g,n+\ell)$. Now we let $r=\sum_{\alpha\in I}r_\alpha$, we let $D_1,\ldots,D_r\subseteq X$ consist of $r_\alpha$ copies of $D_\alpha$ (union over $\alpha\in I$), and we let the $x_i$'s be the intersection points $u^{-1}(D_\alpha)$ (union over $\alpha\in I$). For the purposes of the present argument, let us reindex $\{x_i\}_{1\leq i\leq r}$ as $\{x^\alpha_i\}_{\alpha\in I,1\leq i\leq r_\alpha}$. Now since $C$ is a curve of type $(g,n+\ell)$, it corresponds to a point in $\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n+\ell}$. Choose an \'etale map $\overline{\mathcal M}\to\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n+\ell}$ covering this point, and choose a point $s\in\overline{\mathcal M}$ and an isomorphism $\iota:C\to C_s$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick stabilizing divisor D, minimal l, divisors D_i and the etale chart.

nodes.name: Define E and lambda
nodes.statement: Now for every $\alpha\in I$, there is a unique map: \begin{equation} \tilde\phi_\alpha:\overbrace{\overline{\mathcal C}^\circ\underset\overline{\mathcal M}\times\cdots\underset\overline{\mathcal M}\times\overline{\mathcal C}^\circ}^{r_\alpha\text{ times}}{}\underset\overline{\mathcal M}\times\overline{\mathcal C}^\circ\to\overline{\mathcal C}_\alpha \end{equation} defined in a neighborhood of $\{x_1^\alpha\}\times\cdots\times\{x_{r_\alpha}^\alpha\}\times C_s$ so that $\tilde\phi_\alpha(x^\alpha_1,\ldots,x^\alpha_{r_\alpha},\iota(\cdot))=\phi_\alpha(\cdot)$ and $\tilde\phi_\alpha(y_1,\ldots,y_{r_\alpha},\cdot)$ classifies the curve in the last factor after forgetting the last $\ell$ marked points and adding $y_1,\ldots,y_{r_\alpha}$ as marked points (this follows from the fact that $\overline{\mathcal C}_\alpha\to\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n+r_\alpha}/S_{r_\alpha}$ is \'etale). We let $E:=E_I=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}E_\alpha$, and we define: \begin{equation*} \lambda\biggl(\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}e_\alpha\biggr)(\{y_i^\alpha\}_{\alpha\in I,1\leq i\leq r_\alpha},\cdot,\cdot)=\sum_{\alpha\in I}\lambda_\alpha(e_\alpha)(\tilde\phi_\alpha(y_1^\alpha,\ldots,y_{r_\alpha}^\alpha,\cdot),\cdot) \end{equation*} in a neighborhood of $\{x_i^\alpha\}_{\alpha\in I,1\leq i\leq r_\alpha}\times C_s\times X$ (and then we simply cut it off to be zero elsewhere).
nodes.statement_short: Extend phi_alpha and define lambda as the sum of the lambda_alpha.

nodes.name: Identify neighborhoods
nodes.statement: Finally, we observe that with this definition, a neighborhood of $(s,u\circ\iota^{-1},\{x^\alpha_i\}_{\alpha\in I,1\leq i\leq r_\alpha},\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}e_\alpha)\in\overline{\mathcal M}(X)$ coincides with a neighborhood of $(C,u,\{\phi_\alpha\}_{\alpha\in I},\{e_\alpha\}_{\alpha\in I})\in\overline{\mathcal M}^\beta_{g,n}(X)_I$ (note that the point $(C,u,\{\phi_\alpha\}_{\alpha\in I},\{e_\alpha\}_{\alpha\in I})\in\overline{\mathcal M}^\beta_{g,n}(X)_I^\mathrm{reg}$ has trivial automorphism group by definition of $\overline{\mathcal M}^\beta_{g,n}(X)_I^\mathrm{reg}$).
nodes.statement_short: Neighborhoods in M(X) and in the GW thickened moduli space coincide.

nodes.name: Deduce the proposition
nodes.statement: For $E'=E$, under this identification of a small open set in $\overline{\mathcal M}^\beta_{g,n}(X)_I$ and a small open set in $\overline{\mathcal M}(X)$, we have $\overline{\mathcal M}(X)^\mathrm{reg}\subseteq\overline{\mathcal M}^\beta_{g,n}(X)_I^\mathrm{reg}$ (for this it is important that we chose $\ell$ as the \emph{minimum} number of points necessary to stabilize $C$). It follows that Theorem \ref{mainresult}(\ref{openness},\ref{orientation}) implies Proposition \ref{GWgluingneeded}(\ref{GWgluingopen},\ref{GWgluingor}) (note that over this small open set, we have an identification $\mathfrak o_{u(p_{n+i})^\ast N_{D/X}}=\mathfrak o_{T_{p_{n+i}}C_s}$ and that the latter is canonically trivial using the complex structure on $C_s$). Taking the above construction with $J$ in place of $I$ and setting $E':=E_I\subseteq E_J=E$, we get Proposition \ref{GWgluingneeded}(\ref{GWgluingsubmersion}) from Theorem \ref{mainresult}(\ref{manifold},\ref{submersion}) as well.
nodes.statement_short: Regular loci match; parts of Theorem B.1.1 give the parts of Proposition 9.2.9.

nodes.name: First term
nodes.statement: The first term $\bigl(\nabla\xi+T_\nabla(\xi,du_\alpha)\bigr)^{0,1}_y$ comes from differentiating: \begin{equation} \mathsf{PT}_{\exp_{u_\alpha}\xi\to u_\alpha}\left[\bar\partial_y\exp_{u_\alpha}\xi\right] \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Differentiate the transported del-bar term.
nodes.section: B.5 Based \texorpdfstring{$\bar\partial$-section}{del bar section} \texorpdfstring{$\mathcal F_{\alpha,y}$}{F\_alpha,y} and linearized operator \texorpdfstring{$D_{\alpha,y}$}{D\_alpha,y}

nodes.name: Middle terms
nodes.statement: The second two terms come from differentiating: \begin{equation} \mathsf{PT}_{\exp_{u_\alpha}\xi\to u_\alpha}\left[\lambda(e_0)(\alpha,y,x_1,\ldots,x_r,\cdot,(\exp_{u_\alpha}\xi)(\cdot))\right] \end{equation} where we use the fact that $\frac d{dt}x_i(\exp_{u_\alpha}(t\xi))=-\operatorname{proj}_{TC_\alpha}\xi(x_i)$.
nodes.statement_short: Differentiate the lambda(e_0) term, using the derivative of x_i.
nodes.section: B.5 Based \texorpdfstring{$\bar\partial$-section}{del bar section} \texorpdfstring{$\mathcal F_{\alpha,y}$}{F\_alpha,y} and linearized operator \texorpdfstring{$D_{\alpha,y}$}{D\_alpha,y}

nodes.name: Last term
nodes.statement: The last term comes from differentiating: \begin{equation} \mathsf{PT}_{\exp_{u_\alpha}\xi\to u_\alpha}\left[\lambda(\operatorname{proj}_E\xi)(\alpha,y,x_1,\ldots,x_r,\cdot,(\exp_{u_\alpha}\xi)(\cdot))\right] \end{equation} We leave the calculations to the reader.
nodes.statement_short: Differentiate the lambda(proj_E xi) term.
nodes.section: B.5 Based \texorpdfstring{$\bar\partial$-section}{del bar section} \texorpdfstring{$\mathcal F_{\alpha,y}$}{F\_alpha,y} and linearized operator \texorpdfstring{$D_{\alpha,y}$}{D\_alpha,y}

nodes.name: Reduce to nabla^{0,1}
nodes.statement:
The operator $D_{\alpha,y}$ equals $(
abla\xi)^{0,1}_y$ plus compact terms (by Lemma ef{linearizedformula}), so it is equivalent to show that $\xi\mapsto(
abla\xi)^{0,1}_y$ is Fredholm (and we may forget about $E$). Here $
abla$ is really the pullback of $
abla$ via $u_\alpha$. Thus it suffices to show that if $V$ is a smooth complex vector bundle over a nodal Riemann surface $C$ equipped with a smooth connection $
abla$, then the horizontal maps:  egin{equation}  egin{tikzcd}[column sep = large] W^{k,2,\delta}(C,V)\ar{r}{\xi\mapsto(
abla\xi)^{0,1}}&W^{k-1,2,\delta}(	ilde C,\Omega^{0,1}_{	ilde C}\otimes_\mathbb C V)\ W^{k,2}(C,V)\ar[hook]{u}\ar{r}{\xi\mapsto(
abla\xi)^{0,1}}&W^{k-1,2}(	ilde C,\Omega^{0,1}_{	ilde C}\otimes_\mathbb C V)\ar[hook]{u} \end{tikzcd} \end{equation} are Fredholm.
nodes.statement_short: Up to compact terms, it suffices to treat (nabla xi)^{0,1} for a bundle over a nodal curve.
nodes.section: B.5 Based \texorpdfstring{$\bar\partial$-section}{del bar section} \texorpdfstring{$\mathcal F_{\alpha,y}$}{F\_alpha,y} and linearized operator \texorpdfstring{$D_{\alpha,y}$}{D\_alpha,y}

nodes.name: Bottom map Fredholm
nodes.statement: For the bottom map, the Fredholm property is standard. Indeed, $W^{k,2}(C,V)$ lies inside $W^{k,2}(\tilde C,V)$ as a closed subspace of finite codimension, and $\nabla^{0,1}:W^{k,2}(\tilde C,V)\to W^{k-1,2}(\tilde C,\Omega^{0,1}_{\tilde C}\otimes_\mathbb C V)$ is Fredholm by elliptic regularity on the compact Riemann surface $\tilde C$.
nodes.statement_short: Elliptic regularity on the normalization.
nodes.section: B.5 Based \texorpdfstring{$\bar\partial$-section}{del bar section} \texorpdfstring{$\mathcal F_{\alpha,y}$}{F\_alpha,y} and linearized operator \texorpdfstring{$D_{\alpha,y}$}{D\_alpha,y}

nodes.name: Top map Fredholm
nodes.statement: For the top map, the Fredholm property follows from results of Lockhart--McOwen \cite{lockhartmcowen} concerning the Fredholmness (in weighted Sobolev spaces) of elliptic operators on manifolds with cylindrical ends. Specifically, $W^{k,2,\delta}(C,V)$ lies inside $W^{k,2,\delta}(\tilde C,V)$ as a closed subspace of finite codimension, and the map $\nabla^{0,1}:W^{k,2,\delta}(\tilde C,V)\to W^{k-1,2,\delta}(\tilde C,\Omega^{0,1}_{\tilde C}\otimes_\mathbb C V)$ is Fredholm by the theory of Lockhart--McOwen \cite{lockhartmcowen}. This uses the fact that the weight $\delta\in(0,1)$ is not an eigenvalue of the asymptotic linearized operator in any end (the set of eigenvalues in any end is precisely $\mathbb Z$, corresponding to the powers $\{z^n\}_{n\in\mathbb Z}$ on $D^2\setminus 0$). Let us also remark that both of these Fredholmness statements are easier at $p=2$ than for general $p\in(1,\infty)$, since for $p=2$ one can use Fourier analysis (after localizing the problem with a partition of unity).
nodes.statement_short: Lockhart-McOwen theory, since delta is not an eigenvalue of the asymptotic operator.
nodes.section: B.5 Based \texorpdfstring{$\bar\partial$-section}{del bar section} \texorpdfstring{$\mathcal F_{\alpha,y}$}{F\_alpha,y} and linearized operator \texorpdfstring{$D_{\alpha,y}$}{D\_alpha,y}

nodes.name: Easy halves
nodes.statement: Now it remains to show that the induced maps on kernel and cokernel are isomorphisms. The map on kernels is obviously injective, and the map on cokernels is easily seen to be surjective (use the fact that the image of the top horizontal map is closed and the fact that the rightmost vertical inclusion is dense).
nodes.statement_short: Kernel map injective, cokernel map surjective.
nodes.section: B.5 Based \texorpdfstring{$\bar\partial$-section}{del bar section} \texorpdfstring{$\mathcal F_{\alpha,y}$}{F\_alpha,y} and linearized operator \texorpdfstring{$D_{\alpha,y}$}{D\_alpha,y}

nodes.name: Reduce to regularity
nodes.statement: For the surjectivity of the map on kernels and the injectivity of the map on cokernels, it suffices to show that if $D_{\alpha,y}\xi=\eta$ for $\xi\in W^{k,2,\delta}$ and $\eta\in W^{k-1,2}$, then $\xi\in W^{k,2}$. To show $\xi\in W^{k,2}$, it suffices to argue locally on one side of a given node.
nodes.statement_short: Suffices: weighted solutions with unweighted RHS are W^{k,2}.
nodes.section: B.5 Based \texorpdfstring{$\bar\partial$-section}{del bar section} \texorpdfstring{$\mathcal F_{\alpha,y}$}{F\_alpha,y} and linearized operator \texorpdfstring{$D_{\alpha,y}$}{D\_alpha,y}

nodes.name: Error distribution at nodes
nodes.statement: Certainly (the vector field part of) $\xi$ extends continuously to $C_\alpha$ (by definition of $W^{k,2,\delta}$), and this continuous extension satisfies $D_{\alpha,y}\xi=\eta+\epsilon$ where $\epsilon$ is a distribution on $\tilde C_\alpha$ valued in $\Omega^{0,1}_{\tilde C_\alpha,j_y}\otimes_\mathbb C u_\alpha^\ast TX$ and supported inside the (inverse images of the) nodes. By elliptic regularity, it suffices to show that $\epsilon=0$.
nodes.statement_short: The extension satisfies the equation up to a distribution epsilon supported at nodes.
nodes.section: B.5 Based \texorpdfstring{$\bar\partial$-section}{del bar section} \texorpdfstring{$\mathcal F_{\alpha,y}$}{F\_alpha,y} and linearized operator \texorpdfstring{$D_{\alpha,y}$}{D\_alpha,y}

nodes.name: Error vanishes
nodes.statement: Now for smooth test functions $\varphi$ supported inside a small neighborhood of the support of $\epsilon$, we have: \begin{equation} \langle\epsilon,\varphi\rangle=\langle D_{\alpha,y}\xi-\eta,\varphi\rangle=\langle\xi,D_{\alpha,y}^\ast\varphi\rangle-\langle\eta,\varphi\rangle \end{equation} We thus obtain the bound $\left|\langle\epsilon,\varphi\rangle\right|\leq c\left\|\varphi\right\|_{1,1}$ since $D_{\alpha,y}^\ast$ is a first order operator and $\xi,\eta$ are bounded (as they are continuous). On the other hand, $\epsilon$ is supported at a finite set of points, so it is a linear combination of $\delta$-functions and their derivatives. Hence $\epsilon$ does not satisfy the bound $\left|\langle\epsilon,\varphi\rangle\right|\leq c\left\|\varphi\right\|_{1,1}$ (recall that $W^{1,1}\hookrightarrow\hspace{-\arrowwidthawesome}\nrightarrow C^0$ since we are in two dimensions) unless $\epsilon=0$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: epsilon is bounded by the W^{1,1} norm, impossible for a nonzero combination of delta functions.
nodes.section: B.5 Based \texorpdfstring{$\bar\partial$-section}{del bar section} \texorpdfstring{$\mathcal F_{\alpha,y}$}{F\_alpha,y} and linearized operator \texorpdfstring{$D_{\alpha,y}$}{D\_alpha,y}

nodes.name: Away from necks
nodes.statement: Away from the ends/necks of $C_\alpha$, the expression is zero when $y=0$ (since $(0,0,u_0,\{x_i^0\},e_0)\in\overline{\mathcal M}(X)$) and more generally it follows easily that its $j$th derivative is bounded pointwise by $c_j\left|y\right|$. In the ends of $C_\alpha$, the expression is zero.
nodes.statement_short: Error bounded by |y| away from necks, zero in ends.

nodes.name: Localize in the neck
nodes.statement: In a given neck $[0,6S]\times S^1\subseteq C_\alpha$, argue as follows. Recall that $\lambda$ vanishes in the ends/necks, so we just have to bound $\bar\partial_yu_\alpha$. Now $\bar\partial_yu_\alpha$ is only nonzero over $[S-1,S]\cup[5S,5S+1]$; by symmetry we may just work over $[S-1,S]$.
nodes.statement_short: Only the cutoff interval [S-1,S] contributes.

nodes.name: Exponential decay of u_0
